--- Page 8 ---
**Francis Bacon, Book 3, Chapter 4, from *On the Advancement of Learning*.**

One is moved to wonder at Aristotle's confidence, who, stirred by a certain impulse of contradiction, and declaring war on all Antiquity, not only usurped the liberty of coining new terms of art at will, but also strove to extinguish and destroy all ancient wisdom. So much so that he nowhere names ancient authors, nor makes any mention of their doctrines, except to criticize men or refute their opinions.

A little after.

Concerning a man so excellent indeed, and admirable for his sharpness of intellect, Aristotle, I would readily believe that he received this ambition from his disciple, whom perhaps he emulated; so that if the former subdued all Nations, the latter might subdue all Opinions, and establish for himself a kind of Monarchy in Contemplations:
A fortunate plunderer of doctrine, not a useful example given to the world. ——

[Stamp: Bayerische Staatsbibliothek München]

**DEDICATION.**
...it pleased me to acknowledge myself bound. A tri-

it bears only the title of a transla-
tion; but it hopes for some splendor from
its author and your patronage; you who both love studies of every kind,
and are accustomed to kindly embrace the efforts of a developing
talent. Things more worthy and equal to your praiseworthy Name were not
found from the meager account of my progress. And so, while
I strive thus to prove my diligence and faithfulness to the Readers, I also wanted
this to stand as a pledge of our veneration for you. Farewell, Most
Noble Sir, and may you long survive for your family and your praises,
by virtue of your family's hereditary patronage of the Muses.
Middelburg, Zeeland. September 1st, 1648.

THE TRANSLATOR
T O T H E R E A D E R.

[Large decorative initial F]RANCIS BACON of Ve-
rulam's Natural History
has long been a desired work in Latin. Printers have more than once earnestly sought its translation, even at a price. Hitherto, the variety of the subject matter, entangled with many difficulties, has deterred everyone; a variety which would also exhaust Englishmen and scholars. No confidence in my studies, whose harvest is barely in the blade, nor a deeper knowledge of the English language, has driven me to this, but fortune; whether it will turn out well or ill, rests with you, kind Reader;

4 Reader;

--- Page 12 ---
L E C T O R I .
Reader; if you would allow my endeavors, conscious of their own slightness, and never intended for the press, yet brought here by the gentle importunity of friends, from which it is not possible to retreat, to be safe within the hope of pardon; while I am unwilling that the Latin academies of philosophers should longer lack the work of that Illustrious Man, most useful for constructing the rules of Physics, which makes things correspond to Nature. For after I decided to devote the leisure cut off from occupations and relaxations to exercises of the pen, seeking things real, so to speak, and somewhat removed from the insubstantial clamor of words, I fell upon these things, indeed most pleasant, and opportune for fostering my medical studies; but elsewhere not infrequently intricate to one turning them over, indeed even desperate, unless to the Learned—

--- Page 13 ---
L E C T O R I.
...unless the kindness of very learned men (whose names are too worthy to be affixed to this vestibule) had from time to time extended a helping hand. Having struggled through the entire course of difficulties, when the papers, now reduced into a small volume, reached the hands of those whom it would be a matter of conscience for me not to obey, I immediately felt efforts being made, until the fruits of my diligence were no longer permitted to remain private. Thus therefore I finally come forth, with the work of a Latin interpreter for Bacon having been diligently performed; which indeed feared to be called a servile herd, and took care not to translate word for word; but so that a freer style might render clarity to the attentive reader, not obscured; which itself does not run everywhere with the same thread, in some places more concise, in others more expansive; so that
        * 5                for-

--- Page 14 ---
L E C T O R I.
...so that perhaps it might present a varied likeness of our former reading. Nevertheless, I do not dare to promise that I have entirely achieved what I diligently pursued. Indeed, some things will be found which will easily testify how not everywhere I have satisfied myself. Thus you will see certain English words added to the pages, even where Latin is not lacking; sometimes even where I despaired of being able to express it. But here and there, kind Reader, I expect from you a remedy for the unsound passages; if perhaps, through the benevolence of the learned age, the hope of a second and more improved edition shall not have been unreasonable, and if in a difficult work and in rendering into Latin matters of nature so abstruse, some ignorance is beyond blame, nay, even if a slumbering attention also errs, it is within the hope of pardon.

W. RAWLEY

PREFACE
*translated from English.*

[Decorative initial C] SINCE in this collection
my Lord the author did not
deign to dedicate his own
little work, I feel myself
publicly bound, that (with his
consent) I should prepare the way
for the Reader, by indicating those
things which pertain both to the
form of the work and to its
publication. I remember it was
often used by him in conversations,
that if he had consulted only his
own reputation, it would have been
better to condemn the Natural
History to private obscurity, than
to publish it for individual public
use. For it seems only an undigested
mass of particulars, removed from
that splendor which a precisely
observed Method usually confers
on books. But whatever human
consideration prevailed over the
desire for his own honor...

--- Page 17 ---
P R E F A C E.
whether it might serve the advantages and security [of mankind]. Nor was he ignorant that no other way remained by which mortal genius might be asserted into liberty, bound and enchanted by the fallacies of notions and speculations, which utterly lost the good fruit of operations; but that above all, deference must be paid to sense and experiments, at least at the beginning. Moreover, he owed an example of Natural History, as if it were the designated third part of his Instauration. My Lord repeatedly stated that it would happen that many of those things which he would embrace in this writing, men would consider to be vile, unworthy, trifling, and feigning utility. Therefore it is to be wished that it may continually be present in their thoughts what is now to be done, and what difference there is between this Natural History and the lucubrations of others in this kind. For whatever of this subject

--- Page 18 ---
P R E F A C E.
For whatever of this subject is read, it indulges in the pleasantness of descriptions and showy treatments, pretentiously vending rare miracles and affected secrets. But our hero composed a Natural History, from the foundation of which true philosophy may be aroused, which may both illuminate the intellect with a torch, favor the building of axioms, and hold the principal parts in the direction of operations. For thus he believes he has discharged his obligation, by propagating the boundaries of the sciences and faithfully caring for their augmentation. Since he has here gathered material suitable for the structure, and in the Novum Organum (the second part of which shortly awaits the public Reader) has suggested instruments and rules, men will have been unjust to themselves, unless they raise the arts to that pinnacle of perfection to which human ingenuity can attain. And hence sometimes arose my Lord's complaints, when, having discharged the duty of an Architect,

--- Page 19 ---
P R E F A C E.
having discharged [the duty of an Architect], he thought himself soon also to be driven to the lowest labors of a workman, indeed (following the example of the Israelites after their exodus from Egypt) to collect straw through the fields and burn bricks. For he persuaded himself that it was hoped in vain by another, men being hardened in their stubborn contempt for those things which they received as beneficial. As for the fact that the dignity of experiments does not everywhere consist in the opinion of some, elsewhere indeed becoming common, it must be considered that they are honorable enough insofar as they acknowledge God as their author. If they are criticized as if obvious, it must be known that clear experiments, free from all doubts, illuminate the solid structure of axioms. It is also customary for our Hero to render most clearly explained those things which present themselves as admirable, and not to arrange things of this kind so that they appear admirable. Moreover, experiments into mi-
                                    nute details

--- Page 20 ---
P R A E F A T I O.
...even in minute details, he used to say, they must be broken down, lest they remain whole, and as they were in their original state. As for their use; my Lord often repeated the distinction of experiments, by which some are called 'fruit-bearing' and others 'light-bearing'; and he thought that whoever acknowledged no use of light, because it is diffused immaterially, did not have a sound mind. Furthermore, experiments elsewhere have reasons appended, so that the work of interpreting Nature, which is being undertaken, and the axioms to be elicited, might be more readily at hand. He considered the reasons given by himself to be more solid than those usually given by others: not because he boasted of any excellence of intellect above others (as he used to say), but because of his familiarity with Nature and experiments. Furthermore, by scattering causes, he did not want men (who impatiently bear being stopped as if by an obstacle at the ignorance of causes) to wander endlessly in a vast forest, but to linger with them for a little while until

--- Page 21 ---
P R E F A C E.
until more certain and more trustworthy axioms emerge. I also have this from my Lord's private conversations, that he interrupted the series of the methodical work, and did not wish to fulfill the law of strict order (although a certain hidden order will not easily escape the reader's attention), so that anyone might conceive the confidence to attempt something similar and devote effort to collecting experiments. If he had digested his own things more carefully, the useful labor of imitators would have been cut short by the despair of achieving that endeavor. How scrupulously indeed he urges method, the book *On the Advancement of the Sciences* will prove, pursuing that thread of order (if I see correctly) which scarcely anyone else has presented more exact, or I am greatly mistaken. My Lord's saying will close the preface, that the world as it is in itself and as the work of God is presented here, with all rashness and license of imagination proscribed.
                                   READE-

TO THE READER
Greetings.

[Illuminated initial I] I once came across a French book, titled "Histoire Naturelle de Mre. François Bacon, &c." And because in its Preface I remembered there were some things not irrelevant to this place, I wished to offer these things also to the Reader's judgment. Thus, however, stand the French words, soon to be changed into Latin speech:

I will also be very glad that the Reader be warned that in this translation I have not punctually followed the order observed in the English original, for having found too much confusion in the arrangement of the subjects, which seem to have

TO JACOB GRUTER
*Brother*
ISAAC GRUTER
*Greetings.*

[Large decorative initial R] EM, my Brother, you have undertaken a task which, while easily approved by fair assessors of things, will nevertheless be troubled by harsher judgments when you encounter ill-occupied Censors, a large part of our age. From this group, even those who receive you most mildly will cry out that this whole genre of translation is useless, a genre which bestows upon the Latin world writers as far removed by origin from Antiquity as they are in character from the genius that produces enduring books. But there was no reason why a malevolence, searching out every hidden corner, should deter you from your undertakings, you who (if by chance you err) do so following greater precedents, whose authority in literature is bene-

--- Page 26 ---
...whose authority in literature will kindly defend the expenses of your leisure. For, eager to temper the intervals of reading with writing, you drew the lines of your pen, and (as he says) "furrows *in not sterile dust*", in the chosen field of your, that is, your Physical and Medical practice, having established a marriage of pleasantness and severity, by an exchange of matter and words. Thus you were at leisure from reading authors by a slight separation of literary diligence, so that an account of studies in another genre might be established for you; and yet reading complains of nothing having been withdrawn from it, as it finds its own parts even in writing. I am a witness that the hope of glory – perhaps to be contended for here more boastfully by others, or at least to be attempted more ambitiously – was not proposed to you, if in a brother's business a brother, a *suitable witness* (οἰκεῖος μάρτυς) is to be heard. Things offered to the public, which, not having been inspected privately by foolish judges, seemed likely to be not unwelcome to the chairs of philosophers; with you refusing publication, which others would eagerly pursue—

--- Page 27 ---
...were urging. I joined those who, from their hiding-
places, fleeing the cares of the world and burying them-
selves, thought you should be drawn out,
since in a very widespread, as it were, applause,
everything of that Man had always pleased me,
to whom you have now rendered the service of a Latin inter-
preter. Here, the method of refined discussion, in the
select variety of its argument diffused through many things,
pleased me, being far removed from the nar-
rowness of today's Peripatetics, who fabricate no-
tions rarely consistent with Nature. Nor
yet do I think *Verulam* (Bacon) sur-
passed the mists of human intellect, so that, established
in clarity, he always had things he could present
as certain. He led the
way for the aroused industry of others to follow,
which will render tribute to diligence,
if anywhere either explored novelty will en-
large the boundaries of knowledge, or doubts inextri-
cable to predecessors will receive
light from the good fortune of a succeeding age. But
this is the subject matter of your dissertation,
into which I feel I have fallen by a hidden departure,
having touched upon it with sparing words, while con-

--- Page 28 ---
...while other matters, presented by the need to hasten this writing, by chance take precedence over the congratulation I had conceived. To bring this letter to a close – a letter which, if the thoughts previously stirred within me had corresponded to the outcome into which I am rashly carried by the sway of the occasion, would not have been sent from these confines – know that nothing could have happened more pleasing to me than to see the fresh sheets from the press, with the brief announcement of the work's completion added. May God grant that him whom we now diligently praise for his efforts in another's work, fame may soon advance with kindly auspices as he attempts something of his own.
Farewell. August 7, 1648.

FIRST CENTURY.

Various experiments pertaining to the percola-
tion and penetration of one body
through another.

[Decorative initial E] DIG a well, a little above
where the outermost wave of the sea
runs out, with that depth
which corresponds to the lowest ebb
of the sea's decrease; the tide will fill
this with fresh water suitable for drinking.
This is popular in the coasts of Mauretania.

--- Page 42 ---
2          OF FRANCIS BACON
is confirmed by popular experience, where it alone compensates for the lack of fresh water. Julius Caesar understood this well when he was besieged at Alexandria. For by digging wells on the shore, he thwarted the laborious efforts of the enemy, who had diverted seawater into the fountain of Alexandria; and thus preserved his army unharmed, when the hope of safety seemed to have vanished. Caesar, however, ignorant of the cause, believed that there was a spring of fresh water in the sands of the sea, but it is manifest that this should be ascribed to the seawater, which fills the well in proportion to the rise and increase of its tide, and having entered the sands, deposits its saltiness by percolation.

     2. I remember reading of an experiment in filtering salt water through earth, with ten vessels placed one above the other, yet it did not remove the saltiness enough to be fit for drinking. The same Author relates from the account of others, that salt water drawn through twenty vessels proved to be sweet. This experiment seems to contradict the other concerning wells dug on the shore; yet he says that if repeated twenty times, it is not without effect. But it is worthy of note how wretched our imitations are found to be, as we commonly set about experiments, unless they are guided by great judgment and a certain light of axioms. For first,

--- Page 43 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 3
for, there is no small difference between
the passage of water through twenty small vessels, and
the distance such as appears in rising and falling
water. Secondly, there is a great dif-
ference between sand and earth. For
all earth contains a certain kind of nitrous salt,
of which sand is usually devoid.
Furthermore, earth does not filter water as exquisitely
as sand. But a third reason now
remains, which is equally suspect to me as the other
two. This is, however, that in the expe-
riment of the transmission of seawater into
wells, the water ascends, and in the experi-
ment of the transmission of water through vessels, it de-
scends. It is now established that the more
saline parts of water (if once thoroughly imbued
with salt) penetrate to the bottom. And therefore it is not
strange if the derivation of water by descent
does not render it sweet: Furthermore,
I somewhat doubt whether the impact of water driven
from the sea is more suitable for shaking out
the saline parts, than when water flows
by its own motion.
3. Percolation or transmission seems
a certain kind of separation, which not only
separates the coarse from the fine, and the dregs from
other parts, but also much more subtle
natures; and it is varied, according to the bodies
that exist, through which the transmission is carried out;
A 2 as if

4 FRANCIS BACON
as if through a woolen sack liquid deposits fat, if through sand, saltiness. They report concerning the separation of wine from water, transmitted through ivy wood, or a similar porous body, but it is not confirmed.

	4. Gum of trees (which to us mostly appears translucent and clear) is only a thin transmission or percolation of the tree's sap through the wood and bark; and similarly, diamonds endowed with angles, and carbuncles collected from rocks (which also shine more than gum) are subtle exudations of stone.

	5. Aristotle gives a foolish reason why the feathers of birds are of more vivid color than the hairs of animals; for no beast has green hairs representing the color of lapis lazuli and living flesh. The reason is, he says, that birds are more frequently in the sun's rays than beasts. But that is manifestly false: for cattle spend more time in the sun than birds, which mostly live in forests or shade. The truest reason is that the excrementitious humor of animals, which equally constitutes feathers in birds and hairs in beasts, is transmitted in birds by a thinner and more delicate filtration than in beasts; for feathers pass through quills, but hairs through the skin.

SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 5

6. The clarification of liquids by adhes-
ion is like an internal percolation, and it occurs
when some glutinous body, mixed with the liquids,
is agitated together with them. This motion causes
the coarser particles to adhere to the glutinous body;
and in this way, the finer particles are separated
from the coarser ones. Thus apothecaries clarify
syrups with egg white, mixed and
agitated in the juices to be clarified, because the
albumen collects all the dregs and coarser parts,
and after the syrup is placed on the fire, the
egg whites harden and are removed. In this way,
Hippocratic wine is clarified if it is mixed with milk,
thoroughly agitated, and then passed through a
woolen sack, which they call Hippocrates' sleeve.
And that which is glutinous in the milk draws to
itself the aromatic powder and the coarser parts of the liquids.

7. The clarification of water is an experiment
conducive to health; besides the fact that crystal-
line and clear water delights the eyes; it is done,
however, by throwing and placing stones at the source
of a spring, so that the water may be filtered through them.

8. Perhaps percolation also brings about sweetness
and flavor, not only clarity and brilliance.
For that also follows

is likewise achieved with clarity, when coarser parts are separated from others. So also it is found that the sweat of a man of a warmer nature, and who delights in bodily exercise, and keeps his body clean, and has a thin skin, emits a sweet odor; as is related of Alexander, as we commonly see that gums contain sweet odors.

Various experiments pertaining to the [blackletter font: motion] of a body from pressure.

9. Take a glass filled with water, and move a moistened finger around the rim of the glass, pressing it rather firmly. The finger, having been moved around for a short space of time, will cause the water to ripple and to leap up in fine drops. This instance remarkably demonstrates the force of compression in solid bodies. For if ever a solid body (such as wood, stone, metal, etc.) is compressed, an internal commotion of its parts arises so that it may free itself from the compression. And this is the cause of all violent motion. And it is worthy of the greatest admiration that this motion has never been observed, although it is most obvious among all motions, and the principal root of all mechanical operations.

--- Page 47 ---
SYLVA SYLVARUM. Century I. 7
radix. This motion first operates in a circle, as if trying, seeking a way to free itself, and in its progress explores if a more facile liberation is given anywhere. This motion is manifest in liquids. For all liquids form circles, and strike them against themselves; but in solid bodies (which are not broken) it is so subtle that it escapes sight. Nevertheless, it reveals itself by various effects: as in this example which we have in hand. For the pressure, facilitated by the moistening of the finger (since it adheres so much more easily to the rim of the glass), after some time, excites all the particles of the glass to action, so that they strike the water sharply; which striking generates a leaping of the waters.

      10. If you strike or pierce a solid fragile body, such as glass or sugar, it is not only broken in that part where the force was most directly impressed, but it is shattered all around into segments and fragments. The motion from pressure, exploring all paths, shatters where it finds the body most weak.

      11. Gunpowder, expanded into such a flame, which does not suffer compression, moves circularly (for flame consists of the nature of a liquid body), sometimes receding, sometimes shattering the cannon, but generally exploding the ball,
                                 A 4

--- Page 48 ---
FRANCIS BACON'S
ball, which in that place finds the easiest release.

	12. This motion of pressure, and that of tension which corresponds to it, I am accustomed to call (by a common name) the motion of liberty; which is, when some body returns from an unnatural extension and dilation to its natural state, and restores itself. Thus, if a bladder filled with air is compressed, it springs back, and stretched leather and cloth rebound. These two motions (concerning which infinite instances can be given) we shall treat in their proper place.

	13. This motion from pressure is also excellently demonstrated in sounds, as a struck bell emits sounds, which immediately cease when a hand is placed upon it. So also the sound of a harpsichord ceases as soon as it feels the edge of a cloth thrown upon it. For these sounds are produced by a subtle percussion of the smallest parts of the bell or string impressed upon the air; just as water leaps out from the subtle percussion of the smallest parts of the glass into the water, about which we spoke a little earlier in the ninth experiment. Nor indeed should you imagine that a local tremor of the bell or string effects that, as we shall abundantly declare in that treatise concerning Sounds.

Various experiments concerning the separa-
tions of bodies by weight.

14. Take a wide-bellied glass with a long neck. Fill the belly partly with water. Take also another glass, into which you pour red wine mixed with water. Invert the first (glass) with its belly turned upwards, and stop up its neck with your finger. Then insert its opening into the other glass, and remove your finger. Retained in this state for some time, it will separate the wine from the water; the wine will ascend and remain at the top of the upper glass, the water will descend and settle at the bottom of the lower glass. The transition is obvious to the eyes; for you will see the wine emerge upwards in a slender (so to speak) vein. Therefore, for convenience (since the experiment requires little time), it is expedient to suspend the upper glass from a nail. For as soon as so much pure and unmixed water has collected at the bottom of the lower glass that the opening of the upper (glass) is immersed in it, the movement will cease.

15. If there is wine in the upper glass and water in the lower, you will be able to experience no movement at all. If there is pure water in the upper (glass), and colored water in the lower, or vice versa, no movement will occur. But it is established by experience.

--- Page 50 ---
10        OF FRANCIS BACON
[It is established by experience], even if the mixture of wine and water in the lower [vessel] consists of three parts water and one part wine, no impediment to motion arises. This separation of wine and water is known to exist by weight. For an unequal weight of bodies is required, otherwise the operation is frustrated. And the heavier body is always in the upper glass [for the separation to occur]. But note, that the water is made suspended, and a great weight of water in the belly of the glass is, as it were, supported by a column of water in the neck of the glass. For this cause excites motion; for even a longer delay hardly separates water and glass in one glass.

    16. This experiment can be transferred from a mixture of various liquids to simple bodies, which consist of various but similar parts. Therefore, use in the experiment brine or salt water and fresh water, pouring the salt [water] (which is heavier) into the upper glass, and see if the fresh [water] ascends. Try the same with sugar and pure water, and observe whether the water that ascends deposits its sweetness: for which purpose a siphon would be needed in the belly of the upper glass.

Various experiments concerning accurate
    infusion both in liquids
            and in air.

    17. In bodies containing more subtle spirits, which
are easily dissipated, when you prepare an infusion, observe these things.
A short stay of the body in liquids receives the
spirit; a longer one confounds it, because it draws out
earthly parts at the same time, and corrupts the more subtle ones.
And therefore it is an error in physicians
if they rely only on a longer stay
as strengthening the virtue. But if you require
a strong infusion in bodies
which consist of more subtle spirits, let the
rule be that a longer stay not be allowed,
but that the infusion of the body be repeated often.
Take violets, and infuse a proper handful of them
into two pints of vinegar. Let them stand for
three quarters of an hour, and then remove them,
and renew the infusion seven times with a similar
quantity of violets; it will make the vinegar so
fragrant with the smell of the flowers, that, if after twelve-

--- Page 52 ---
12      FRANCIS BACON
18. This rule, which we have prescribed, is of excellent use for the preparations of medicines and other infusions. For example, the leaves of Borage are potent with an excellent spirit for dispersing the vapors of melancholy, and therefore they cure insanity; nevertheless, if the leaves remain infused too long, they only provide a crude substance, devoid of all virtue; therefore I suppose that if Borage is macerated for a short space of time in must or the yeast of beer while it ferments and is not yet decanted, with new ones added repeatedly, I would make a most efficacious potion against melancholic affliction. I also hold the same opinion concerning the flowers of the bitter orange.

19. Rhubarb clearly contains parts with mutually contrary operations, namely purgative and astringent to the body. The former are easily separated, the latter adhere more firmly. So that if Rhubarb is infused for an hour and thoroughly pounded, it will purge better and will astringe the body less after purgation, than if it is macerated for 24 hours; as experience has taught. I also conceive that by repeated infusion of Rhubarb often (as was said concerning violets), with only a short duration allowed each time, an equally strong purgative can be produced as by Scam-

SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 13
Scammony. Nor will it be of slight aid in
medicine to be able to render Rhubarb and
more benign medicines as effective as those
which are not without malignity.
20. The most purgative part of purgative
medicines resides in the finer spirit, as appears
from the fact that they suffer no ebullition
without great loss of virtue. And therefore it
will be of good use in medicine to be able to
retain the purgative power, and to remove the
harsh taste of the purgative. And it seems that
this can be done by observing a frequently
repeated series of infusions for a short period
of time. For it is probable that the harsh and
unpleasant taste adheres to the coarser particles.
21. In general, operation by infusions is
crude and blind, unless it is observed which
parts of the substance exit more quickly, which
more slowly, so that by proportioning the time
for each, you may remove what you desire, and
leave the quality. To understand this, one must
pursue a twofold method. The first is, that you
should experience what a long or short delay
effects, as already said; the second, that you
should observe in order the infusions of one and
the same substance in various liquids succeeding
one another. For example, take orange peels, or
Rosemary,

And so, in infusions of things which have vehement spirits, it would be better to reject the first infusion after a short time, and to use the subsequent one.

Experiment concerning the tendency of continuation in liquids.

24. Bubbles have the form of a hemisphere, air within, a thin membrane of water without. Nor is it a thing unworthy of admiration that air can swell up so suddenly when enclosed by water, and so, when it has gathered itself into a peak, be contained by such a fragile covering as a bubble is. As for the swift ascent of air enclosed in water, the motion is one of percussion from the water, which itself descending propels the air upwards, not a motion from lightness in the air. Democritus calls this a motion of impact. In this obvious experiment, the cause of the bubble closing itself on all sides is that the tendency resisting separation and discontinuation (which is strong in solid bodies) is also found in liquids, although weaker and more relaxed;

--- Page 56 ---
16      FRANCIS BACON'S
and weaker; as can be seen in this motion of a bubble.
It can also be observed in small transparent bubbles made from
saliva, which boys make from reeds; and
in the castles of bubbles, which they prepare by blowing
into water, which has acquired some degree of tenacity
from soap. The same is evident in drops of water, which, having acquired enough
to flow down, is drawn out into a thin thread
lest it separate; if that fails, it contracts into round
drops; a shape most effectively preventing the discontinuation of the body. The cause
of roundness in a bubble is the same both regarding
the membrane of water and regarding the internal
air. For air likewise avoids separation,
and therefore rolls itself into a round shape. The persistence
of the air and its brief delay, shows that air by itself with slow or
no appetite is carried upwards.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning Artificial*
*Fountains.*

25. The rejection of experiments, which
I sometimes use, even if it does not appear, is varied.
But if an experiment proves its use in operation,
I accept it, but I hand it over as of doubtful
reliability. An unknown man describes a method
for preparing an artificial fountain. Seek out
sloping ground, where conveniently a swift
flow-

--- Page 57 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 17
...run-off for rainwater. Arrange a channel half-full of stones of proper size to a depth of three or four feet in the same ground. Let one part be placed on the rising ground, the other on the sloping ground. Fill the channel with a suitable quantity of ferns, pour sand on the surface. You will see (he says) after several repeated showers, the lower part of the channel gushing forth like a spring. Nor is it surprising if this happens, while rainwater is flowing. But he adds that it will last for a long time after the rain has ceased flowing; as if the water is multiplied, helped by the air through coldness, the condensation of the earth, and the association of the previous water.

*A solitary experiment concerning the*
*poisonous quality of human flesh.*

26. The French (from whom the Neapolitan disease received its name) report that during the siege of Naples there were wicked merchants who sold the flesh of men recently killed in Mauritania, preserved in jars, in place of tuna; and that the origin of this disease is ascribed to such foul and heavy nourishment. Nor does it deviate from the truth; for it is known that Cannibals in the West

--- Page 58 ---
18 FRANCIS BACON
to eat human flesh; and that India,
when first discovered, suffered greatly
from this disease. In our time too,
poisons, which are most potent to the
West Indians, consist of a mixture of
human blood, fat, or flesh. Many
Witches and sorceresses, both among
pagans and Christians, feed on human
flesh, (as it seems) for strengthening
their imagination with foul and sharp
vapors.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*the conversion and transmutations*
*of air into water.*

27. These seem to be the most probable
reasons for changing vapors or air into
water. The first is cold, which condenses,
as shown by the condensation of air in a
calendar glass, where it becomes somewhat
more like water. We also see in the
generation of springs, to which the
ancients (very probably) attributed their
origin from the conversion of air into
water, facilitated by the stillness which
the air enjoys in these parts of the earth,
so that it cannot dissipate, and by the
coldness of the rocks; for springs are
mostly generated in those places. The
same is evident from the effects

--- Page 59 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 19
...ffects of cold in the middle (as they call it) region of the air, which produces dews and rains; and by the experiment of the change of water into ice with the help of snow, niter, and salt (about which we will speak later), which can be transferred to this conversion of air into water. Let an experiment be made whether a greater quantity of water comes forth from the return than there had been before. If this happens, the increase is from the conversion of air. Fill the bottom of the Alembic with water, the neck being stopped, but first having ascertained the weight of the water. In the middle of the alembic, suspend a sponge, and see how much water you can squeeze out of it. Whatever more or less there may be, let it be compared with the water consumed. For it must be known, if any change can occur, it happens most easily where the pores are small; and this is the reason why a sponge is prescribed to be

*A solitary experiment on how a good*
     *physical condition and stature may be*
               *produced.*

     28. Some of the Ancients relate that
puppies or other animals, if they are enclosed when young
in such a cage or box that they cannot fill
the proper measure of their kind, but grow
in breadth or height, grow to the shape of their place.
If we are not deceived by the report of the ancients,
and if it can happen that tender offspring, compressed
in this manner and held more tightly, do not die,
a method would be found which might produce
dwarfs of monstrous and exorbitant figure.
That is beyond controversy

This has been established by long-term observation,
that by pressing, the formed parts of the
tender fetus depart significantly from their natural form.
Thus the foreheads of infants, handled
by hands (which was noted by the ancients) make
macrocephali; which form of head
was then in esteem. A moderate elevation of the bridge
of the nose prevents the deformity of a flat nose.
This observation, thoroughly examined, shows
the means by which men and women in many ways
may become more graceful and shapelier,

allow. Thus the retraction of the calves upwards
causes them not to droop, but to sustain themselves. The fore-
head likewise, a retraction upwards makes it spacious
and not low. The common custom
of wrapping infants in swaddling bands makes them more slender as
they grow up, and of better form. For we
see young women use tighter body
constriction against stoutness.

*A solitary experiment concerning the mixture of flame and air, and its great power.*

30. Flame and air do not easily mix except in an instant, or in vital spirits and living animals. In gunpowder, its vehemence was attributed to the rarefaction of the terrestrial substance in the flame. Up to this point true, and then (indeed) another element emerges, whose form occupies a greater space, whence necessarily follows dilation, and, lest two bodies fill one place, the necessary expulsion of a globe, or the blowing up of tunnels. But these speculations have something crude and stupid about them. For flame, if nothing else were present, nor would it prevail in the greatest quantity, it can be suffocated by another hard body, such as an iron ball or the barrel of a gun. So that flame by a hard bo-

--- Page 64 ---
24      OF FRANCIS BACON
body, is not sufficient for expelling a body, but a hard body extinguishes the flame and does not allow it to ignite or disperse. But the cause of such a violent motion is in saltpeter (which we otherwise call salt of Peter), which, containing within itself a crude and expansive spirit, first expands itself with the heat of fire (nor are we unaware that simple air, thinned by heat beyond its nature, will make room for itself, dissolving and dispelling obstacles with its blast); secondly, when the saltpeter has expanded itself, it propels the flame outwards with a blast, like an internal bellows. And therefore we observe that sulfur, pitch, camphor, wildfire, and other flammable materials besides, although they burn with a vehement and scarcely extinguishable flame, yet they do not excite such fiery blasts as gunpowder. On the contrary, we see that Mercury (a most crude and watery body), when heated and tightly enclosed, possesses the same force as gunpowder. As for living beings, it is most certain that their vital spirits are a substance composed of airy and fiery matter. And although air and flame do not easily mix by themselves, they nevertheless do not refuse to be coupled in a fixed body, which is evident in two bodies (which are their foods): water and oil. For those too of their own accord do not

A solitary experiment regarding the hidden nature of flame.

31. Take a wax candle and place it in an iron
or bronze tube. Afterwards place it upright in a dish
full of spirit of wine and heated. Then, with the candle
and spirit of wine simultaneously set on fire, you will see
the flame of the candle expand, and swell four or five times
more than it was accustomed to before; and it appears
in a round, not pyramidal, shape. Moreover, you will observe
the internal flame of the candle maintaining its color,
nor will it take on anything blue towards the color of the
external flame in the spirit of wine. This is a remarkable
instance, supplying two things worthy of note.
The first is, that a flame enveloped by a flame is not
extinguished, but is a fixed and continuous body,
like air or water. Therefore the flame will continuously
ascend with equal magnitude,
                                B

--- Page 66 ---

    *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
        *the differing power of flame in*
            *the Middle and at the Sides.*

    32. Hold an arrow placed in the flame for the space of ten pulses. Then, when it is removed, you will find the outer parts of the arrow towards the flame more scorched and blackened, and for the most part turned into charcoal; whereas what was in the middle appears only to have been touched by fire. This instance leads to many observations regarding the elucidation of the flame's shape; and clearly demonstrates that the flame burns more intensely around the sides than in the middle, and, what is of greater moment, that violent or wild heat or fire does not exist, except where it is compressed and thins itself. Therefore, the Peripatetics (although their opinion about an element or fire above the air has been deservedly exploded) here acquit themselves very well. For to those who object that if a fiery sphere were given, which would envelop the world in such close embrace, it would not be possible but that all things would be exposed to be consumed by fire,

they reply that pure elemental fire, in its
natural place, and not irritated, is only of
moderate heat.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning the di-*
*minution of the natural motion of gravity*
*at a great distance and a certain*
*depth of the earth.*

33. It is the constant assertion of many,
confirmed by obvious experiment, that in the
bottom of a mine shaft a mass of crude metal
can be moved and rolled by the work of two
men, which, when moved to the surface of the
earth, would require the combined strength of
at least six men to be moved from its place.
It is a noble instance, and it is expedient that
a more exact account of this experiment be
had. For it is very probable that the motion
of gravity operates slowly both at a great
distance from the earth and in the interior of
the earth. The former happens because the
appetite for union of dense and compact bodies
with the earth is weaker at a distance. The
latter, because the body has in some part
acquired its own nature, from the fact that it
has been under the earth at a certain depth.
But as for motion towards a certain point or
place (which is the opinion of the ancients), it
is utterly vain.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the contraction of a corporeal mass or*
*bulk from the mixture of liquid*
*bodies with solid ones.*

34. It is strange that, since the ancients admitted experi-
ments on the faith of others, they were able to build things of great mo-
ment upon them. This is one of their most trustworthy obser-
vations. They boldly assert that a vessel filled with ashes
receives the same quantity of water as if it were empty. But it is plainly false:
for it does not imbibe a fifth part of the water. I attribute this difference
to the ashes being placed more loosely or more tightly; as we see
that ashes by themselves and unmixed, if they are compressed,
occupy less space; so also ashes are held in a looser space
with air, and in a tighter one with water. I have not yet
ascertained whether the water itself, with ash or powder mixed
in, contracts into a narrower space.

     *Various Experiments concerning*
          *purgative medicines.*

   36. The operation of purgative medicines
and their causes have hitherto been relegated among
the secrets of nature; and therefore the profound
ignorance of men attributes them to occult
properties, specific virtues, and a fourth quality,
and similar hiding places of ignorance. The causes
of purgatives are various, all open and
clear, and thoroughly proven by
experience. The first is, whatever cannot
be processed and digested by the heat of the
stomach, the stomach expels either by
vomiting, or sends down to the intestines, and
the expulsive motion of the stomach and intestines
provokes other parts of the body (such as the orifices
of the veins and similar) to expulsion
by consent. For there is no in the human

...human body a more familiar and frequent motion than that by consent. The overloading of the stomach is caused either by the quality or the quantity of the medicine. Quality is of a threefold difference: either it is extreme bitterness, as in Aloe, Colocynth, etc.; or nausea from a most unpleasant and acrid taste, as in Agaric, Black Hellebore, etc.; or a hidden and hostile malignity to the human body, often not manifesting itself by taste, as in Scammony, Mechoacan, Antimony, etc. It is to be observed that if any purgative medicine reveals none of these qualities, a just suspicion of poison is aroused. For it either effects this by corrosion, or by latent malignity, and a certain repugnance with nature; and therefore caution must be exercised both in preparing and taking medicines of this kind. The quantity of what is taken also excites purgation, as we see in a large quantity of freshly drawn milk, and even in excessively consumed foods; for too eager an ingestion of foods often turns into purgation, both upwards and downwards. Therefore, we generally observe that the operation of purgatives succeeds after two or three hours from when the medicines were taken, because the stomach first attempts to digest them.

Note also that besides the sympathy between purgatives and humor, there is another cause why certain medicines draw a humor agreeable to themselves more than another. It is this: that some medicines operate more quickly than others, and those which act quickly, draw only the thinner and more fluid humors, but those which draw slowly, exert their power on the more tenacious and viscous humors. Therefore, caution must be used in how rhubarb and similar things are to be used, not by themselves, nor with nothing mixed, nor habitually. For it quickly carries away the thinner part of the humor, leaving behind the more stubborn mass of humors. Something similar can be said of absinthe, so greatly celebrated.

*Various experiments concerning food*
    *and drink, especially the most nutritious.*

    45. We have dealt with the evacuation of the body,
now we pass to its repletion from restorative
substances in consumptions and emaciating diseases.
In vegetables, one part surpasses another in nutritive
faculty. Thus grains and roots nourish more fully than leaves,
so that the Order of the Folianators was rejected by the Roman Pope,
inasmuch as he considered leaves unsuitable for the nutrition
of the human body. Whether also the flesh of animals
differs thus, has not yet been properly explored;
for example, whether livers and other viscera nourish more
than external parts. Among the Romans, I find that goose liver
was a delicacy, so much so that they even had an art
by which it might be rendered both more elegant and
larger; but whether it nourishes more fully,
is not apparent. It is established that marrow nourishes more
abundantly with fat, and I conceive that a decoction
from bones and nerves, crushed and well
filtered, is a very nourishing broth.
Thus is also found Scotch

51. That fresh milk contains great nutritive power, is well-known; it is likewise a good remedy for treating emaciation. But let two small bags be placed in it while the cow is being milked, one with mint powder, the other with powder of red roses. For these in some way preserve the milk in the stomach from coagulation: Add sugar also for the same reason, and partly for the sake of flavor. I judge cow's milk prepared in this way to be preferable to ass's milk, because (without doubt) it is not so prone to change, but is somewhat acidic. Mare's milk is more effective against acrimony of the urine, and ulceration of the bladder, and is also soothing for all. Woman's milk is also prescribed for others who are failing; but I do not consider it among good foods, as it is somewhat too close to the juice of the human body, except for infants, for whom it is natural.

The poultice loosens the pores and renders the humor suitable for exhalation. Fomentation draws forth humors in the manner of vapors, but with respect to the path made by the poultice, it extracts moderately and draws none from elsewhere besides. For it is a gentle fomentation, and it has a mixture and appearance of stupefaction, though slight. The plaster is moderately astringent, which repels in such a way that no new humor may enter. The poultice alone renders the part softer and more apt for receiving the defluxion and the impression of humor. Fomentation alone, if it were less efficacious without a path made by the poultice, would extract little; if too strong, it would draw both to the part and from the part. The plaster alone would restrain the humor contained in the part, and thus would both exasperate it and prevent the access of new humor. Therefore, they ought to be applied in order, as has been said. The poultice is to be applied for a space of two or three hours; the fomentation to be applied very warmly for a quarter of an hour or a little longer, and to be repeated seven or eight times; the plaster to be applied continuously until the part is strengthened.

   *A solitary experiment regarding*
           *cure from habituation.*

   61. There is also a certain hidden method of curing, not yet brought into use, derived from habituation to a thing harmful in itself. Poisons have been rendered familiar to some, as has been said. Those who commonly take care of people suffering from plague are rarely infected by contagion. The toleration of torments from habituation renders them lighter. The digestion of excessive food or wine, when turned into a habit, prevents indigestion and drunkenness. In general, chronic diseases, such as coughs, consumptions, certain types of paralysis, lunatics, etc., are most dangerous in the beginning. And therefore it is the part of a prudent physician to consider whether the disease is incurable, and whether its exact cure is free from danger. If there is danger, let him resort to palliation, let him alleviate the symptoms, not too much occupied with a perfect cure: often, however, this method (provided the patient only has patience) achieves more than expectation would have promised itself; as also if the affection can overcome the symptoms in a paroxysm, and turn patience into a natural disposition.

Moreover, such excesses excite and irritate nature, which thus rises more vehemently against the disease.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning the*
*cure of diseases which are contrary to*
*the predisposition of the body.*

64. Hippocrates' aphorism, namely "in diseases less, etc.", contains a good and profound speculation. For it indicates that diseases contrary to the constitution of the body, age, sex, season of the year, and diet are more dangerous than those which agree with these. Someone might think the opposite, for where the symptom of the disease and the natural disposition, as it were, offer mutual aid, the disease will be more vehement; nor is there any doubt about that, presupposing a similar quantity of matter. But what the Aphorism asserts is that such diseases indicate matter more abundantly collected, and therefore can turn natural inclinations to the contrary. And therefore in such a state of diseases, the physician should look to purgation more than alteration, since the fault is in quantity, and the qualities spontaneously return to order.

A Solitary Experiment concerning preparation before purgation, and the complete restoration of the body.

65. It is a prudent observation of physicians to apply preparations before proper purgations; for it is indeed true that the body is often greatly harmed if both the preliminary and subsequent measures are neglected. The harm from a defect in preparation is the tenacity of non-fluid humors, and their inconvenient exit; which causes great disturbances in the body and adverse occurrences while the purgative is at work; whence the strength of the medicine is dulled and diminished, so that it does not purge sufficiently. Therefore, the double function of preparation is to render the humors mature and fluid, and the passages more pervious; for both facilitate the exit of the humors. As for the former, syrups are most beneficial; as for the latter, decoctions or preparatory broths. Clysters also ensure that medicines do not stick in the intestines and operate by dislodgement. But it is true that bodies full of humors and fat, and clear and calm weather are in themselves preparatory, and render the humors more fluid. But let the physician attend to purgations to be administered during cold weather,
                                 C 3                      das,

--- Page 94 ---

[...to be administered in cold weather,] and to slender bodies, unprepared. For whatever harm exists after purging, arises from humors badly obstructed elsewhere; for indeed it is true that some humors fixed in certain parts of the body rest without harm, while to other parts (especially the ducts) they bring much injury. Therefore, it will be advisable after purging to use decoctions and broths, not so much opening ones, as before purging, but to resort to cleansing and purifying clysters, so that the remnants of humors which could descend to the lower region of the body may be removed.

66. Blood is stopped in various ways. First, by astringent and repercussive medicines. Secondly, by drawing spirits and blood inwards; which is effected by cold, as iron or a stone applied to the neck stops blood from the nostrils. It has also been found that testicles inserted into strong vinegar repel spirits and stop blood. Thirdly, by the regression of blood through Sympathy. For it has been found by experience that a part, emitting blood, inserted into a freshly dissected capon or egg, and which

Fourthly, by habit and the lapse of time. Thus, the wound first inflicted by a Spaniard on the Prince of Orange overcame the medicines and bandages applied to stop the blood. Finally, the opening of the wound having been stopped up by the thumbs of men succeeding each other for the space of at least two days, habit repressed the blood. There is also a fifth method, that blood be drawn in the opposite part by revulsion.

*Solitary Experiment concerning the change of foods and medicines.*

67. The change of medicine as well as food is beneficial; nor should one persevere in the frequent use of either. The reason is, because that continuation produces satiety in nature, so that its appetite and operation are blunted. Thus we see harmful things become harmless by habituation: as poison, for digesting which some have a stomach capable of handling it from continuous use. Therefore it is not surprising if some salutary things lose their helping power by habituation. But the same intermission with change...

*A solitary experiment concerning diet.*

68. Experience dictates that diets strictly instituted from Guaiacum, Sarsaparilla, and similar substances afflict the patient more at the beginning than in the progress. Hence, most of the more delicate ones stopped in the middle, deceived by this opinion, that they would not be able to endure them until the end, if the beginnings caused such great disturbances. But the reason is, because such diets dry out humors, catarrhs, and similar things, and they cannot dry them out unless they first attenuate them. And while the humor is attenuated, it becomes more fluid than before, and disturbs the body, until it has been dried out and consumed. Therefore, patients ought to wait a proper amount of time, and not be troubled by the beginnings.

*Various experiments concerning the production of cold.*

The production of cold is most worthy of inquiry, both on account of its use and the knowledge of its causes. For heat and cold are the two hands with which nature principally operates. We have heat readily available, with respect to fire. Cold must be waited for until it arrives,

--- Page 97 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 57

...until it arrives, or must be sought in caves, or on the highest mountains; and when all things have been attempted, we cannot obtain it in the highest degree. For furnaces heated by fire far surpass the heat of the Sun; but vaulted places and hills do not greatly excel in the cold of winter frost.
      69. The first cause of producing cold is that which nature supplies to us, namely, a cold exhalation from the inner parts of the earth in wintertime, when the Sun is not able to overcome it. For the earth (as has been well noted by some) is primarily cold. Both ancient and modern philosophers assert this. Parmenides was of this opinion, and the author of that discourse in Plutarch (for I do not acknowledge Plutarch as its author) concerning the primary cold. Telesius felt the same, who revived the philosophy of Parmenides, and among modern thinkers, he is commended above all.
      70. The second cause of cold is the contact of a cold body. For cold is active, and passes into adjacent bodies, like heat; which is evident in those things which snow and cold things touch.    A solitary experiment concerning
      the conversion of water into air.

                                                                 from

of a thin cloudlet of exhalation or

misty haze is suddenly dispersed and dissipated.
But a similar cloudlet, applied to oily or

it adheres more tenaciously, but because air preys upon water,
and flame and fire (prey upon) oil. Therefore,
for removing grease spots, they use char-
coal wrapped in blotting paper, because
fire acts upon grease or oil, as
air (acts) upon water. We also see paper
smeared with oil, or wood coated with oil,
or something similar, retain moisture for a very long
time, but things moistened with water dry out more quickly
or rot. The reason is that air with diffi-
culty mixes with oily moisture.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning the Nourishment of Living Things before they are Born.*

94. It is a work of providence, most truly observed by some, that the yolk of an egg contributes little to the generation of a bird, but only to its nourishment. For if a chick recently hatched is dissected, you will find many remnants of the yolk; and it is necessary that birds, which are generated outside the womb of females, have in the egg both material for nourishment and that from which the body is generated. For after the egg is laid, and separated from the body of the hen, it receives no further nourishment from the hen, but only the vivifying warmth from her incubating it. But beasts and man need no internal nourishment, because they are generated within the womb of the female, and are continuously nourished from her body.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the Efficacy of Fire.*

99. It is certain that heat is the chief of all faculties, both in the fabric of nature and in the works of art. It is also clear that the effects of heat are most promoted when it exerts its force upon bodies without dissipation or detriment of matter, which confounds reasoning. Therefore it is true that its efficacy can best be perceived in distillations, which are performed in closed vessels and receptacles. But there is nevertheless a certain higher degree: for although distillations preserve bodies in cells D 4 &

--- Page 120 ---
80 FRANCIS BACON
and in closed vessels, lest they be dispersed, yet they allow space for bodies to change into vapors, and reciprocally return into liquids, and separate from each other; as nature is accustomed to expand, although it does not enjoy full liberty, with the result that the true and ultimate operations of heat are not obtained. But if bodies can be altered by heat, and yet do not admit such a reciprocation of rarefaction, condensation, and separation, it is probable that this Proteus, as if grasped by the hands of matter, will transform itself into various metamorphoses.

Take therefore a square iron vessel, in the form of a cube, which has thick and solid sides. In it, place a cube of wood, which fills it very tightly, and let it have an iron lid as strong as the sides, and let it be sealed with clay in the manner of the Chemists.

Then place the vessel on burning coals; keep it well heated for a few hours. I believe that, when inflammation and evaporation are entirely prohibited, with the body continuously transforming within itself, one of these will follow: either the body of the wood will be converted into a kind of malagma (as the Chemists call it), or the thinner parts will be changed into air, and the thicker parts, as if cooked and encrusted, will adhere to the sides of the vessel,

--- Page 121 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 81
adhere, consisting of denser matter than the raw wood itself. Let another experiment be made; take water and and place it in a similar vessel, sealed as before, but with milder heat to be used, and the vessel then to be removed from the fire; and after a short space of time has elapsed, when it has cooled down, the heat is to be renewed; this alteration is to be repeated several times; and if you can ever bring it about that water, one of the simplest bodies, changes its smell or taste by heat, as in composite bodies, be assured that you have produced something great in nature, and made an entrance worthy of observation to wonderful mutations and productions of bodies, and discovered a method by which fire may produce in a short time what the Sun and age accomplish in a long course of time. But concerning the wonderful operations of this closed distillation (for thus indeed we call it), which is not dissimilar to the uteri and matrices of living beings, in which nothing exhales or separates, we will treat more fully in its proper place. Not that anyone should think that we are pursuing the pygmies of Paracelsus, or prodigious trifles, but that we may know that the effects of heat are such that they scarcely enter human thoughts, if all its force is retained enclosed.

100. Nothing is more certain in nature than that it is not possible for any body to be utterly reduced to nothing; but just as it was the work of God's Omnipotence to create something out of nothing, so too it is entirely within His Omnipotence to destroy it. And therefore it was well said by a certain obscure writer among the Chemists, that there is no other way of producing wonderful transmutations of bodies than if, by all means, reduction to nothing is urged and attempted. Here is a great secret for preserving a body from change. For if you can prevent them from turning into air, because no air can enter, nor from passing into adjacent bodies, because they are entirely heterogeneous, nor from completing a circuit within themselves, they will never change, even if by their nature they are most perishable and mutable. For we see how flies or spiders find a more lasting tomb in amber than the preservation afforded to a royal corpse by balsam. I feel the same about bodies placed in Mercury. *Various Experiments concerning Tones;*
*and first, the nullity and entity*
*of sounds.*

Perspective has hitherto been diligently treated, nor has that felicity been wanting concerning Music for the nature of sounds; which, however, generally observed, has superficial and perfunctory observations. It is reckoned among the most subtle secrets of nature. It is my intention, as I have previously advised, to subjoin to the inquiry into things immersed in matter, either things immaterial, or participating less in matter; such as that concerning sounds; so that the intellect may neither be confused, nor cling tenaciously to one thing.
115. First, it is to be observed, that great motions are performed in natural things without noise.

--- Page 133 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. II. 93
noise. The heavens are rotated most rapidly, yet no sound is perceived; although in the dreams of some it is said to excite the sweetest music. Likewise, the movement of comets and fiery meteors (such as a falling star, etc.) produce no sound. If anyone thinks great distance is the reason why sound does not reach us, let him consider that lightning and flashes of light generated in a space not very distant from us are seen without any sound at all, although they do not occur without the percussion and tearing apart of the air. Winds in the uppermost region of the air move clouds with a movement imperceptible to us here, and pass without sound. Winds blowing lower down on the plain, unless they are violent, produce no sound; however, their sound is perceived among trees. In general, when winds produce sound, they always do so unevenly with intensity and remission, and sometimes, when they are fiercer, they tremble at their greatest force.
    Rain and hail falling even with great force do not make a sound by passing through the air, unless they strike the ground, water, houses, or something similar. The rapid course of a river through its bed, if it is deeper, does not make itself heard, but flows silently. An in-

120. It is rumored among popular discourses that a certain white powder is found for exploding cannons without sound. Certainly a dangerous thing, if the truth does not fail, since it could be useful for clandestine murders. But it seems to me that it cannot happen that expelled air, which is compressed, should rush into the open without sound. As for the white powder (provided a means of extinguishing and removing sound is found), it seems to obtain a certain mixture of saltpeter and sulfur without charcoal: for saltpeter itself catches fire. If anyone thinks that sound can be abolished and extinguished by the air, which was enclosed, exploding before it reaches the mouth of the cannon and the open air, he conceives things that reason flees from, since they ought to render sounds all the more divided. As if a transverse tube were hollowed out in the barrel of a musket, it could emit various sounds, both through the front opening and from the sides. But my mind dictates that if such a thing could be brought about, so that the air around the mouth of the cannon would not be compressed, the ball would fly out with little or no sound.

     134. Take some silver vessel, and another of wood, both full of water; then strike the arms of the tongs, as before, a hand's breadth from the bottom; you will find the sound from the silver vessel clearer than from the wooden one. If, however, the vessel is empty, the collision produces no difference between the silver and wooden vessel. Hence, besides that observation of great importance, that no sound is produced from air, these two things can be gathered: first, that the sound is communicated to the bottom of the vessel; second, that such communication passes better through water than through air.

That rebound motion is swift and sharp, while the former [motion] is soft and dull; thus the plectrum continuously twists the string, and for that reason makes it vibrate perpetually.

  138. If someone blows a whistle into one

The cause is the diffusion of sound in a circuit,
which, otherwise to be dispersed through the air,
if it is confined by a certain channel, will
necessarily generate a greater sound. In which
experiment it is to be noted that by compressing
receptacles, sounds are not only preserved, but
also increased and sharpened.
  139. A hunting horn, wider at one end,
will intensify the sound more than if the
opening were entirely equal. The reason is
that the air, having first entered narrower
spaces, is contracted, then, having found
larger ones, pours itself into a wider exit
and expands itself. Also in its exit, striking
more air, consequently it is more powerful
and weighty. And thus hunting horns, which
are sometimes made straight, not curved,
always open wider towards the lower parts.
An experiment could be made with pipes
wider below, or with a certain capacity,
then ending in a straight concavity.

140. There is in the fields of St. James a brick canal, to which a certain low ceiling is contiguous, and at whose end is a round house of stone.      155. Water supplies a most certain experiment: if someone enters a bath, having taken a bucket, the mouth of which, with its bottom inverted and equally depressed, he should lower to the surface of the water, then depress it under the water to the width of one and a half hands, maintaining a continuous equilibrium, lest any part be raised, which would allow air to escape.

Then let him, standing in the bath, immerse himself in the water to such a depth that he can insert his head into the bucket, and so much air, exciting bubbles, will burst forth as the space of his head requires. Then let him utter a voice, clearly to be perceived by another standing outside the water, but with such a thinness as is customary for puppets, yet so that the sound, articulating words, is not confused.

It should be noted that this can be done much more skillfully if the bucket is placed on the head of a man who has not yet entered the water, who then sinks down, the bucket being depressed along with him; let him also lean on his knees, or sit, so that the water becomes deeper.

Perhaps not idly might someone conjecture that the Sicilian poet had knowledge of this experiment, when he narrates that Hylas, the servant of Hercules, having gone out to fill his bucket with water from a most pleasant spring in the vicinity of the shore, was, by the Nymphs, seized by love for him, stolen alive beneath the waters. Various experiments regarding the communication of sounds.

The communication of sounds (in the cavity of a tortoise shell, an empty vessel, etc.) has only been touched upon in the amplification of sounds; but it claims a peculiar title, and deservedly so.
166. A notable experiment, by which the communication of sounds may be demonstrated, is in the striking of a bell. Here, if you strike its uppermost part with a hammer, then the middle, then the lowest, you will perceive a sharper and deeper sound responding from the hollow interior, although the percussion is only external.
167. Although sound is produced between the breath of the mouth and the air contiguous to the pipe, nevertheless it obtains some communication with the sides of the pipe and the spirits contained therein. For one sound arises from a wooden pipe, another from a brass tube. A pipe also clothed with cloth or silk will produce a different sound from that which it would give by itself; also, moistened somewhat, it sounds differently internally than when dry.

*Various experiments concerning the equa-*
*lity and inequality of sounds.*

In the preceding (where we considered Music), we dealt with musical sounds, from which either harmony or dissonance of two parts arises, which we call tones; and likewise concerning non-musical sounds; the reason for which was given by us, that the former are generated from equality, the latter from inequality. We also added what bodies were equal, producing tones, and what were unequal and lacking tones. Now indeed we will treat of that kind of equality of sounds which is not from the nature of bodies, but is accidental; whether from the roughness or obliquity of passages, or repeated percussion, or trepidation of motion.

*Solitary Experiments concerning Sharper*
*and Graver Sounds, and Musical Sounds.*

178. It is evident that when a greater quantity
of air is struck, the sound is grave; when a smaller
quantity, acute. The striking of a greater
quantity depends on the magnitude of the
striking body, the width of the hollow space
traversed by the sound, and its length. Hence,
hypate is greater than nete; flutes for grave
sounds have larger holes than those for acute
sounds. And these flutes and similar instruments
produce a graver sound the further down the
holes are and the further they are from the
mouth, and the closer to the mouth, the more
acute the sound. Moreover, a solid body,
such as [a] an andiron, struck at the top will
produce a sharper sound; in the lower parts,
a graver one.

We observe the same in strings, which, the more they are stretched and twisted (whence a faster rebound), the sharper the sound produced. Thus, a thicker string, more stretched, and a thinner string, less stretched, produce the same sound.

180. Boys, women, and eunuchs produce thinner and sharper voices than men: the reason is not that the latter have a larger head, from which a stronger voice might emerge (for the efficacy of voice or sound contributes to difference in clarity or softness, but minimally to tones) but a more dilated organ; heat also contributing to this dilation, as is well established. But the reason why the years of puberty change the voice, escapes us more. It seems to happen because, with much of the body's moisture, by which the parts were previously more fully irrigated, being driven to the seminal vessels, heat begins to abound in the body, which renders the passages more dilated; since all the effects of heat occur, such as hairiness, roughness of the skin, and hardness of the skin.

Various experiments concerning internal and external sound.

Moreover, there is another difference of sound, which we call internal and external, which is neither low nor clear; nor deep nor high-pitched; nor musical nor unmusical; although it is true that the internal sound does not possess the power of generating a tone; but on the contrary, the external sound is musical or not. And therefore we will rather devote our efforts to enumeration than to exact distinction; even if (so that we may in some way sketch our opinion) the internal is for us more truly an impulse, or a contusion of air, than its elision or section; so that percussion differs less with respect to the other, as a blow from a cut.
188. In human speech, a whisper, whether clearer or softer, is called internal sound;
F 5

--- Page 170 ---
**130 FRANCIS BACON**
the pronunciation itself is an exterior sound; and
therefore a tone or song never arises from a whisper, as it does from speech. Thus respiration or a
blast, which occurs by mouth, bellows, or winds,

by means of a pipe or hollow object, however soft, is
exterior. By the same reasoning, very strong winds,
if they are not confined or blow through a hollow,

whence if a hollow wind blows, it is a sign
of rain. A flame when it moves within itself
or is inflated by bellows, produces a murmur or an
interior sound.

*Various Experiments concerning*
*articulated sounds.*

192. It is evident, and also reckoned among the most admirable secrets of sounds, that sound, undiminished in any part of itself, is dispersed through the entire air, and adheres whole even to the smallest particles of air; so much so that the skillfully articulated diversity of sounds, both from humans and from birds, passes unconfused even through the narrowest crack.
193. The unequal agitation of winds, and similar things, even if they provide a vehicle for sound, carrying it to more or less distant places; nevertheless, they disturb the distinctions of sounds not at all within that space where they can be perceived; although perhaps they are the cause why sounds are heard less far than in a tranquil sky; as was partly said before.
194. Too great a distance confuses articulated sounds, as is clear from the fact that, perceiving the voice of a preacher or similar, you cannot distinguish the speech, and one articulated sound is confused with another, as happens when many speak at once.
195. In that experiment, if someone under
water

--- Page 172 ---

if one utters a voice under water, a thin voice is produced; but so that the articulated sounds of words may be distinguished, as we said before.

**196.** Thus I conclude with myself, that a sound extremely thin, or extremely grave, cannot be articulated; but the articulation of words requires a moderate sound; because both excessive thinness of sound confuses articulation by contraction, and excessive lowness by dispersion. And although (as said in the preceding) an articulated sound can entirely after production be contracted in passing through a narrow fissure, nevertheless the prior articulation requires a greater dimension.

**197.** Observation has taught, that a preacher in a place or chapel vaulted above and below cannot be heard as conveniently as in other places. The reason is, because subsequent (sounds) arrive before preceding (sounds) vanish; and therefore articulated sounds are more confused, even if the quantity of sound is greater.

**198.** The movements of the tongue, lips, throat, palate, etc., which serve for the varied pronunciation of the letters of the alphabet, are worthy of inquiry, and pertain to the present investigation of sounds. But since they are subtle and require a long description, we deem them to be omitted, and among

The Hebrews showed diligence, designating which letters were labial, dental, guttural, etc. But the Latins and Greeks applied a distinction between semivowels and mutes, and among the mutes they made others tenues, mediae, and aspirates; nor in vain, but not exactly enough. For the special movements and impacts, from which the formation of these sounds arises, were investigated too little diligently; as, for example, that the letters B, P, F, M cannot be expressed unless by contraction of the mouth or by closing the mouth; that the letters N and B cannot be pronounced without the letter N being changed into M, so that Hecatonba becomes Hecatomba. That M and T cannot be pronounced unless P intervenes, as 'emtus' is pronounced 'emptus', and many similar cases. To such an extent that by applying themselves more deeply to this investigation, they will discover that fewer movements are required for the formation of an entire alphabet than there are letters counted.

   199. The lungs are the most spongy of all parts of the body, and therefore most suitable for contraction and expansion.       200. A certain kinship has been observed
between sounds from inanimate bodies or
animate ones which do not produce articulate
voice; and various letters of articulate voice.
For usually they designate these sounds
by referring to similar articulate voices. Thus, the trem-
bling of water has a certain similarity with
the letter L; the ringing of metals
with the letter Z; the growling of dogs with R; the sound
of an owl with S. H.; the sound of cats with
the diphthong 'eu'; the voice of the cuckoo with the diphthong
'ou'; the sound of strings with N. G. If therefore
anyone should apply himself to this curiosity or novelty,
so that he may wish to impart the pronunciation of a
word to a puppet or a corpse fashioned by himself,
he must first consider the movements
of the instruments of voice, then fashion similar ones in
animate bodies, and attend to the cause
of the conformity of that similarity;
and thus the notion of that effect will become clear.
