Various experiments concerning the motions
of sounds in any line, circular,
oblique, straight, upwards, downwards,
forwards, backwards.

201. [Decorative initial O]All sounds, of whatever kind
they may be, move in a circle;
that is, in all directions, up-
wards, downwards, forwards, backwards;
which all instances show.
202. Sounds do not require that they be carried
to the sense in a straight line, as
visible things do, but it can be curved; al-
though it is true that they move most strongly
along a straight line. Nor, however, is this
due to the straightness of the line, but to the smaller
interval; for a straight line is the shortest.
Hence if someone from the other side of an intervening wall
part

--- Page 176 ---
136      OF FRANCIS BACON
side utters a voice, it can be heard from the other; not because the voice penetrates the wall by passing through it, but because, being curved, it ascends over the wall.
     203. A sound that is obstructed and reflected will reach the other side by an oblique line. Thus, if a curtain is lowered on one side of a carriage and raised on the other, if someone begging speaks to the closed side, he will seem to be standing at the open, not the covered, side. Also, a small bell or a large bell, for example, placed on the northern side of a room, and a window on the southern side, he who is in the room will perceive the sound as if from the south.
     204. Although the movement of sounds is circular (for indeed a circle or spherical area is given to them), nevertheless it is most vehement, and is carried furthest along the forward lines, and by the first local impulse of the air. And therefore the voice of a preacher is more conveniently perceived from directly in front of the pulpit than behind or to the sides, even if it is unobstructed. So also a musket or a cannon will be heard further forward, directly from the mouth (of the barrel), than backwards, or to the sides.
     205. It might be called into doubt whether sounds move better upwards than downwards. Pulpits are erected and stand out; and Empero-

It is strange that a man standing on the ground sees those who are on the top of St. Paul's as of smaller stature, and cannot distinguish them; whereas the contrary happens to one looking down from the summit, where neither is the stature so much diminished, nor does all distinction entirely vanish.    *Various Experiments concerning the duration*
      *and evanescence of sounds, and the time*
         *necessary for their generation and transmission.*

   207. The production of sound is momentary,
between which and its fading away a little time intervenes.
And here a strange error of men is detected,
of those who consider that to be a continuation of sound,
which is nothing other than a renewal. For the percussion
of a body imparts a vibration to its minute parts,
and thus renews the percussion of the air. You may
clearly gather this from the fact that the dying sound
of a bell or a struck string, which is considered a
continuation, completely ceases, as soon as the bell
or string feels a hand laid upon it, as in harpsichords,
where the damper falls and touches the string, the
sound ends. Also, if a small bell is touched after
being struck, the sound ceases. Here a twofold (thing)
must be distinguished

the sound dies with the breath. Nor

the bellows, namely, previously inflated, subside.
208. It is certain that the sound of a cannon
of war, which has overthrown many, can be carried through twen-
ty at least miles on land;
much further on sea; which will reach the ears
not at the very moment of the explosion,
but after an hour or much later.
Necessarily this is a continuation of the prior sound,
since no vibration is detected
from which it could be renewed, nor will the contact of the can-

greater sounds the continuation is more than
momentary.

210. It is known to all from observation that the object of sight moves faster than that of hearing; since the flash of a cannon is perceived by the eyes sooner than its sound by the ears; which also usually happens in splitting wood, where, standing a little distance away, one will see the hand raised for the second blow before one has heard the sound from the first; and the greater the distance, the greater the anticipation; just as the flash of thunder, very far removed from us, precedes the crash by a considerable interval.

211. When colors present themselves to the eyes, they do not usually fade or diminish gradually and by degrees, but a continuous vigor and efficacy persists, while sounds gradually perish: the reason is that colors do not participate as much as sounds with the motion of the air; and that sound communicates somewhat to its local motion (as an indispensable cause) is also shown by the argument that it perishes so quickly; since the cut and impelled air is continuously restored and reunites itself, which also happens in water, but not with equal speed.

Various experiments concerning the passages and interceptions of sounds.

In exploring the passages of sounds, or conversely, you must observe that an exit in some body does not deceive you on the side for a straight passage through, and therefore the intercepting body must be closed very tightly, since sound escapes even through the narrowest crack.

212. Wherever sound passes through a solid and well-closed body (such as water, a wall, metal, as in stopped bells, etc.), that solid body must be thin and slender, lest it completely extinguish the sound. Therefore, when someone speaks under water by means of air, the voice below the water must not be greatly suppressed, so that it can penetrate. So also if a voice is uttered towards the other side of a closed wall, excessive thickness will prevent it from being heard on its other side. Imagine a barrel to be empty, with sides two feet thick, and its opening closed; I conceive that the sound by which it resonates from the communication of the exterior air with the interior would be faint, or no sound at all; only a perceptible noise from the exterior percussion, as if the vessel were full.

213. It is certain that when sounds pass through solid bodies, the spirit or parts

--- Page 182 ---
142          FRANCIS BACON
the pneumatic parts of that body. But
this will be observed much more accurately if the sides of a hard body are struck, than if they are struck from within, without an impact on the sides.
Take therefore a bell, whose openings are stopped, and let it be suspended in a glass flask, the mouth of the glass being very tightly closed with wax. Then, the glass being shaken, observe whether the sound of the bell is perceived, and how faint. It is to be noted that instead of a thread, a metallic cord [a] should be used; or else the capacity of the glass should be such that the agitation occurs without striking the sides of the glass.
     214. It is clear that by a long and perpendicular arc (the sound-carrying line), sound is entirely extinguished; so that what can be heard beyond a wall, is not perceived beyond a temple; nor is it perceptible at any distance from the wall, but is felt very close to the wall.
     215. Soft and porous bodies primarily stifle sound, so to speak, at its birth. For an impact on cloth or hides renders the sound faint, as we have said. Various experiments on how much the shape of
pipes or cavities, or conveying

How much the shapes of pipes, or cavities for
sound to pass through, or conveying bodies, contribute
to the variety and alteration of sounds; whether a
greater or lesser quantity of air received in the cavity
is considered; or the space through which sound is
carried shorter or longer, or other circumstances, we
have treated under other headings. Here is the place
due to examining shapes, which I conceive as lines
permeable to sounds. Such are straight, oblique,
angular, circular, etc.
221. The shape of a bell is not unlike a
pyramid, except that its delineation and expansion,
as it were, descends and spreads out more quickly.
The shape of hunting horns and flutes is oblique.
Straight horns are also found, with as many oblique
holes, but with little difference in sound; except that
straight ones are blown more vehemently. The shapes
of flutes and pipes are straight; but these consist of a
smaller and larger hole above and below. A trumpet
has the shape of the letter S, by which that strident
sound is produced. In general, the straight shape G

--- Page 186 ---
146          FRANCIS BACON
straight produces the purest sounds; the oblique more hoarse and discordant.
     222. An experiment could be made with a sinuous tube, having four bends; but also with a tube shaped like a cross, open in the middle; likewise with an angular tube, to see what variety of sounds they generate. Furthermore, let there also be a circular tube, precisely curved in its roundness, with a hole inserted as a receptacle for the blast; to which let another be joined not far off, with an obstacle placed across, so that the blast may pass through the circle and thus reach the second hole. Moreover, solid bodies of various shapes are to be tested by striking them, such as globular, flat, cubic, cross-shaped, triangular, etc. Let their combination also be made; flat against flat; convex against convex; and convex against flat; and let the differences in sounds be accurately noted. Also to be explored are sounds produced by hard bodies of various thicknesses. I have found that the sound of a golden bell is excellent, not inferior to silver or bronze, indeed, better. However, the sound of a gold coin is duller than a silver one.
     223. A lyre consists of a hollow, not along the length of the strings, but transversely; nor is any instrument so gradually failing in sound through rather long intervals, as.

Therefore, I propose that if a harpsichord is formed with a double concavity, the former along its length, the latter at the end of the strings, as in a lyre, it would necessarily result in a more perfect sound, not so muffled and discordant. This should be attempted without a substratum board, only in the manner and form of a lyre, at one end of the strings; or finally with a double concavity, one at each end of the strings.

Various experiments concerning the mixture of sounds.

224. A clear distinction appears among those things which are perceived by sight or hearing, that visible things pass through the medium unmixed, while others are confused in the medium. For when the eyes sweep across the sky, many stars, trees, hills, people, beasts, all fall under a single gaze at once; nor is an image emanating from one thing disturbed by others flowing together to the eye. Sounds, however, emitted from various parts, follow the predominance of one. Also, the mixture of dissenting voices is tempered into harmony; which is denied to colors. But nevertheless, the lesser light is extinguished by the greater light, so that it escapes sight; just as the light of a glow-worm G 2 light

--- Page 188 ---

the lights tinted with these colors will be mixed,
and will impress upon white paper a purple
color. Also, the mixture of colors weakens
with debility; for a place is illuminated more
from whitewashed walls than from black ones, etc.
But the reason which carries sounds confusedly,
and the images of visible things unconfusedly,
is that sight operates through a straight line
and produces various cones; and in that
way no coincidence can occur in the eye or
visual point. Sounds, however, moved through
oblique and tortuous lines, must necessarily
coincide, and thus disturb each other.

    225. The sweetest and best harmony

Various experiments pertaining to
the imitation of sound.

236. It is a certain miracle of nature, if one gives it sustained attention, that boys and some birds are able to express voices by imitation with astonishing dexterity. For birds, the mouth of the speaker and its movements are unobserved, yet they are taught no less correctly in a dark or bright place. It is a matter of some exquisite curiosity concerning sounds from speech, the study of which might not seem devoid of difficulty. But the difficulties presented at the beginning gradually decrease in such a way that repeated attempts, with the passage of intervening time, overcome them. But this does not remove the novelty of the thing. Perhaps someone might think (although, to tell the truth, it could provide a just cause for admiration) that there is a certain transmission of spirits, which, moved in the teacher, generate a predisposition in the spirits of the pupil so that he is invited to imitation, which is thus gradually perfected. But the operation due to the transmission of spirits (the greatest secret of nature) awaits its treatment elsewhere; especially where an inquiry concerning the powers of imagination will be instituted. As far as imitation is concerned, to deny entirely

   *Various experiments concerning the re-*
          *flection of sounds.*

   There are three kinds of reflections in sounds:
concurrent reflection, iterating reflection, which is Echo,
and super-reflection, an Echo from a previous Echo.
The former having been treated under the heading of
the magnitude of sounds, the latter two are now to be
discussed.
   242. The reflection of effluvia from visible
objects can be directed by mirrors, inasmuch as,
having issued forth and advanced in straight lines,
they can be led to some point, but the reflection
of sounds scarcely allows itself to be governed,
because sound more loosely fills space with curved
lines...

--- Page 197 ---
      SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. III.     157
filling space, does not admit such direction,
whence the method of preparing artificial echoes
has not yet come into use; and whatever
Echo has hitherto become known does not
admit return in a narrow place.
   243. Natural Echo is generated in walls,
woods, rocks, hills, and banks. Water,
however, where it is near, creates a con-
current Echo; where it is far distant, it
produces an iterating one. For concurrent and
iterating Echoes are distinguished in no other
way than by the swiftness or slowness of their
return. But it is beyond controversy that just
as water promotes the carrying of the original
sound, so it serves to carry the Echo further.
   244. It has been said in previous sections
that when a voice is uttered through a body
permeable to sound, with one end of it
stopped, the return of the breath can be felt
at the mouth, but not the sound: the reason is
that the preservation of the original sound by
the obstruction does nothing for the preservation
of the reflected sound; moreover, the generation
of echoes, except from clear sounds, is altogether
rare. Hence, the compression of air in a
narrow cavity removes all hope of an artificial
echo. However, it is established by experiments
that if someone leaning over a well 25 cubits
deep speaks softly, yet not so softly as to be a
whisper, a sufficiently perceptible Echo is
returned from the water. Let it be

Whether Echo also produces this (that is, whether someone standing to the side of the reflecting body hears better, or indeed where the voice is uttered, or anywhere in a straight line) could be tested; likewise if one stands closer to the place of reflection than the speaker, or vice versa. At the same time, it would become known whether Echo, like the original and primary sound, is stronger nearby.

Various experiments concerning the agreement and disagreement between those things which are perceived by sight and hearing.

255. Both spread themselves circularly, and fill a complete orb, but not beyond certain and determined limits of progress; they languish and gradually die out according to the proportionate distance of objects from the sensory organs.

256. Both sustain an entire and undiminished species/form, and insinuate themselves into any minute parts of the air and the medium; and just as species/images introduce themselves unconfused into narrow cracks and pass through, as is evident, in the pointer of a balance instrument as regards sight; and in fissures and cracks as regards sounds.

257. The sudden and easy generation and propagation of both, with equal speed of vanishing, namely, when light is removed, and bodies emitting sound (are removed).

258. Both receive and carry with them exquisite and accurate differences, such as colors, figures, motions, distances in visible things; and the tones of articulate voices, songs, vibrations in audible things.

259. Both seem to pour forth nothing of a corporeal effluvium into the medium, by which it might complete the sphere of its activity, nor evidently...

--- Page 204 ---
164      OF FRANCIS BACON
evidently to impress local motion on the medium through which it passes, but merely to carry away spiritual propagations with itself. Since the industry of investigators has not hitherto fully applied itself to the cause of this matter, it will merit examination in its proper place.

260. Both appear generative of no effect, except that which is appropriated to their object and sense; and, except for that, the rest seems sterile.

261. But both, by their proper action, manifestly produce three effects; the first of which is that a species more (so to speak) quantitative and of greater impression may subdue the smaller and weaker one, as the light of the sun (subdues) the light of a glow-worm, the roar of a war engine (subdues) a voice. The second, that any object in excess and overpowering may destroy the sense, as the light of the sun (destroys) the eye, a violent sound near the ear (destroys) hearing. The third, that both admit repercussion, as in mirrors, and Echo.

262. Neither destroys or impedes the species of the other, although meeting in the same medium, just as light or color does not remove sound, or vice versa.

263. Both affect living beings with objects moving the senses in diverse ways, according as they may be pleasing or displeasing; which, however,

_Various Experiments concerning the Spiritual and Subtle Nature of Sounds._

**287.** The repercussion of sounds (called Echo) strongly demonstrates the spiritual essence of sound. For if it were corporeal, the generation of the secondary sound or repercussion would be the same, as regards the manner and instruments, as that of the primary. But the pronunciation of words requires various and exquisite instruments, which no structure of a similar kind recognizes their return; but a mere impediment, whence repercussion.

291. The dissolutions of metals exhibit [*a*] vivid and pure colors; gold excellently yellow, Mercury exceedingly green, tin intensely blue. The same is observed in their putrefactions or rust, such as minium, green color, Bise, cirrus, etc., as well as in vitrifications; the reason is that their hardness, whether enduring fire or strong waters, allows them to be held in an equal position; they also retain a part of the principal spirit; which two, namely, an equal position and an agile spirit, hold the chief place so that bright colors may be rendered.

*A solitary experiment concerning the diverse operations of fire and time.*

295. Some things, having undergone fire, first
soften, then harden, like the crumb of
bread; some things fire hardens, then afterwards softens,
like the crust of bread, biscuit, sweet-
meats, salt, &c. The reason is, that in those things which
are hardened by time, the operation of fire is a
kind of liquefaction. But in those things
which are softened by time, the operation of fire
is a kind of cooking, and time in some way
dissolves all things cooked by fire.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
            *contagious diseases.*

   297. Some diseases harm by transition, others do not; those (that do) especially attack the spirits, nor do they so much have their seat in the humors, whence they are transmitted from body to body, such as pestilential diseases, eye inflammations, and similar ones. Secondly, they also infect the soul with a manifest migration from body to body, for they do not escape sight, unlike those which affect the spirits. In this kind is consumption of the lungs, etc. Thirdly, they also penetrate into the skin, in which they manifest themselves, the contagion being transferred into the air, or an adjacent body; especially those whose (skin is) somewhat fatty, nor

Such are poison, the French disease, and the bite of a mad dog.

   *A solitary experiment concerning*
      *the incorporation of powders &*
               *liquids.*

   298. You will see that most powders cohere more tightly when water is mixed in than when oil is, although the latter is a thicker body, such as flour, etc. The reason lies in the compatibility of bodies, which, the greater it is, makes for more perfect imbibition and incorporation. And this compatibility in most powders is greater with water than with oil: however, painters' colors and ashes are better incorporated with oil.

   *A solitary experiment concerning*
          *bodily exercise.*

   299. Frequent movement and exercise are beneficial to some bodies, to others rest or gentler movement. To a warm body, and one that does not abound in humors, excessive agitation brings harm; and in this, physicians err...

--- Page 224 ---
184          OF FRANCIS BACON
physicians, in that they encourage men of such a bodily habit
to exercises, which will be harmful to them,
especially those living on a stricter diet. But as
exercises increase, a fuller diet should correspond;
for those more sparing in food, such should also be the
exercise; whose advantages are these: First, that it
transmits nourishment more to the parts to be nourished;
then, through sweats, it facilitates excretion, whence
a more perfect assimilation in the parts; third, that it
renders the body more solid and more compact, and less
subject to predatory spirits. The contrary evils are: that
it inflames the spirits, makes them predatory; that it
absorbs and too much attenuates the body's humidity;
that it shakes the internal parts too much, especially
violent exercise, which (the internal parts) rather enjoy quiet.
In general, if exercise is excessive, it is adverse to the
prolongation of life; whence women are longer-lived
than men, because they move less.

   *Solitary Experiment concerning*
      *foods which induce satiety.*

   300. With certain foods one may use often and for a long
time without satiety, such as bread, meat not
fatty or putrid, etc. Certain ones, though
pleasant, accelerate satiety, such as sweet
and fatty foods, etc. The reason is, because the empty
or astringent mouth of the stomach excites appetite,

inasmuch as it is cold and dry. But sweet and fatty foods satiate more, and cling more around the opening of the stomach and fluctuate, nor do they descend as quickly, and they are more easily changed into bile, which is hot and always destroys appetite. Another cause of disgust lies in frequent use, since appetite is stimulated by new things, and therefore foods too often repeated produce nausea. If anyone moreover wished to give causes of satiety, pleasantness, novelty, and not only distinguish foods and drinks, but also movements, loves, companionships, pleasures, studies, which we enjoy from habit, or which we dislike, he would enter a very ample field of inquiry. But as for foods, the cause is attraction, which is swifter, and is more stimulated towards new things, than towards those whose lingering taste from previous use has not yet, as it were, vanished from the judgment of the palate. And in general this is the reason, that custom reconciles us to those things which were unpleasant in the beginning, and vice versa; but things pleasing at the beginning of use suddenly produce nausea.

Various experiments concerning the clari-
fication of liquids, and the acceleration
thereof.

[Decorative initial V]To anticipate by artifice the time of nature's operations in accelerating its effects is deservedly to be reckoned among the Great Works of Nature. Moreover, after the creation of matter from nothing, that, so to speak, anticipation of time holds the second place in relation to divinity. Therefore, our inquiry proceeds to explore these innermost secrets; setting aside for another place the acceleration of germination, for which we reserve a general treatise on Plants. Now we shall pursue accelerations concerning other matters.

301. Very many liquids, permeating the whole
body, at first appear turbid, exhibiting dregs,
such as must, beer not sufficiently boiled,
                                                                    or

--- Page 227 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. IV. 187
or the chyle of beer, expressed juices of fruits and herbs, etc. Waters, in the course of time, when they have settled, are allowed to clarify. To achieve this more quickly than usual is among those things which commend themselves most by their own importance. For by applying stimuli, we urge nature on, into whose order we thus rush, perverting it. That thing also has the best use in drink, and in the speedy preparation of potable things and condiments, and other things pertaining to the same. But it is necessary to set forth the producing causes of clarification before understanding the aids that promote it. Separation provides the first cause, by which the somewhat thicker parts of the liquid are separated from the thinner ones. The second (cause is) the equal distribution of spirits in liquids with the tangible parts; which itself also by itself is effective in rendering bodies non-turbid. The third (cause is) the attenuation of the spirits themselves, whence transparency is brought about for the liquid.

302. Separation is accomplished by weight, as we observe in the obvious sediment of liquids; (also by) heat, motion, precipitation or sublimation (that is, the propulsion of various parts upwards and downwards, a kind of attraction); adhesion, as when a more viscous body mixed with a liquid is agitated,

--- Page 228 ---
188 FRANCIS BACON
is stirred, which afterwards, being separated, contracts the thicker parts; finally, percolation.

303. Equal distribution of spirits is achieved by moderate heat, and motion (the time for which these operations are performed by way of anticipation is not specified), and the mixture of another body, which has the power of opening the liquid, and renders the spirits capable of permeating.

304. The attenuation of spirits is also accomplished by heat, motion, and a body mixed in, endowed with the faculty of attenuating. Now, however, after the causes have been explained, so that the acceleration of clarification to be instituted may proceed generally, attention must be paid to these instances and experiments.

305. It is obvious, by drawing off, to free wine or beer from dregs, so that they may more quickly obtain clarity. For dregs, although they are useful for preserving the strength of the drink and for warding off corruption longer, nevertheless they likewise produce something thick. And this instance relates to separation.

306. On the contrary, I do not consider it a useless experiment, what dregs, not native to a liquid, contribute; which, although generally they disturb liquids, nevertheless attenuate spirits. A solitary experiment concerning
the making of gold.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Hitherto, the hope of making gold has shamefully deluded the world,
which I determine not to be vain, nor to exceed the narrow limits of human
faculty. But the means destined for that effect suffer from deceptions
and errors as regards practice, and from concepts embracing nothing
sound as regards theory. For the claims that nature is said to intend
the conversion of all metals into gold, and would not deviate from this
goal if freed from bonds and impediments; and that metals, once
crudities and impurities are purged and roughness removed, would turn
into gold; and that a moderate quantity of the Medicine injected into
base metals would suffice to change a great number into gold and
multiply them – these are mere dreams; and the remaining foundations
of Alchemy are consistent with them. In order that this fable may be
speciously adorned, Alchemists call to their aid many vanities from
Astrology, and have other subsidiary aids from natural magic, from
superstitious interpretations of scripture, auricular traditions, fabricated
testimonies of the ancients, and other things of this kind. On the
other hand, it cannot be denied that not a few good

--- Page 239 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. IV. 199
...experiments of produce, and a certain
restoration of the world. But we, indeed, about to discuss the transmutations of bodies
and experiments pertaining to metals, will show true and nature's well-worn paths, and certain guiding traces, from which light may shine forth upon such a notable work. We praise the industry of the Chinese, who, having despaired of the making of gold, toil hard in preparing silver, diligent even to madness. For that former (gold), certainly the heaviest and among metals most materialized, has difficulties not easily explained, such as you would not find in others that least equal the weight and matter of gold; and it would be an easier task to prepare silver from lead or mercury, even though they exceed the weight of silver, since rather a greater degree of fixation is required than any condensation. Meanwhile, while we encounter axioms pertaining to maturation, we will provide a demonstration for maturing metals by a method of exchange, by which some of them may turn into gold. For thus I am persuaded that if metals have been properly boiled, digested, and matured, easy paths for producing gold lie open. And here it occurs to me that a German became known to me, whom, by his boasted knowledge of preparing gold, more closely to a distinguished man and an intimate familiar—

   *Various experiments concerning the pro-
      duction and acceleration of
            putrefaction.*
   To overcome the impediments to the maturation of putrefaction has something most worthy of universal and very widely diffused inquiry, since corruption, conversely, corresponds to generation, and those two are like terms circumscribing operating nature, and boundaries within which it entirely encloses itself; a twin guide to life and death.
   Putrefaction is the action of spirits who attempt departure from the body, so that, dispersed into the air, they may enjoy the free Sun.
   That attempt of the spirits to gather into the body of the air (which makes a step of egress) has five indications of different effects.
   If a more vehement motion solicits the spirits detained in the body, colliquation follows, as in metals, etc.; if a milder one, digestion or maturation, as in drink and fruits.
   If the spirits are not completely detained, but are moderately pushed forth by a confused and disorderly motion,

But if that motion proceeds in a certain order, it is vivification and figuration, as animated beings generated from putrefaction teach, and those of that kind which are more perfect. If an exit is open to the departing spirits, desiccation, induration, consumption, etc., follow, as bricks show, and the evaporation of a liquid body.

329. The aids which contain the causes of putrefaction and accelerate it are what the following context explains. First, if a raw or watery humor is added, as evidenced by the moistening of any flesh, apple, wood in water, etc., since preservation is due to somewhat oily and fatty substances.

   *Various Experiments concerning the pro-*
      *hibition & anticipation of putre-*
               *faction.*

   Those things by which putrefaction is warded off, and by which we preserve the integrity of bodies, have a most worthy use in inquiry. These bodies are subject to a twofold danger of dissolution, namely, desiccation or consumption, and putrefaction. Moreover, this [putrefaction], in human bodies and other living things (through fevers, worms, pulmonary phthisis, apostemes, ulcers both internal and external), occupies the greater part of the books of Physicians and Surgeons. Therefore, we assign those things constituting this inquiry to a special title, which will range through medical experiments of every kind. To the others we assign this place, to which the preceding [discussions] can shed light, where we treated of accelerating putrefaction by artificial means. For by removing the causes of putrefaction, putrefaction itself is excluded.
   341. The first thing that wards off putrefaction is cold, since food and drink remain uncorrupted longer in winter than in summer. Flowers also and fruits
                                             in snow

--- Page 249 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. IV. 209
...in snow conservatories preserve their vigor unimpaired; the volatile spirits, namely, being held back, and the tangible parts compacted.

342. Secondly, astringency, which resists dissolution, since astringent medicines generally prevent putrefaction. The same principle of astringency causes a small quantity of oil of vitriol to prevent water from putrefying. This astringency inheres in the substance, whose virtual cold it is, and which operates almost in the same way as cold.

343. Thirdly, the exclusion of air, and its admission, which, though naturally tending in opposite directions, are nevertheless the cause of the same effect (as often happens), depending on the condition of the material in question. Thus, wine or beer from accurately closed bottles acquire a certain durability. Underground granaries preserve grain longer than above-ground ones. Fruits enclosed in wax do not lose their freshness; bodies immersed in honey or flour remain fresh; and liquids of drinks and juices, with oil poured over their surface, do not cease to be fresh. Conversely, in clothes not exposed to air, moths are bred and they become moldy. The reason for the difference is that the exclusion of air, where there is a need for the retention of spirits, for bodies

--- Page 250 ---
210        FRANCIS BACON
to bodies it grants that they remain whole, which drink and grain prove; but where the emission of spirits is required by expelling the humor which is superfluous, those bodies which need to be exposed to air feel harm.
    344. Fourth, motion and agitation are adverse to putrefaction, which requires rest. For the subtle and imperceptible motion, which causes putrefaction, is disturbed by agitation, and local motion preserves bodies and their parts whole. Thus a granary, where grain is winnowed, or turned over, as in an hourglass from a higher place to a lower, prevents the problems of its initial good quality. Flowing water lacks putrefaction; which (putrefaction) the human body also expels with frequent exercises. On the contrary, rest, lack of motion, or obstructions (by which obstacles the flow of humors and the motion of perspiration are stopped) promote putrefaction, as we partly indicated a little earlier.

   *A solitary experiment concerning*
        *the acceleration of childbirth,*

353. Acceleration of childbirth in animals

*a] A Fortnight.*

--- Page 256 ---

353. The acceleration of birth in living creatures has a double aspect; if either maturity and hastened perfection are granted to the embryo, or some way of expediting from the maternal confines is given. In the first way, there is something not unpraiseworthy, which testifies to strength; the second is malignant, and moreover has a symptom or disease as its cause. Therefore, a true observation of the ancients is that a seven-month birth is usually vital, but an eight-month birth is for the most part fatal. But the reason assigned is fabulous, namely, that the eighth month begins the period of Saturn's reign, a planet, according to their fictions, malignant; but in the seventh month, the Moon reigns, a more benign planet. But from truth, this reason is given: if the birth anticipates the ordained time by such a long space, this is to be ascribed to the vigor of the infant; but if by a shorter [space], it is a defect of maternal weakness.

*Solitary Experiment concerning the acceleration of growth and stature.*

354. The increments of human stature are rapid, either from a fuller diet, or from the nature of the nourishment, or from a more vigorous and excited heat, which nature confers. Regarding the former, excess in food is harmful, inasmuch as it rather distends the body and into breadth,

--- Page 257 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. IV. 217
rather than in length, as it progresses. Of which thing there is an analogy in plants, which rarely attain height when, while tender, they begin to spread out widely. As for the nature of the nourishment, let it not be too dry, because infants fed with milk, in regions where its use is frequent, surpass in height those for whom nourishment from bread and meat is more frequent. It is also a common saying that [a] daisy roots boiled in milk (which have a remarkable drying faculty) make dogs small. Nor is it disputed that too dry food causes a retardation of stature. Furthermore, let the food be potent in its opening power, whereby the humors are thinned, and the spirits are promoted upwards. Nor is it without reason that Xenophon so highly commends the use of cardamom in educating Persian infants, as it contributes to growth and a more agile bodily constitution. Cardamom is called nasturtium in Latin, which herb, when it is tender, is pleasant for eating. The excitation of native heat occurs especially through exercises, so that consequently in frequented schools the sedentary life of boys detracts from their growth, while country people, not sent to similar gymnasia, are generally of a better stature. *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*Chameleons.*

360. The chameleon is almost the size of a common lizard, with a head not proportionate to its size, and huge eyes. It moves its head with its neck unmoved, I know not how it bends, as happens with pigs. Its back is curved, its skin sprinkled with tubercles, less prominent towards the abdomen. Its tail is slender and

(these things are fabricated from dreams of sympathy) since,
because it feeds on air, it is believed to possess great power
to generate an impression in the air itself.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*subterranean fires.*

361. Someone among the ancients relates that in a certain region of Media, flames erupt from the plain, which are pure, and he denies that they are enveloped by a quantity of belched smoke, ashes, or pumice, such as mountain caverns vomit forth. The definite reason is that there is no compression for the flames, as in mountains, or in earthquakes that become fiery and eject flames. And blind fires emerge, unaware of how to flame, and finally bursting forth when oil is poured on them. The reason is that the fire seems to be so suffocated that it cannot remove a stone, and it is heat rather than flame, yet sufficient for igniting oil.

*nitre.*

362. It is recorded that water in some lakes is found to be so nitrous that clothes thrown into it are spontaneously cleansed of adhering dirt, but if kept there longer, they are reduced to ashes.

*Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the congelation of air.*

363. Take the largest bladder you can,
fill it with air, tie it around the neck
with a waxed silk thread, and moreover
seal it very tightly with a thick wax stopper,
so that even if the neck of the bladder dries out,
air is prevented from entering and exiting. Then
bury it four or five feet deep in the earth,
in a vault or snow-house, so that snow is
excavated around the bladder. After the space
of fourteen days, see if it has contracted. If
this happens, it appears from the surrounding
cold of the earth or snow that the air has
condensed and become more like water. The
significance of this experiment is wide-ranging.

*Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the congelation of water into crystal.*

364. It is reliably reported that in inner
caverns, hanging crystal is found, and that a

onto it. In some others, but more rarely,
it is said to originate from below. Although cold-

Nor do these serve merely for illumination, but they prove themselves useful and convenient; for these lights bring great advantage to economy, if they could be prepared so that in light and beauty they might contend with others, and in duration they might even excel. 375. The fifth way of aiding duration is in the nature of the air in which the candle burns, whether it is hot or cold, humid or dry. Be that as it may, it at least creates a weaker light, and for that reason, an aid to continuation is supplied.

*Various experiments concerning burials and infusions of various bodies under the earth.*

376. Burials under the earth provide no small use for the preservation, densification, and hardening of bodies. That method of burying which does not prevent contact with the earth serves for densification and hardening; and it is customarily applied to the art of preparing porcelain vessels, etc. Nor dissimilar

--- Page 274 ---
**FRANCIS BACON**

Nor is the method dissimilar in preserving hard and solid bodies, such as clay, wood, etc. But if you aim for bodies to soften and become tender by being preserved, then the other of these methods must be tried: that, stored in cases, they cannot touch the earth, or that, built into an arched structure, the earth may hang over them without touching them. If this happens, putrefaction will follow from humidity rather than their being preserved by the cold virtue of the earth insinuating itself, unless the earth is both extremely dry and sandy.

377. An orange, a lemon, and a common apple, wrapped in linen and buried under the earth for a space of 14 days, at a depth of four feet, in a place however humid and with a rainy sky, we took out uncorrupted and not moldy, but which had hardened a little more than usual, with their color otherwise fresh, but with a withered taste. Kept there beyond the said period of time, they showed the beginning of putrefaction.

378. Of beer buried in a full bottle, as before [*a*], the taste was good, more lively and clear. The same happened to a bottle containing wine, and also of vinegar, similarly buried in a bottle, there was greater liveliness and fragrance, with a taste almost resembling violets. After a full month, those three from their hidden place—

379. That would be a fruitful experiment, if oranges, lemons, and pomegranates could be preserved until summer, at which time they would be of any price. And in general I establish, that he who is about to devote himself to exploring the effects of cold, needs three aids: a snow-pit or snow-chest, an arched underground space twenty feet deep, and also a deep well.

380. They say that gems, corals, and jasper recover lost color underground. Truly of wonderful benefit, if the success corresponds. *A solitary experiment concerning the af-*

to movement, producing an effect contrary to the North wind. The reason is, because the former wind renders the humors as if liquid and fluid, so that the parts, by lying upon [each other], become heavy, which wood and other things teach us; these the South wind makes swell. Moreover, the movement and agility of the body principally consist in the nerves, which the South wind relaxes more.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
        *summer and winter diseases.*

   382. It is commonly known that more people fall ill in summer, and more die in winter; unless a plague is raging, which usually invades in summer or autumn. The reason is, because heat, for the most part, gives origin to diseases, which are mostly cured by sweats and purges, the summer season contributing to this; they are more easily provoked, and as for pestilential diseases, the reason why most people die in summer is this: because that season of the year is most fertile for generating them. Otherwise, for those seized by such a plague in winter, the fear of immediate danger is not lacking.

...and humid [years/conditions] are generally present, from which the generation of plague is suspected, by this weak argument, that putrefaction originates from heat and humidity. In England, this belief struggles, since that plague reigned with great destruction through many summers notable for dryness; the reason perhaps is, that dryness in the bodies of islanders, accustomed to humid air, exasperates the humors, and inclines more to putrefaction or inflammation. Moreover, it generally infects waters and renders them less wholesome. Add to this, that in Mauritania plagues rage in the summer months, with a hot and dry climate.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning a popular error about Epidemic diseases.*

384. For many diseases, both Epidemic and others, there is its own and proper time for manifesting. This is falsely attributed to the constitution of the air at that time, since the cause lies hidden in the circuit and series of preceding time, which unfolds into the present and connects the seasons of the year. Therefore Hippocrates in his prognostics has good observations of diseases, which testify to the nature of past time.

A solitary experiment regarding
[a] Hesitation.

386. It is known that many are stutterers. The cause may perhaps be a cooling of the tongue, from which comes a slowness of natural movement. And therefore we observe that delirious people usually stutter, and stutterers also, after drinking a moderate amount of wine, stutter less, because it warms them up. Nor are we unaware that stutterers stumble more with hesitation at the beginning of a speech than in its progress, the tongue, of course, warming up little by little through movement. In some, however, the cause may perhaps have been (though rarely) dryness of the tongue, an equal impediment to movement, along with coldness, a frequent affliction for wise and illustrious men, such as Moses, a man of impeded tongue. Very many stutterers are found to be very choleric, with cholera inducing dryness of the tongue.

Various Experiments concerning odors.

389. The fragrance of odors is greater in free air and from a moderate distance than if they are brought to the nose, as previous [experiments] have shown elsewhere; the reason is twofold: first, a more subtle mixture or incorporation of the odor. Thus, sounds are most pleasing to the ears if any part, being distinct and separate, does not strike the sense. Second, because all fragrance consists of and is carried by crude and earthy odors mixed in. From distance, a sweetness is achieved, which comes from a greater spirituality, carrying away whatever earthy [matter] accompanied it.

388. Crushing reduces the latent sweetness of odor in dry substances to maximum vigor. Thus, pricked orange and lemon peels render them more fragrant. In general, motion and agitation elicit fragrance from bodies, even uncrushed ones, as with a scented sachet if it is shaken. The reason is twofold: first, a more copious effluvium of spirits, facilitated by crushing, pricking, compression, and to some extent, by motion, in their egress; the second includes another, namely the impulse of air, hence a directed vehicle of odor.

389. Plants whose flowers produce the greatest delights of odors, but whose [plants themselves are] entirely
                                             odorless

Such [water] is usually supplied by large rivers accustomed to navigation, and also by large and pure lakes; the efficacy of the sun reigning more here, than in the sources and narrower rivers. I would assign the next place of goodness after this to chalky water, for preparing drink from it. It also benefits digestion if it is drawn from a deep well, namely, for removing the crudities of the water. But chalky water near the surface of the earth is too corrosive, as appears in the washing of clothes, which the use of such water gradually eats away.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the dark color in Ethiopians.*

399. The heat of the Sun dyes men in certain places with a blackish color, as in Ethiopia, Guinea, etc. That this is not an effect of fire, glass-makers show, being continually occupied at the fire. The reason perhaps is that fire acts upon the spirits and blood, so that they exhale, and thus renders men pale and somewhat dark. But the more benign heat of the Sun draws the blood only to the outermost parts of the body, and rather digests it than melts it away. Hence all Ethiopians are of a fleshy indeed, but ill-proportioned bodily habit, and with thick lips, which indicate moisture retained, not drawn out. We also see them born in regions abounding in water because of rivers and other causes. For Meroë, the metropolis of Ethiopia

*A solitary experiment concerning movement*
*in the very few moments after death.*

400. Some animals, when decapitated, move for some time,

worms, flies, etc. Firstly, therefore, it is established
that the immediate cause of death is the dis-
solution or extinction of the spirits, the destruction
or corruption of the organs being mediate.
However, some organs are so absolutely
necessary that their destruction is immediately
followed by the extinction of the spirits, with the
intervention of the shortest possible time. Some
of the ancients, a classical writer, neither suspec-

Of similar authority is this account: that with the head of a piglet opened, the brain, removed and placed on someone's palm, palpitated, with no part of the brain injured and without separation from the spinal cord. During this entire interval of time, the piglet appeared dead and was deprived of all movement. A little later, with the brain replaced in its spot and the piglet's skull closed, it walked about a little. Nor is it unknown that an eye, gouged out by the law of retaliation, hung for some time from the optic nerve, deprived of the power of seeing during that time, but a little later, by restoration, the act of seeing returned. Therefore, the spirits are contained primarily in the head and the ventricles of the brain, which both man and beast have large and capacious, with the result that when the head is dissected, they move little or absolutely not at all. But the heads of birds are very small, and therefore the spirits are more dispersed through the nerves, whence movement in them is a little more prolonged. So much so that histories have recorded that a Roman Emperor, for the purpose of showing his skill in shooting, aimed a huge forked arrow at an Ostrich while it was crossing the Theater at a swift run, and took off its head, and with the head removed, nevertheless

416. Fourth, to bare the roots around the Lord's nativity for several days. The reason is clear, because for some time the ascent of sap is prevented, and the restraint being removed afterwards, if the root is covered by earth thrown over it, the ascent of sap follows, but slower.

417. Fifth, to take the tree out of the earth for several months before it puts forth buds. The reason is, because after removal, time is required before, returned to the earth, it draws sap, which, while it elapses, delays the flowers that are about to emerge.

These experiments in as many ways should be transferred to other things, both trees and flowers, with the necessary changes.

421. Some people hold a plausible
opinion, namely, that if you graft a late-ripening fruit onto the trunk of an early-ripening tree, the fruit will ripen earlier; as if a peach is grafted onto a cherry tree, and conversely, if a notable early-ripening stock is grafted onto a stock that ripens later, the adopted scion will exhibit its native character, as if a cherry is grafted onto a peach tree. But the authors of this opinion are deceived by vain imaginings. The reason is that the scions have dominance over the stock, which behaves passively, providing neither nourishment nor impetus to the scion.

*Various experiments concerning the ripening*
*of fruits in trees and plants.*

Now we will proceed to show how to impart to fruits, flowers, and roots the bounty of increased yield, and a sweetness beyond the usual, and how to procure for trees height, size, and, beyond the character observed in practice, a hastened precocity. To this inquiry, undoubtedly, much significance will be added from the preceding experiments on accelerating ripening, and the treatise which we have at hand will provide mutual illustration in return for the former, both effects being referred to the increase of vigor in the tree.

--- Page 300 ---

growth, but so that, avoiding the danger of confusion, each thing might be given its due, where reasons are more appropriate to one effect and less so to another, they had to be treated separately.
    422. It has been proven by experience that ferns or stones piled up at the roots of a wild tree (such as oak, elm, ash, etc.) when it is first planted, cause the speed of its usual growth to be doubled. The reason is, because they prevent the moisture, which comes to the tree from above, from flowing away, nor do they allow it to evaporate from the incident heat of the sun. Furthermore, they protect the tree's warmth, and ward off cold winds and frost, as if by an interposed shelter. Perhaps also its continuous retention from the very beginning contributes something to this. It should be investigated whether straw placed around the body of the tree to a certain height increases the speed. Although the root is the dispenser of sap, yet it is drawn to be distributed throughout the whole body. But _it should be noted_, that if stones are applied to the stem of a lettuce or other softer plant, it is suffocated by too much moisture, so that it is corroded by worms.

433. A more abundant yield from a tree is produced not only by grafting onto tender stocks, but also by grafting onto various branches of an old tree, which offers a sure hope of great fertility; this hope, however, diminishes when grafting onto only a single stock.

434. Nowhere hitherto has the annual digging around the roots come into use; yet it is destined to be of great importance for making the fruit both early and better. It has only been applied to vines, but if it were frequently practiced on other trees and shrubs (like roses, etc.), it would add speed to their maturity, as I indeed conceive the matter.

435. It is established that a fruit-bearing tree, whose roots have been greatly loosened (or dug around) and then re-established, has greatly increased the yield of the following year. No other reason can be given except the loosening of the earth, which is beneficial to the tree. This benefit can conveniently be derived in other plants, outside of fruit-bearing trees, since their transplantation into new soil is more difficult than that of flowers and herbs.

**Various Experiments concerning the compo-**
**sition of fruits and flowers.**

In living things that distinguish sexes, we observe various outcomes from various matings, and as it were a certain composition in creatures. Thus a mule is generated from a horse and a she-ass; and other changes of species occur, which are called monsters, but are rarer. Also that proverb, *Africa always produces something monstrous*, is not thought to have flowed from any other origin than that the scarcity of spring water in a parched region gathers various beasts from all sides to a watering place, which, having quenched their thirst and being refreshed, very frequently mix with a species not their own. The variety of composition and mating in plant genera has not yet been thoroughly investigated by experiments, which, however, if it can be attempted, is more subject to our control than that of animals, with their creeping itch of pleasure and spontaneous movement rushing into mating. Therefore, it will be a most noble pursuit if such a composition of plants can be achieved, inasmuch as it promises diverse and new names for fruits and unknown flowers. Grafting (inoculation) does nothing for this purpose, merely improving fruit and doubling flowers, etc., but it is ineffective for generating a new species, as the scions predominate over the stock.

*Various experiments concerning the sym- pathy and antipathy of plants.*

Many traditions and observations from deep antiquity have flowed down to us, accepted by public belief, concerning the sympathy and antipathy of plants; namely, that some rejoice in the vicinity of others, becoming more vigorous from sympathy, while others flee, faring poorly from antipathy. But these concepts betray ignorance, falling short of a true knowledge of causes, as many experiments concerning sympathy and antipathy teach. In plants there is no such agreement from friendship or disagreement from enmity as people invent for themselves with vain imagination, and which they designate with the utterly erroneous nomenclature of sympathy and antipathy. On the contrary, here all things happen, with sympathy declining into antipathy, and vice versa, when in this manner

--- Page 325 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. V. 285
it happens. If a plant draws its own sap, [a] as it qualifieth the Earth, so that what is left behind, separated from the former, is unsuitable for another plant, proximity is beneficial, because of the contrary [nature] and not [the need for] nourishment of the same kind. But if, however, two plants are nourished by the same sufficiently copious sap, proximity is harmful, one defrauding the other.

480. Therefore, any plant whatsoever that feeds largely from the earth, and so [b] soaks the Earth, exhausting it, harms all placed near it; such as large trees (especially the ash) and all those which send roots not far from the earth's surface. Thus, between the cabbage and the vine there is not only discord, though not unknown to the ancients, but also this [cabbage] agrees poorly with other trees, inasmuch as it preys upon the richest saps of the earth as much as possible. And, if it be true, that the vine, creeping near the cabbage, turns its path elsewhere, the cause could be the worse nourishment it encounters; and although the root may be in the same place with it, nevertheless (I doubt it nonetheless) the plant to be nourished will turn itself away.

481. Plants not of one nature, and to be nourished by different sap, rejoice in friendly conjunction.

a] as it qualifieth the Earth.
b] soake the Earth.

they thrive, as we have said; and many of the ancients write that rue, placed near a fig, grows very successfully and is rendered more efficacious. This happens, as I believe, not from agreement, but from the extraction of a contrary sap, which one draws out to sweeten itself, the other to become bitter. From their account also we have, that a Rose is rendered more pleasing by the vicinity of garlic, or even for this reason, that the more fetid sap enters the garlic, and the more fragrant sap enters the rose.

      482. It is also manifest that flowers grow among grain, which, when planted, very rarely or never arise elsewhere, except in the place we have mentioned; such as the cornflower (blaveolus), a species of yellow marigold (calendula), wild poppy, and fumitory. Nor does cultivation of the soil achieve this by plowing or furrowing; just as certain herbs and flowers only grow in new ditches, which untouched and unplanted earth would not produce with spades; so much so that the grain seems to imbue the earth with a quality, and prepare it for those about to grow.

**486.** Intersperse cucumbers or gourds, as it were, sparsely among muskmelons, so that you may try whether the taste of the melons becomes more wine-like and more pleasant. Moreover, mix a cucumber with radishes planted around it, and observe whether it increases the pungency of the radishes.

493. Some ancient and modern writers from the school of natural magic have observed a sympathy between the Sun, Moon, and principal Stars, and herbs and plants. Hence, names derived from the Sun and Moon have arisen, and other things which, ostentatiously adorned from the storehouse of absurdities, they have sold. It is known that some herbs have a twofold relation to the Sun, so that they either open themselves or close, or bend or incline their head. For marigold, tulips, pimpernel, and most flowers expand their leaves at the splendor of the Sun; partly they contract at the approach of evening or at the sense of a cloudy sky. Nor should the reason be so pompously assigned, that they rejoice at the Sun's presence and are saddened by its absence, since closure is nothing other than the weighing down of the leaves and swelling around the lowest parts from moist air, which, when dry, extends them. And they consider it a kind of miracle that garden clover hides its stem when the Sun is shining, when it is only the fullest expansion of the leaves.

A question is put forward as a pretext for impostures that are to be handled more cautiously, for example, 'Which woman in this assembly is of outstanding beauty?' or 'Who hides a glove or playing cards?' Meanwhile, another person is ordered to recite various names, and at the naming of each person, the cross is fixed in the box, having first been applied to the mouth, as if for the sake of enchantment; yet it is not moved when they come to the person designated within themselves; while they apply the cross to the mouth, they touch the oat-beard with the tip of the tongue and moisten it, and thus the cross is fixed in the box. Afterwards, it is seen to turn gently and calmly four or five times, which arises from the unfolding of the oat-beard due to the moisture secretly applied. These things will be more evident if the cross is fixed between the fingers, instead of the box. Therefore it is clear that this movement from slight moistening is more effective than that contraction of leaves, or the inclination of the head in the marigold.

*Various experiments so that herbs and fruits may be adapted for medical uses.*

499. Vain and akin to fictions are the tales told about altering the smell, color, taste of fruits by infusion, mixture, or grafting into the bark or root of a tree, flower, or herb, whose substance, imbued with this or that color, might be aromatic or medicinal; the reason being that all these things have completed their period and do not nourish, and any such alteration of qualities in vegetables must necessarily arise from that which can contribute to the plant's nourishment. But it is true that if cows are fed on wild garlic, the milk is permeated with the taste of garlic. Sheep meat also is more pleasing to the taste if the sheep is fed on wild thyme and other very healthy herbs. Galen mentions cow's milk in the cure of scirrhus of the liver, when the animal's food consisted solely of certain herbs. Spanish honey almost smells of Rosemary or Orange, from where the bee collects it. From the ancients came that story about a girl nourished by Aconite (than which, among all vegetables, a more potent
                                                              more

a] Exp. 462.

--- Page 335 ---
magis venenum non eſt) and continuous use had rendered it harmless to her, while it killed others who partook of it. Others have observed that Bezoar is found to be both potent and of no efficacy, a disparity also discernible by sight; and that one kind is collected from animals accustomed to graze in the mountains, where there are theriac (antidotal) herbs; the other, ineffective of course, from those whose pasture is in the valleys, where such herbs are not found. Hitherto I am of the opinion that just as maceration renders wines and beers medicinal, and moreover, a certain tempering of powders imbues bread; so too can foods (meat, fish, milk, eggs) be reduced to the role of medicine and a dietary aid, if the animal, bird, or fish is fed with things chosen for this purpose and suitable for the disease. However, the matter would not be without danger in secret poisonings. But doubts prevent asserting that these things can be referred to plants and herbs, inasmuch as their sap, their nourishment, being more common, reluctantly admits a quality not assimilated by the plant.

500. But lest the prejudice of incredulity hinder most useful experiments (especially since many of the ancients have committed them to writing), we have deemed it worthwhile to briefly propose four methods from their invention, so that plants may become medicinal.

Thus it is likewise evident that the whitish flowers of trees are for the most part odorless, such as those of the cherry, pear, plum, and the flowers of the cultivated and wild apple; while those of the almond and peach are reddish and fragrant. The reason is, because the substance of the flower is from that which is most delicate and purest in the plant, whence, painted with such pleasing color, it shines. If that (substance) is too sparse and meager, an ineffective odor will languish, except in very succulent plants; so that a diminution of nourishment is required rather than an augmentation, if one strives to achieve fragrance. This is observed in the white satyrion, or white orchids, of a very delicate odor, and in the flowers of peas. *Various experiments concerning the degene-*
*ration of plants and the transmu-*
*tation of one into another.*

518. It has been frequently proven by experience that plants degenerating from lack of cultivation become worthless within the same species; sometimes to such an extent that a change of species follows. To this contribute: 1. A long stay in the same place, not frequently changed. 2. Dryness, unless the inherent moisture of the earth suffices. 3. Transplantation, and removal, as it were, to a more malignant colony, or the omission of those things which pertain to the composition of the soil. Thus, through neglect, curled mint is changed into garden mint, and cabbage into a turnip.
519. Any fruit grafted onto a root or shoot, if compared, will depart from its former nature. Grapes, figs, almonds, pomegranates, if planted from their stones, produce degenerate and wild fruits. Again, most fruits of the grafted kind, if you expect them from planted kernels or stones, you will see degenerate. It is true indeed that peaches (as previous sections have taught) grow more successfully from planted stones than if they are inoculated; but this exception from the rule

--- Page 349 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VI.      309
the rule is that any plant that delights in much moisture will promise better growth from a stone or kernel than if it is grafted. For although the nourishment from the stock is thinner, it provides less, while the earth nourishes more abundantly.

      520. Very old seeds, yet not entirely deprived of all vigor sufficient for a plant, usually degenerate. Hence industrious gardeners test the viability of seeds by placing them in gently bubbling water; which, within the space of an hour, if they are viable, will germinate.

      521. It is remarkable what they relate about basil, namely, that if it is exposed to too much sun, it turns into wild thyme; although those herbs acknowledge no natural affinity. But basil is a very hot plant, with rich and succulent leaves. If this oily nature is drawn out by the stimulating sun, it seems probable that a change will arise from it.

among the miracles of nature; since among the pronouncements of common philosophy it is said that it cannot happen; and
indeed the matter is one of no light labor and of scrutiny
probing the innermost recesses of nature. But
several instances drawn from experiments refute the opinion of impossibility, so that an examination of the causes may be undertaken. Living creatures generated from putrefaction, such as

argued that living creatures not born from seed
can change their species. For nature, which
intimately constitutes the seed, prevents the creature
from deviating, as if by injected bonds.
So that it may be concluded that, since the
earth produces plants without seed, a migration
of those plants from species to species can occur.
Therefore, since obvious instances are lacking,
we will endeavor to lay down a method of investigation,
through experiments that introduce probability. And generally
we ask all readers who approach this work of Sylva
Sylvarum, that they keep causes for wonder far away,
and not attribute to haste, as if crude impulses,
the fact that we here give place to particulars not
yet brought to the test of experiment. For
I hold the contrary opinion, namely, that such
particulars have that dignity

--- Page 352 ---

...dignity, by which they (the particulars) may surpass what has been attempted hitherto, and by which (through them) things may become thoroughly known; since these (particulars), from the latter category, as they are presented, should be admitted; while the former (established knowledge), by directing, may sharpen the investigation of causes and help the formation of axioms.

    526. Above all, it must be known that if you apply yourself to the transmutation of plants into one another, it is necessary that the nourishment should predominate over the seed; which in this experiment is required, being most contrary to the nature of the herb, yet so that the faculty of growing is not hindered. Let the seed also be very weak and of minimal vigor. Therefore, it would be advisable to plant marsh plants on hill ridges and in open places: which plants, on the contrary, delight in much moisture, (and thus) to expose them to the dryness of sandy soil; thus, let tree mallow and sedge be transferred to hills; cucumber, lettuce seed, and cabbage to a sandy plain; conversely, let thorn be planted; heather, white hellebore, and fern in a marshy place. I also establish that edible and garden herbs on hill ridges become more medicinal, yet less suitable for eating than before. Perhaps also, herbs which are wild by nature may be changed into salad plants. Let this be the first rule for transferring, as it were, substance into another.

527. The second method is to commit a small amount of the seed of that herb, whose intended conversion is to be achieved, to the earth mixed with other seeds, so that you may ascertain whether the sap of other seeds imbues the earth with such a quality from which the seed, towards which the intention of imitation is directed, may be altered. For example, let purslane seed be sown mixed with lettuce seed, or lettuce with purslane; or basil among thyme seed. Let a change in taste or anything else be observed. But you will do best if you wrap it in a small linen cloth, and exclude the foreign seed from that whose mutation you are preparing.
528. The third method is the preparation of the earth by mixing bruised or otherwise comminuted plants, whether in leaf or in root. For example, mix bruised cabbage leaves into the earth, into which plant cultivated thistles or parsnips. Likewise, into earth prepared with bruised marjoram, oregano, or wild thyme, cast fennel, etc. In this operation, the process of nature will be continuous (as I indeed believe), not because the herb to be changed will be nourished by the sap of the foreign one (for I rejected that in the preceding sections), but the matter will pass into a new [a] confection of compounded earth; from which perhaps the seed may be altered, without the species of the former herb persisting.

*Various experiments concerning the height, and the art of making dwarf trees.*

532. It is certain that cultivated trees in groves grow more upright, and with branches less luxuriant in their lower parts, than those which occupy fields. The reason is, because there is a natural movement in plants so that they may enjoy the Sun. Add to this that they are not saturated with too much nourishment, the wood drawing part of it to itself, repletion always being harmful to stature. Finally, they are kept warm, which is a great impetus for the height of plants.
533. Trees hottest by their nature (and their flammable gum shows their heat), such as fir and pine, are carried upwards by spontaneous growth until they have filled the summit, with no branches on the side detracting anything from this. The reason is partly in the heat, partly in the thinness of the sap,
O 2

--- Page 356 ---
316 FRANCIS BACON'S
both prerogatives transmitting sap upwards. Juniper is only a shrub, nor of such thickness that it can contribute to height.
	534. They report that good and strong hemp, spread over a tree nourishing low shoots, when it begins to put them forth, will make it dwarf and spread it out. The reason is manifest, because every plant proportions its extension to the capacity of the place.
	535. The matrix of trees from which they are born are either roots or a nucleus. If you place their shoots in the earth (as is permitted in some, especially by custom), some of them will germinate; but (as they say) the trees will be dwarf. The reason is, because a shoot does not draw nourishment as strongly as either a root or a nucleus.
	536. Every plant, quickly pushing forth sap, has a body not proportioned to its length, and therefore they are twisted or rambling, like ivy, bryony, hop, honeysuckle, whereas the art of making dwarf trees requires a slower pushing forth of branches, and a lesser impulse to ascend.

Various Experiments concerning the Rudiments and Excrescences of Plants, or
Superfetation [a] in Plants.

The Sacred Scriptures relate that Solomon wrote a natural history, from the cedar in Lebanon to the moss growing in the valley, as the best versions have it. And it is true that moss is only the rudiment of a plant, as if the mold of the earth or of bark.
537. Moss is produced especially by buildings covered with tiles or thatch, and by the extremities of walls, which present a clear and pleasing greenness. It grows on slopes, because just as water and moisture generate moss, so it desires flowing, not stagnant, water. The growth on walls or tiles is due to the dryness of the place; because its moisture is not sufficient for producing a plant, it germinates by pushing forth moss. Although if, softening due to age or other causes, they (the walls/tiles) disintegrate, they sometimes produce plants, such as wall-pellitory; and almost all moss has a tiny stem, besides the villi and fibers in the lower part.
538. Moss grows in walkways, especially those exposed to cold and facing north, as in various open arbors. Again, if they are frequently trampled,

*Various Experiments concerning Foreign Plants.*

574. It is reported that earth from the Indian climate and distant regions, exported for ballasting a ship to some Italian soil, produced exotic herbs, unknown to Europeans. Also, from their roots, barks, and seeds crushed together and mixed with other earth, and thoroughly irrigated with warm water, herbs not dissimilar to others arise.

575. Plants transplanted from warm regions and transported to others struggle in pushing out their shoots at the time proper to their own climate. Therefore, so that harm may be averted, nothing more is required than that they be safe against the harm of retardation from cold. It also stands on historical record that grains from warm soil, transferred to colder soil, surpass in precocity that common grain of colder land. It is likely that the success of the experiment will be better with grain than with trees, since grains are only annual, from which the virtue of the seed does not con-

   576. Many plants, which the air of a milder climate produces, having experienced the harshness of a more rigid climate, will nevertheless sprout at the end of spring, with the sprout remaining intact for the greater part of summer, as the seed of the orange, lemon, etc. shows. Their seeds, sown in the ground at the end of April, will yield most pleasing [a] salads, mixed with other herbs. Nor do I doubt that the seed of the clove, or pepper, etc., if it could be had green here at the time of sowing, would prove the same.

*Various Experiments concerning the Duration*
*of Herbs or Trees.*

583. Durability is most conspicuous in those
which have a very large body, such as
oaks, elms, chestnuts, [a] the lotus
tree, etc. But this applies to trees; for in
herbs the opposite often holds true: since
borage, cabbage, melons, though of quite large
bulk, are of short duration, and hyssop,
savory, germander, thyme, sage persist intact
for a long time. The reason is, because the vitality
of trees depends on the measure of their vigor and the quantity
of their sap, being otherwise sufficiently protected
by the circuit of their bark against injuries
from the air. Herbs, however, are nourished by languid
sap, armed with soft bark, and those which excel
in longer life have a pungent odor and a woody
stem.
584. Gland-bearing trees surpass fruit-bearing ones
in the prerogative of durability; especially
those whose fruits are more humid; such
as oak, beech, chestnut, walnut, almond,

   a] *the Loat-Tree.*

--- Page 377 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VI. 337
gdalus, pinus, &c. surpass in durability
apple, pear, plum, &c. The cause is
the fatness and oiliness of the sap, which
resists decay more than watery sap.
585. Trees which leaf out later,
and shed their leaves later, exceed in longevity
those for which leaves emerge sooner, and
fall. The cause is, because slower production
indicates a more fixed moisture, the other
a looser, and more easily dissolvable one: the
same reason holds, why wild trees
live longer than garden trees;
and in the same species, those with sour fruits,
than those with sweet ones.
586. Nothing is equally conducive
to prolonging the life of trees, shrubs, and
herbs as frequent pruning, which, as often
as it is repeated, renews the plant's sap so that
it does not luxuriate so widely spread out, nor
grow so languidly, than if it had lacked pruning;
so much so that plants accustomed to living a year, if

*Various experiments concerning various*
*figures of plants.*

588. We leave the particular figures of plants
to descriptions specifically occupied with
them, content generally with the observa-
tions instituted by some concerning these matters.
Trees and herbs in producing branches do not
have a definite shape, nor do they follow an order.
                                                            Cause

--- Page 379 ---
        SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VI.    339
The cause is, because the sap repressed in the bark does not burst forth at once (as in the bodies or trunks of trees or the stems of herbs) until they put forth branches; and when they burst forth, they emerge by chance, by whatever way is given in the bark. It is true that some emerge with more scattered branches, as is usual for the holly, winter pear, quince apple, medlar, citrus, some are tapered into a more exact pyramid and yet rise into a [a] boss, such as the pear (whose origin Critics derive from πῦρ, fire), orange tree, fir, service trees, lime trees, citron tree, some are more expanded, such as the beech, [b] female beech, etc. The rest behave more indifferently. The reason why they thus scatter their branches is the hurried eruption of sap, whence they do not produce a body of proper height, but with branches wandering about the ground. The cause of the pyramid shape is the repression of sap long before it sends out branches, and its consumption in an equal degree as soon as they emerge.
Dispers

...namely, in producing leaves; as being distinguished by joints and nodes, which are so many obstacles to growth, demanding stages for it to advance itself, such as the simple-flowered carnation, fennel, wheat, reeds, and canes. The cause is the unequal ascent of sap, so that it is as if retarded by obstacles in the way and stops. They also seem to harden with a more compactly formed stem, whence an impediment to the sap tending upwards, until it has collected itself into a node, from which it emerges more concentrated and is urged to produce. Hence most of them are hollow, with a dry stem, like fennel, straw, and reed.
