\*Various experiments concerning the principal differences of plants.\*

591. Few plants flower before they leaf out, such as almond, peach, dogwood, blackthorn, etc. but for most, leaves precede flowers, as shown by apple, pear, plum, cherry, hawthorn, etc. The cause, in those where flowers precede, is an acrid spirit (therefore they usually produce fruit earlier in spring, but whose maturity is later, like most of the aforementioned particulars) or an oily sap, more suitable for producing leaves than flowers.

   *Various Experiments concerning the method*

   595. That which first offers itself and is the

those which are applied in moderate measure to
the earth. The method of manuring that comes

being turned by the plough, receives the scattered
dung immediately before ploughing or sowing,
and so is covered by ploughing. For if it is cast
long before over the fields, the Sun consumes
much of its richness. If the land is pasture,
scatter it somewhat later and near the approach

But these things are done solely for the benefit of meadows which have a river far distant. Another is, the derivation of water from lands where springs are found, down slopes into lower ground through channels, from which, when cross-channels are made, the water may flow out more widely dispersed. And this drawing off creates hope of profit from a more fortunate yield of grain and grass; the more splendid, the more fertile the sloping land is, because it carries away with it something scraped off from the richness of the earth. But however it may finally be viewed, it never lacks utility. Generally, where marshes and anything similar to them, as if by a flood of water, emerge, that overflow, through the winter increases of water, provides fertility for the following summer. The reason may be that it both preserves the heat of the earth and nourishes the earth itself. But those experienced in marshes affirm that ditches or channels should be kept in such a way that too long a stay of stagnant water does not produce marsh sedge and rushes. For then the land, like a grove, excludes the Sun, whence the remaining moisture prevents the grass of that year from being as desired. So much for irrigation. Things pertaining to avoiding and draining off an excessive quantity of water, and aids to the land in that kind, will not escape our diligence elsewhere.

Various experiments concerning the affini-
ties and differences of plants and
inanimate bodies.

601. [Large decorative initial Q] Whatever difference there is between animate and in-
animate things, we will carefully consider under a heading to which
we set aside a treatise on life, vital spirits, and
faculties; content here with a cursory narration.
Therefore, these differences are reduced, as it were, to two main points,
since spirits and a pneumatic part are present in all bodies.
But two things especially distinguish animate and inanimate things.
The first is, whatever spirit animates living things,
it moves undivided in a continuous flow into veins and hidden
channels, like blood; except that it does not only have its own branches,
but

--- Page 391 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VII. 351
but also certain ventricles or receptacles, the seat of the principal spirit, and to which they are, as it were, channeled. But the spirits of inanimate things are enclosed, and cut off from the tangible parts, impervious to one another, as air exists in snow.
   The second [difference] is, that all spirits of animate things are more or less kindled and have something subtle of flame mixed in, and become airy in substance. But inanimate bodies nourish spirits that know not how to be inflamed. Nor does this difference designate the heat or cold of spirits; for cloves, and other aromatics, naphtha or petroleum consist of very hot spirits (far exceeding the heat of oil and wax) but are not kindled; and whatever among these bodies, which foster more temperate and languid spirits, is inflamed, it becomes intensely hot compared to others where they are not inflamed, besides light and motion, etc.
   602. Secondary differences, and which arise from the former as from radical ones, are these. All plants have a definite shape from a determined conformation, not so inanimate bodies. For note, as far as the spirit can be continuously dispersed, and does not abandon its series, so far does the configuration proceed, and its limits from the utmost endeavor

--- Page 392 ---
352      FRANCIS BACON'S
receives. Then, plants are nouri-
shed, but not inanimate bodies; they have accre-
tion, not alimentation.
Thirdly, the vitality of plants is enclosed within a fixed
period, which is not fixed for animated
bodies. Fourthly, plants preserve their species
by the secondary propagation of individuals among
themselves; which is not observed
in inanimate bodies.
      603. Plants and metals or fossils, which
I reckon among inanimate things, besides the four modes mentioned
before, also differ in these ways. Plants
yield to metals in longevity. Secondly,
in solidity and hardness. Thirdly, the former possess a double climate
above and below ground, while the latter, being only
subterranean, are content with one.
      604. You would see few things that plants and metals
share in the fellowship of both natures.
Coral is most closely related to both species, as
is vitriol; which grows most
readily from moisture.
      605. Another special difference is between
plants and putrefaction; namely, that all of the latter
(if it does not end in desiccation)
turns into plants, or into animals accustomed to being born from putre-
faction. For it seems to me entirely
certain that moss, fungi, and
agaric, and other things of the same kind, are

But flesh, fish, and the plants themselves, and many other things which can be referred to here, when putrefied or corrupted, generate worms. Putrefactions which resemble the nature of plants are distinguished from them by the fact that they do not revive in successive progeny, although they are nourished and expire at their own period, nor are they entirely without form.

606. When I was enjoying the sought-after temperate seclusion of the summer quarter, I had by chance left a cut lemon in a place closed on all sides. When I returned, I saw capillary tips, a thumb's length, grown out from the cut pith, with tiny black heads, resembling grass.

*and difference of plants*
*and animals, and in what confines*

607. The following will show by what natural fellowship plants and animals are joined, and by what contrariety they differ from each other. Both push forth spirits branching out in a continuous flow, and possess those apt for inflammation, but which in animals have ventricles and receptacles,

[unclear symbol]

--- Page 394 ---
354      FRANCIS BACON'S
they have, not in plants, as we said before [a].
Secondly, their spirits communicate more with flame than those of plants.
And these are the primary differences; now take the secondary ones. Firstly, we see plants raised in close companionship with the earth, while animals, separated from the womb, subsist by themselves.
Secondly, animals possess the faculty of locomotion, not plants. Thirdly, animals draw nourishment from their upper parts, especially through the mouth; plants from their lower parts, namely the roots. Fourthly, seeds and seminal vessels, which turn upwards, are parts of plants; in animals, these are the parts which are situated downwards. Therefore it is said not only elegantly, but also philosophically, that man is an inverted plant; for what is the root in plants, is the head in animals. Fifthly, animals are more exactly configured than plants. Sixthly, there is a greater diversity of organs within their body, and as it were, an interior conformation, than in plants. Seventhly, those possess the faculty of feeling; these lack it. Eighthly, animals have spontaneous motion, which plants lack.

   _Miscellaneous experiments concerning_
               _Plants._

   610. The Indian Fig tree sends down its branches so curved within one year, that it spontaneously puts forth new roots, by which, again growing manifoldly from one another, a single tree presents the appearance of a grove. The cause is, the abundance of sap, and the softness of the trunk, which presses down the branches if they are too heavily laden and not strongly supported. The leaves equal the width of a small shield, the fruit the thickness of a pea. The reason is, that continuous shade helps in increasing the leaves, at the expense of the fruit, which is of a very sweet taste. And doubtless it is from the oily moisture and the tenderness of the sap that renders the branches in that plant so flexible.
   611. Someone among the ancients asserts that there is a tree among the Indians which, with few, but immense

   _a]_ _Bee-Flowers._

--- Page 397 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VII. 357
...is clothed with immense leaves, three cubits in length and two cubits in width, and its fruit, of excellent taste, grows from the bark. It could happen that plants exist which propel sap so strongly that there is not enough time, either in distributing it into various branches, or in forming a trunk that bears fruit. Among us, if a comparison is made, generally trees have small leaves. The fig tree bears the largest, then the vine, the mulberry, the sycamore. Of the last order are the willow, the lime tree, the thorn. But you may find where, among herbs rather than trees, the prerogative of large leaves lies, as in the burdock, gourd, cucumber, cabbage. The cause coincides with that which we gave for the Indian fig: a swift and copious propulsion of sap.

It seems plausible that the sap and tears of certain trees are of a sweet taste.      613. It would be beneficial to try planting a hard tree, such as a service-tree or a fir, in sands.

   622. Today's vines are of a smaller size than that in which they were formerly conspicuous, when cups and the image of Jupiter were fashioned from them. The wood of vines preserves itself from rot for many years. And, what we may wonder at, although no tree has such fragile buds while it is green, yet the dried wood has such flexibility that it provided the service of a staff to Roman Centurions.

625. Fruits untouched and free from harm are perhaps also preserved by small vessels filled with fine sand, chalk powder, flour and pollen, or powder of oak wood and mill-dust.

626. Whatever fruits you intend for longer preservation, their ripeness must be anticipated in picking, and they must be gathered on a clear and dry day around midday, when the south wind is not blowing, and the moon is silent and waning.

627. They say that grapes, suspended in an empty, well-closed vessel, placed not in a cellar but in a dry place, can be preserved whole for a long time. Some say that this is done better in a vessel which is filled with wine in such a way that the suspended grapes do not touch it.

628. Whatever you apply to the stem for preservation, they say, yields to the benefits of the cluster; especially if the stem is inserted into elder pith, provided however that the elder does not touch the fruit.

632. The seeds of most plants excel in taste and smell over leaves or roots. The reason is, because in as many plants as a rough and sharp spirit does not quicken, their virtue increases by concoction and maturity, always conspicuous in the seed. But those which a sharp spirit fosters are more efficacious by themselves, since that [spirit], enclosed in the roots, reigns; and the air and the sun, when perceived, cause it to be dissipated as it languishes. This is obvious in onions, garlic, tarragon, etc. There are also plants with very hot and aromatic roots, but insipid seeds, like Ginger. The reason already stated, namely, the heat of this plant is very dissipable, which, confined underground, gains strength, but exhales evanescently at the touch of air.

636. There are two excrescences accustomed to grow on trees and to be found among fungi. One, called *boletus* by the Romans, found in the roots of oaks, and used as a delicacy for tables. I am easily led to that opinion which persuades that more excrescences arise from a dead or decaying tree, its natural sap degenerating into a preternatural substance.

In general, the best fruits are the lowest, as they are nourished by vigorous and least exhausted sap, which travels the shortest path of nourishment. **643.** Hemlock, tempered for drink, brings death with the least sense of pain; a mild punishment used by the Athenians for those worthy of capital punishment. Nearly a twin to this is the bite of an asp, applied by Cleopatra, impressed upon the body. The reason is that the struggle of the spirits makes the torments of death especially to be feared; for here, as if by a diffused mist of sleep, they gradually fall asleep with the vapors, as usually happens in the death of a decrepit old man. Yet I would think it afflicts less than opium, which has hot parts mixed in.

**644.** Some fruits become sweet before maturity, such as myrobalans. Thus fennel seeds, not yet ripe, are sweet, afterwards aromatic. For some, maturity never brings sweetness, such as tamarinds, hawthorn fruits, wild apples, acacias. The reason is that the former abound in a copious and subtle spirit, easily brought to ripeness, the parent of sweetness. The latter obtain a cold and acidic juice, which the heat of the Sun cannot ripen fully so that it becomes sweet. The myrobalan, however, consists of parts of nature opposing each other; for it is sweet and astringent.

     645. A salty flavor imbues few herbs. On the contrary, the blood of all living creatures is salty. The reason might be that salt, although a basic element of life, cannot maintain the place of a primary flavor in plants, since taste reveals them to be bitter, sour, sweet, or pungent, rarely salty. But those [a] strong flavors sometimes occur simultaneously in the humors of living creatures, not so frequently in flesh or in a substance of a more oily nature, which does not easily allow such flavors to be mixed into it. 650. For most seeds, the pod or husk is hidden around the root; the onion brings it forth with itself into the light, so that it appears not unlike a hood on the top of a young onion. The reason perhaps is that the skin or pod is not easily broken, as the peeling of onions shows how tenacious in substance that skin is.

651. The curled leaves of plants indicate an abundance of moisture, which, breaking forth so continuously, proceeds so that it cannot be reduced to an even distribution, but it is necessary that it remain more neglected elsewhere. The weakest curling is hairiness, as in Roman sage and burdock. The next is that in the extremities, as in lettuce, young cabbage. The third is, in adult cabbage, sessile lettuce.

652. There is a tradition concerning fir and pine, especially those rotted by age, that although, like some corrupted woods, they do not shine, yet in sudden disruptions they sparkle, like hard sugar.

654. Observation has shown that a branch of a certain tree, stripped of its bark for some space from below and inserted into the earth, grew. Certainly, a branch of that kind of tree would not have sprouted unless stripped of its bark and planted. On the contrary, we see a tree die when its body above ground is stripped of bark. 655. Lively and moist bunches of grapes will last the whole winter, with the clusters suspended together in a warm, arched place; especially if, when picking them, you allow a bit of the stalk, broken off with the cluster, to remain attached.

656. A reed or cane is a watery plant, accustomed to growing only in water. It has the properties that it is hollow, that it divides the stem and root with nodes; when dried, it surpasses any wood in hardness and fragility, it produces no branches, with many stalks sprouting from a single root. They are of different sizes; the smallest are used for covering houses, or for stopping up cracks in ships; and that better with glue

Among those whose nourishment is from earth mixed with water, it seems to be nourished by a great deal of moisture; whence also its bark is very smooth and its body very hollow.
     657. The sap contained in trees, if emitted, is of various natures. That of the vine, beech, and pear is more watery and clearer. That of the apple is thicker; that of the cherry is gummier; that of the elm is frothy; that of the fig is milky. The sap of the mulberry usually adheres in the vicinity of the bark, which, when lightly struck with a stone, reveals it, but when an instrument is driven in deeper, it is found dry. Trees whose fruits are very moist generally consist of such a body. Vines and pears are very moist, apples are more spongy, the milk of the fig resembles the quality of rennet. In certain acidic herbs, there is a similar milk, such as serves for forming cheeses in springtime.

662. An observation of some from antiquity, that the winds which the East sends forth, although they are cold and do not blow without harm to fruits, nevertheless the South winds sometimes reign with damaging blast, especially while the tree is in flower and the sky is rainy; so that altogether they stir up excessively humid conditions. Zephyrus is considered most benign, and diligent investigation has also taught that green winters, not bound by frost, harm trees; to such an extent that if such a winter recurs two or three times, it kills almond trees and other trees. The cause coincides with the preceding one, because namely the vigor of the earth, too much consumed, fails; (this is) while some of the ancients, of course, recommend warm winters.

    664. If rains precede maturity a little, they fall happily for succulent and moist fruits, such as vines, olives, pomegranates; but so that they contribute more to abundance than to the quality of the fruits; since dry harvests yield the best wines. Moderate rains, however, are also beneficial for grain, lest the excessive heat of the Sun scorch it. In general, nocturnal rains are preferred over diurnal ones, because the scorching heat of the Sun does not follow so closely upon them. It is also clear from the irrigation practiced in summer that evening irrigation is the best.
    665. The diverse nature of the soil certainly deserves diligent experimental work. That which, when dug or ploughed, emits a sweet odor, is praised in the name of its sap, which it fosters, prepared for vegetables. evil cannot be removed, if it is enclosed in narrow spaces, even if the land extends into wider fields. Nor am I unaware that this has benefited certain farms.
Another disease is the production of sterile darnel and oats, into which grain (barley especially) often degenerates, and it arises from the weakness of the sown grain, which, if it has been too old or moldy, is accustomed to produce darnel. Another [cause is] the satiety of the land, which, continuing the yield of the same grain (I do not mean that which grows there, but grains of the same species, for example, barley, wheat, etc.), falls short of its former fertility; so that it is fitting not only for the soil to rest, but also for the seed to be changed. Also there is a malignant blast of winds, which harms at two times: either while they shake off the flowers, or [harm] the grain in full maturity. Another plague of the farm is great heat when wheat pushes out its ears, rare among us, frequent in hotter regions; so that the calamity of the word [calamitas] may have originated from 'calamus' (reed/stalk), when the grain could not emerge from the stalk. Equally harmful is excessive moisture at the time of sowing, infamous among our countrymen for great scarcity of grain, so that the grain in no way grows; whence they are often forced to sow summer grain in the place where winter grain was sown. Similar misfortune [arises]

frost, especially when the air has begun to turn wintry shortly after the seed has been committed to the earth. The ear produces another worm, especially when heat often bursts forth from the clouds. There are also harmful weeds, either suffocating or shading the grain, which, when suppressed, they either kill or deprive of nourishment. *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the healing of wounds.*

677. I find it noted by ancient writers that skins, especially of rams, recently removed and applied to wounds, cause them not to swell up and become ulcerated, and to heal them once they are consolidated. Egg white possesses the same power. The cause is a moderate agglutination, since both bodies are tenacious and viscous, and by repelling the outflow of humors from the wounds, it does not compress them excessively.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning the fat*
*which is diffused through the flesh.*

678. All flesh can generally be turned into a fatty substance if it is cut into small pieces, and the pieces are placed in a glass vessel closed with a membrane, which is placed in boiling water for six or seven hours. This experiment can be profitable in preparing fat or grease for various uses. But it is necessary that the flesh be unfit for human consumption, such as horse, dog, bear, fox, beaver, etc.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
          *hairiness and feathers.*
   680. Beasts are hairier than humans,
and country people than city dwellers; and the
feathers of birds surpass the hair of
beasts in density. The reason why man has smooth skin,
is not abundant heat and moisture,
although, by Hercules, the origin of hair growing abundantly
is from there; but not so much both of those
are required, as heat and excrementitious
humor, (for whatever is assimilated
is not turned into hair) which prevails in beasts
and in country people. Nearly the same
reason applies to the feathers of birds, since
they assimilate less, and excrete more than beasts.
For their excretions are mostly liquid, their flesh
is generally dry. Add to this that they do not
have proper urinary organs, so that all
excrementitious humor goes into the feathers.
Hence I am not surprised that birds are preferred
to beasts for the table, because

*A Solitary Experiment concerning the speed of motion in birds.*

681. The speed of birds in motion exceeds that of beasts, whose flight for the most part no beast's running equals. The cause is the abundance of spirits in birds, greater in proportion to the narrowness of their small body than in beasts. The reason brought forward by some, that that motion partakes of conveyance, since beasts walk, is invalid, since thus swimming ought to be swifter than running. Nor does that conveyance lack the subsidiary work of wings to be accomplished.

*Solitary Experiment concerning the diverse*
*clarity of the sea.*
682. The blast of the North wind makes the sea more transparent than that of the South wind. The reason is that the surface of salt water is somewhat oily, as the hottest days prove. Furthermore, because the South wind somewhat relaxes the water; so that boiling water is not as clear as cold water.

*Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the difference of heat in fire &*
*hot water.*
683. Fire ignites wood, first by rendering it luminous, then black and fragile, finally it breaks it up and reduces it to ashes. You would expect nothing of the kind from hot water. The reason is that fire attenuates the spirit of the body, and afterwards emits it. Attenuation, however, generates light; emission first causes fragility, then dissolution into ashes, nor does any other body enter in besides. In water, the spirit of the body is not so attenuated; a portion of water also enters, which will increase the spirit, and to some extent will extinguish the fire; as we see happen from hot water. Likewise in bodies, which, with the entry of water prohibited, admit insinuating heat,

--- Page 435 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VII. 395
Likewise in bodies which, with the entry of water prohibited, admit the thing, namely insinuating heat, hot water dissolves parts of the fire. Thus, between boiled and roasted eggs (which absolutely no water penetrates) there is scarcely a visible difference, but it is quite noticeable in fruits and meat, which are somewhat permeable to entering water.

  A Solitary Experiment concerning the tempering of heat by moisture.

  684. The bottom of a vessel full of hot water (as experience testifies) gets so hot that one can bear to move a hand towards and away from it. The cause is, because the moisture of water, just as it extinguishes embers where entry is open, so it tempers the heat, whatever part it has touched. Wherefore it is to be noted, that moisture, although it does not transmit through bodies without communication of substance (as heat and cold usually do) gives credence to its operation, not by entering the body, but by tempering heat and cold, as this instance teaches. We also see that distilled water produced in a water bath (which they call a 'balneum') does not differ much from distilled water produced over fire; just as tin plates filled with water do not easily liquefy; without water, they liquefy entirely. Moreover, butter and oil, which are very easily inflamed by themselves, exhibit the same effect, which is to be attributed to the virtue of humidity.

685. It did not escape the diligence of the ancients, namely, the danger of having one's ears pricked while yawning. The reason is, because yawning stretches the inner membrane of the ear, with the spirit and breath drawn in. For this, like sighing, first strongly draws in the spirit, then expels it.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*hiccup.*

686. From the same workshop of antiquity comes the observation that sneezing expels hiccups. The reason is, because the movement of hiccup is an elevation of the stomach, which sneezing somewhat depresses, and diverts the movement elsewhere. For first we see hiccup arise from too much food ingested (especially in children), whence the distension of the stomach. Acid food and drink also cause the same by irritating the stomach, and this movement ceases either by diverting it or by holding the breath. The former happens in sneezing, the latter is evident from the fact that held breath partially removes hiccup. You will feel the same by turning your mind to serious matters, as is commonly done; and by applying vinegar to the nostrils or gargling, because it constricts and inhibits the movement of the spirits.

  *A solitary experiment observing*
          *sneezing.*

  697. A gaze turned towards the Sun causes
sneezing. The cause is not the heating
of the nostrils, which, being open to the Sun,
would otherwise excite it in a single moment, but
a depression of the humors of the brain, which
suffuse the eyes, from where, by a sympathetic
movement, they are drawn to the nostrils and
create sneezing. Conversely, an internal tickling
of the nostrils draws humors to the nostrils, but
by sympathy to the eyes, which are moistened.
But nevertheless, observation suggests that one
accustomed to sneeze frequently can overcome
sneezing if he rubs his eyes until they are
suffused by a flow of watery humor. The reason
is the diversion of the humor, which was about
to descend to the nostrils, to the eyes.

698. For insects, motion is voluntary, and therefore also imagination. But those among the ancients who said that their motion is indeterminate, and their imagination indefinite, revealed their own negligence. For ants directly seek their hiding places, and bees, not without the admiration of observers, discern the way by which they may seek their hive from the flowering plain of the fields, through two or four miles. Perhaps for gnats and flies, imagination is more changeable and dizzying; just as some of the ancients attributed only touch to small birds. But they erred from the truth; for if they move directly towards something, they must necessarily be endowed with sight. Furthermore, they choose a flower or herb that they enjoy more; therefore, they also possess the sense of taste. Bees are also called back by the sound of disturbed air; which indicates hearing, and, even though their spirits spread diffusely, that the seats of the senses are located in the head.

Moreover, those things which sought to be appended to this subject of insects, along with their enumeration, we relegate to the section on animals in general.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*Running.*

   699. The speed of a runner is increased by a
weight held in the hands. The reason
is, because the weight (namely, a proportionate
one) by contracting the nerves, strengthens
them. Where this contraction is not needed,
the weight will be an impediment; which is evident in a
horse race.
For they carefully take precautions lest one
horse be burdened more than another even by the slightest
weight. In running with a weight, the arms are first
pushed backward, then forward,
with a perceptibly increasing impetus; for the
hands are sent back before they are moved
forward. Inquire whether a movement of the spirits
contrary to the intended movement, and that immediately
before we begin to move in the destined direction,
causes the spirits, more vehemently impelled, to burst forth;
just as a spirit drawn in and held back is expelled more
vehemently. Also in throwing, the arms are
drawn back, so that the rotation may be stronger.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning the Pleasures*
*and Displeasures of the Senses, especially*
*of Hearing.*

   700. We have previously described musicians and
unequal-

--- Page 451 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VII. 411
unequal tones, but not so exactly the pleasures and offenses of the senses. Harsh sounds, such as when a saw is sharpened, the grinding of stone against stone, wailing, a rattling sound, drench the body with horror or trembling, and set the teeth on edge. The reason is that objects of hearing usually immediately affect the spirits either pleasantly or unpleasantly. We see that no color is given which greatly offends the eyes. Spectacles full of terror, such things occur to an excited memory, but painted ones move little. Smell, taste, touch are affected by the body's participation or impulse from the object. Sound alone is that which strikes the sense without any intermediary, nor corporeally. Music will confirm this, whether gently tempered into harmony, or harsh with dissonances. For all sounds, whether high or low, sweetness gives them roundness and equality; harsh sounds have inequality. For what else is dissonance than a harsh concurrence of various voices? It is true indeed, if inequality does not fixedly dominate, but vanishes as if transitory, sweetness is rather increased, as in the whisper of a twisted string, the hoarse clangor of a trumpet, in the pipe or nightingale-flute of the great and royal organ, which the English call 'philomela', and wherever discord

412      FR. BACON'S SYLV. &c.
harmony, soon following, absorbs the discord
of sounds. But if it lingers, it becomes unpleasant
and offends. Therefore, pleasure and of-

of sweet sound, of dissonance, and of harsh sound,
which we designate by various names, such as a screech

dull the teeth, it is clearly evident by what
interval the teeth and the organ of hearing are
distant; as if one end of a bow were
held while the string is struck.

A solitary experiment concerning
medicinal veins of the earth.

701. [Decorative initial M] There is a great variety of minerals and fossils, but medicinal earth has few veins. Its principal species are Lemnian earth, common sealed earth, Armenian bole; but the prerogative of dignity should be owed to Lemnian earth. They are commended for their virtue in the healing of wounds, in stopping blood and repressing defluxions and catarrhs, and in driving away, as it were, poison, contagion, and putrefaction, lest they spread more widely and break out. Of all simple remedies, they possess the most perfect and purest drying efficacy, being mixed with little or no admixture of other qualities.                                 S 3                      heat;

   *Solitary Experiment concerning*
        *the germination of sponges.*

   702. Not far from the bottom of the straits,
many sponges are gathered, collected from the
sides of rocks, which are nothing but abundant
and tenacious moss. These, however,
are all the more noteworthy because, within the compass of a small
substance, imitating the configuration of a plant,
they delight in generative waters; for sometimes
they must be sought at a depth of fifteen cubits.
When extracted onto the shore, they feign the amplitude of a mass;
when compressed, they occupy a very small space.

pierced a wooden board, of eight inches
thickness. It is certain that in naval battles formerly
there were in use short missiles which they called

accustomed to be hurled from muskets,
and penetrated the sides of ships impervious to a lead
bullet. But here a hidden mystery of nature

Various Experiments concerning
sweat.

706. A hot water bath does not draw out
sweat from parts under the water. The first
reason is, because sweat is a kind of colliquation,
which only very dry or very humid heat produces.
For excessive moisture extinguishes heat
to some extent, just as hot water extinguishes
fire; and excessively dry heat closes the pores.
Therefore, someone covered in the sun or by
the fire will more easily emit sweat than
someone naked; and earthenware bottles filled
with hot water provoke sweat more gently in
bed than hot brick baths. Secondly, hot water
causes the skin to evaporate, so that the material
is consumed in the parts below the water before
it is turned into sweat.
                                 S 5                               pro-

--- Page 458 ---
418        FRANCIS BACON
comes forth. Then, heat moderately increased draws forth sweat more copiously than heat initially more vehement and uniformly intense. The reason is that gentle heat opens pores better than violent heat; with these opened, sweat flows out more copiously. Therefore, physicians acted according to rational prescription, who, by applying bottles in bed, provoked sweat through sudorific herbs decocted in hot water, applying heat gradually; so that a less hot bottle would perform the first part, and afterwards, a hotter one would perform the second.
    707. The taste of sweat indicates saltiness. Reason: because the fresh and sweet part of nourishment is changed into blood and flesh, but sweat is an excretory part. Raw blood is saltier than flesh, because assimilation into flesh does not occur without a slight and subtle excretion of blood.
    708. The upper parts of the body emit sweat more than the lower parts. Reason: because those parts swell more with spirits, which propel sweat; moreover, they are less fleshy, and from these drier parts, sweat especially comes forth. Such are the forehead and chest.
    709. Sleep excites sweat more than wakefulness, which nevertheless stops other defluxions rather than incites them; such as catarrhs, loose bowels, etc. The reason is, because sleep [increases] heat and spi-

710. Cold sweats are often fatal and indicators of

cold sweat is caused either by relaxation or by a faintness

711. Those diseases which sweat does not resolve, in

former kind either arises from the labor of the spirits,
and testifies that they are oppressed; or from a movement
by consent, when nature, unequal to expelling the disease
from the place it invaded, attempts an indifferent expulsion
throughout the entire body.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the Glow-worm.*

712. The nature of the Glow-worm has not hitherto been sufficiently explored. It is certain that it is generated chiefly during the hottest months of summer, not in fields, but in brambles and hedges. From this it can be understood that the subtlety of its spirit is such that it cannot be attenuated except by summer heat; and again, that that subtlety easily allows exhalation. Italy and warmer regions produce a fly, which is called *lucciola* there, shining like a glow-worm, and perhaps it is a flying glow-worm; but this fly especially frequents lakes and marshes. However, the two former observations can be applied here. For it is not visible except during summer; and sedges or whatever grows green around marshes provide shade equally good as brambles. Perhaps the cold of other regions does not allow the glow-worm to grow to such an extent that winged ones are found.

*Various Experiments concerning impressions*
*from passions of the mind on the body.*

713. The passions of the mind make impressions on the body, which are to be explained here. Fear induces pallor, trembling, raises the hair,

Tremor from the flight of spirits driven inwards, by which the extremities of the body are abandoned. Because of closed skin pores, there is an erection of the hairs, which, lying obliquely, must be raised. Recoil is the apprehension of terrible things, and thus it is a contractive motion, and as it were an inquiry, what initiates the event; and for this reason it is a raising [motion]. Hence he who prepares himself for sudden listening, recoils, for the spirits are raised to attention. Horror is an appetite for expelling what suddenly struck the spirits. For it must be noted that many motions, although useless for expelling obstacles, are irritations of nature, and produce motions by sympathy, as in groaning and wailing from pain.

714. Pain and suffering excite sighing, hiccuping, groaning, trembling and wailing, or shouting, tears, distortion of the face, grinding of teeth, sweat. Tears, from the contraction of the spirits in the brain, which is followed by the constriction of fluid there, and thus the transmission of tears to the eyes.    726. Smaller draughts intoxicate sooner than large ones; sugared wine less than pure wine. **A solitary experiment concerning**
**caterpillars.**

728. The caterpillar is among the most common worms, usually produced from dew and leaves, for you may see swarms of caterpillars produced in trees and hedges, causing for the most part the calamity of leaves in trees and hedges, because they are both born from them and nourished by them. Springtime especially is infested by this plague, because neither dew nor leaves are then lacking, and they are usually generated if the East wind has blown for a longer time. The cause is the dryness of that wind; since all vivification from putrefaction requires that the matter not be too humid. Moreover, what we see covered with spider webs is a sign of slimy dryness; as in lands which spider webs cover from dew and sun. The inner parts of roses also produce green caterpillars, especially those that have not experienced winds blowing through them, in which the dew becomes moldy, but cabbages produce the largest and most numerous caterpillars, with their thick leaves apt to putrefy. Summer, as it expires, shows winged caterpillars, and changes

There is also a caterpillar with a woolly body,

sponds equally to the parts. Animals accustomed to shedding their skin are the snake, viper, cicada, lizard, silkworm, etc. But those which cast off and renew their scales are the lobster, crab, tortoise, snail, etc. It is known that sloughs are found, but cast-off scales very rarely; so that it seems probable that they desquamate in such a way that they gradually fall off; and the new scales are distinguished by remarkable tenderness and softness, and a somewhat florid color. The cause of sloughing and desquamation could seem to be a huge quantity of material in these animals, which is naturally apt to produce skin or scale; then the looseness of the skin or scale less tightly wrapped around the flesh. For it is certain that the old is pushed out by the new skin or scale. Thus in animals the new horn casts off the old, and in birds new feathers [cast off] the old. Those birds also, which have sufficient material for generating a beak, renew their beaks, fresh-

...through its pores, it is most healthy. The reason is, because
the stomach, thus less pendulous, is strengthened.
For we see that those suffering from stomach ailments,
with their legs drawn up and knees as if brought to
the mouth, are wonderfully helped; and those condemned to
triremes, in their very miseries, are stout
and as if with a well-kept body. The reason is,
because a sedentary life in some way supports the stomach,
which a standing posture and frequent movements
make pendulous. Hence, to choose exercises
conducive to prolonging life, which
move the limbs more than the stomach or abdomen,
such as rowing while sitting, or
sawing back and forth.
734. Rising, rather than sitting, produces migraines and vertigo
from prolonged sitting. The reason is, because vapors, collected
by sitting, seek the head more with sudden movement.
735. He who leans for a long time on some part,
renders it numb, and, as they say, makes it
fall asleep. The reason is, the compression of the part,
with the spirits' freedom of access blocked.
The relaxation of the compressed part causes a pricking sensation
to be felt from the return of the spirits.

pestilential years.

(as experience testifies) are made infamous by the suspicion of plague, and a multitude of frogs, flies, and locusts, etc., persuades that they will be unhealthy. The cause is not to be sought from a hidden place, since these animals, born from putrefaction, show the year, from its general disposition and the constitution of the air, as if conspiring towards diseases and putrefaction. The same prognosis applies (as [a] said before) if worms have formed galls sometimes found in oaks: for these represent a malignant temperament of the air more subtly from close at hand than human sense can penetrate.

   *A solitary experiment regarding*
      *a prognosis of a more intense winter.*

   737. It is an observation of country folk that years in which there has been an abundance of fruit or berries of the hawthorn or the scentless dog-rose, portend harsh winters. They say the cause lies in the secrets of divine providence, which (as the sacred scriptures testify) does not neglect even sparrows falling to the ground, so that it may all the more illustriously provide signs of itself in preserving birds through those seasons of the year. Perhaps this cause may be drawn from the scrutiny of nature: that the preceding summer suffered from a defect of heat and an abundance of moisture;

[a] *See Century 6.*

abundance; which the production of these fruits
proves. Furthermore, it is necessary that cold
vapors remain in great abundance, and are not
dispersed, from which the cold of the coming winter is
intensified.

A singular experiment concerning
medicines which condense
and revive the spirits.

738. Among the Turks, there is a drink in use, which
they call Coffa, from a berry of the same name, which
is black like soot, and has a pungent, not aromatic,
odor. That [berry], reduced to powder,
is taken by them in water so hot that it allows a draught.
They use this drink in their taverns (which are called
Coffa-houses) strengthening the brain and heart
and aiding digestion. Indeed, this Coffa berry,
the root and leaf of betel, the leaf of tobacco, the
tear of the poppy (opium), very common among the Turks,
because they think it removes fear,
condense the spirits, and render them strong and
cheerful. But they seem to be distinguished by various
modes of use; for Coffa and opium are taken internally;
only the smoke of tobacco [is used]; betel
is only chewed in the mouth, with a little
lime. That more of this kind are given, if
inquiry does not slumber nor correction be wanting,
would not be alien from the truth. Inquire about hyoscyamus.

and provoke sleep. *Note*, that the root or seed
of tobacco is not smoked, as they are stronger than the leaves themselves.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
          *the painting of bodies.*

   739. The Turks have a black powder
made from mineral Alcohol, which they
smear on their eyelids with a thin brush to darken them,
so that the white of the eye may shine forth. With the same
powder they dye their eyelashes and eyebrows [*a*] adorned
in the manner of an arch from a perspective view.
Xenophon recorded that the Medes applied
pigments to their eyes. The same dye makes
the hair and beards of the Turks black. Our
countrymen also, so that by dyeing their gray hair
they may counterfeit the beauty of youthful
form, darken their hair with various devised aids,
and comb them with a lead comb or similar aid.
The Chinese, with an unattractive bodily
constitution (for they are olive-colored), dye
their cheeks using the artifice of purple;
especially the King and the Nobles.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*the use of bathing and anointing.*

740. We wonder that the use of bathing, a part
of regimen, has fallen into disuse. For the Romans
and Greeks, it was like food and drink.
Today, among the Saracens, its practice has not perished;
our people only acknowledging it as a part of
medication. I am of the opinion that bathing, in the
manner the Romans used it, was harmful to health, by
softening the body and rendering it susceptible to
consumption. For the Turks, their diet is more suited
to it, since the drinking of water and the rice
they eat, and other food of moderate nourishment,
render their bodies solid and hard, so that the fear that the
use of bathing might debilitate them is groundless.

   *Solitary Experiment concerning*
          *marbled [a] paper.*

   741. The Turks are excellent makers of pa-
per, which we call marbled; an art
unknown to our people. They take various co-
lours dyed with oil, and sprinkle them in drops of water,
and gently move the water, with which then
they moisten thickish paper, which draws
the lines of undulating veins, like cloth or
marble.

   *Solitary Experiment concerning*
          *cuttlefish ink.*

   742. It may be wondered that among birds, all beasts,
and fish, the blood is red,
but only in the cuttlefish is it black like ink. Per-
haps someone might think the cause is from blood
very much overcooked; since we see in
sausages of common use that blood turns black
by boiling. But the cuttlefish is a delicacy,
and eagerly sought after.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*the increase of the weight of earth.*

743. They report, whose trustworthiness it is impious
to question, that earth taken from places adjacent to the Nile,
if both moistening and consumption are prevented,
and if it is tested for weight daily, remains constant
until the seventeenth of June; on which day the Nile
swells; and increases in weight until the river
has reached its proper height. If the truth of the account
is not flawed, it has its cause from nowhere else but the air,
which then begins to condense, and thus is changed
into moisture within the small amount of earth, causing an increase
in weight. It has also been observed with cut and weighed
tobacco, that some of its former weight is lost if it is dried
by fire; and after being exposed to the air, it recovers whatever
it lost. It can be seen that the swelling river causes
some change to the entire body of air flowing around in the vicinity.
For (which is even more astonishing) they truly report
that on that day, when the Nile swells, severe plagues
usually arise in Cairo.

*Various experiments concerning sleep.*

744. Those who are very cold, especially in their
feet.

--- Page 482 ---
442          FRANCIS BACON'S
feet, sleep is hindered for them. The cause
could be that in sleep free
respiration is required, which cold harms by hindering it.
We see that difficulty of respiration
arises from sharp cold. Another cause
might also be that cold summons the
spirits to its aid, so that, thus collected, they cannot
ascend into the head; which sleep always requires.
Whence both pain and noise are likewise obstacles
to sleep, which, on the contrary, darkness promotes.

745. Certain noises (about which we
treated in Experiment 112) favor sleep;
such as the blowing of wind, flowing water, the buzzing
of bees, soft singing, reading, etc. The reason
is that they excite a gentle attention
in the spirits, and whatever promotes this without
heavy labor, calms the spirits which are active with a natural and discursive motion.

746. Sleep nourishes, or at least
preserves bodies for a long time without food. Beasts
which sleep deeply through winter (which
I find noted concerning Bears) grow fat
during sleep, even when not fed. Bats
have been found in ovens and other
caves, packed one upon another, whence the
conjecture was made that they sleep the entire winter,
and eat nothing. Inquire, whether bees
do not pass the winter in sleep, and spare
their honey?

_Various experiments concerning teeth_
_& hard substances in the bodies_
_of living beings._

If a method for restoring teeth were available,
one might boast of having discovered a mystery of nature;
let men direct their thoughts to this matter.
Whatever the case, the nature of a tooth deserves
investigation, just as other parts
of living beings. .

747. There are five solid and harder substances in the bodies of living beings:
the skull, tooth, bones, horns, nails. The
head everywhere displays many instances of this solidity,
because it has a skull made entirely of bone,
teeth, jawbones, and that somewhat hard
instrument of hearing, from which horns
emerge; so that the structure of living beings is
like the framework of a building,
whose walls and other parts are supported by columns and beams,
while the more elegantly crafted roofs consist
of tiles, lead, or stones.
Birds have three things peculiar to themselves: the beak,
of the same substance as a tooth (for teeth

       748. Bones, having attained the measure of their

       749. Most hard substances have receded

In teeth, these things are to be considered: 1. preservation. 2. care for their whiteness, lest it perish. 3. their extraction with less torment. 4. relief and remedy for toothache. 5. artificial insertion where they are missing, having been knocked out; and finally, that very important restoration, where advanced age has consumed them.

*Various Experiments concerning the Genera-*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*tion and Gestation of Animals*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*in the Womb.*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;758. Some living beings reproduce at certain
times of the year, such as deer, sheep,
wild rabbits, etc., most sheep and
fish. Others at any time of the year, such as
man, etc., and all domestic animals, such as horses,
pigs, dogs, cats, etc. The cause of generation
at any time of the year is abundance.
For superabundance promotes generation;
which flows from a double source, either the
nature of the animal, if it is warm, humid,
or sanguine, or from abundant
nourishment. As for the first, man,
horses, dogs, etc., for which any time of the year
is favorable for generation, are more abundant in heat and
moisture, pigeons among birds

--- Page 489 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VIII. 449
The very hot and very moist (animals) most often produce offspring; domesticated animals almost always do so. The deer is a melancholic and dry animal, which its timidity and the hardness of its flesh prove. The sheep is a cold animal, as appears from its gentleness and because they rarely drink. For most birds, the substance is drier than for beasts. Fish are cold; as for the second cause, which is the abundance of food, man, cow, pig, dog, etc. are fed more abundantly; nor is it obscure that wild animals rarely reproduce, while domesticated animals do so more often; which both heat and abundance of nourishment provide. It is certain that wild animals observe September as the time for mating, because whatever food and grass summer provides, yields into this faculty of generation. The earlier September becomes wet with rain, the sooner they whelp; dryness delays it. The sheep also, being moderately warm, reproduces around the same time or a little before. But those for whom generation is fixed and recurring in a cycle, such as birds and fish, devote themselves to spring offspring; contributing to this preparation are both the decline of winter and the warmth and fostering of spring. There is also another reason for generation defined by its period, and it is the relation of gestation to the time of generation, since no animal strives for a new birth while the female is carrying the womb, nor giving birth,

--- Page 490 ---
**OF FRANCIS BACON**
being in heat, or bringing forth young into the light. Therefore experience dictates that if eggs or young are removed from the nest, they return to mating, even repeatedly.

759. For some animals, nature has prescribed a longer or shorter time for carrying in the womb. A woman usually completes nine months; a cow and a female sheep, about six; a deer, nine; a mare, eleven; a dog, nine weeks. An elephant is said to carry its womb for a space of two years; for whatever they peddle about ten years smacks of fable. Two things present themselves in birds that fix attention: what differs from coitus, the laying of the egg, and then from the laid egg, the breaking of the shell. And in birds there is less diversity of time than in other animals; yet there is some. For a hen spends three weeks on incubation, an Asiatic hen, a goose, a duck, a month. Inquire about others. The cause of such great diversity regarding time among animals is either the nature of the species or the constitution of the womb. Regarding the former, those that mature more slowly are carried longer in the womb; as we are taught by the example of man. An elephant requires a long delay to complete the proper measure of growing up. But in most other species, the constitution of the womb (that is, its hardness and dryness) with the former cause

--- Page 491 ---

cause concurs. For a horse foal needs almost four years to mature, likewise a mule foal, and a calf. But puppies, for whom the period of maturation usually comprises nine months, are carried in the womb for the same number of weeks. Birds, just as they distinguish birth in a shorter time, so too do they mature in less time; most of them completing their growth within twelve months.

760. For some animals, a single birth provides numerous offspring; such as dogs, hares, rabbits; etc. Others are unipara, such as a woman, a lioness, etc. This can happen from the quantity of sperm required for the production of one individual of that species; for if less is required, a greater number can be admitted; if more, a smaller number; or from the divided cells of the uterus, into which the sperm is secreted in a divided manner.

Various experiments concerning visible forms.

761. It is beyond controversy that light is equally augmented by refraction as are colored objects. For just as the magnitude of a solid object at the bottom of water increases, so too does that of a candle, which is held placed in a lantern under water. I remember having heard of an experiment where fireflies, inserted into glass and placed under water, were used to attract fish.

--- Page 492 ---
FRANCIS BACON'S
fish. But hitherto it is hidden from me, whether a diver, keeping his eyes open under the waves and floating on his back, sees things situated in the air as magnified or diminished. For it is undoubted that if the eye is in a thinner medium and the object in a thicker one, the presented image increases. On the contrary, if the eye's rays pass through a denser medium, and the object is situated in a thinner one, what will happen is hidden from me.

762. It would be expedient to inquire more deeply whether reflection cannot produce greater refraction than rays emitted directly. For example, take an empty basin, and place a gold coin or anything else in it; then move further back from the basin until the sight of the coin vanishes, as it were, being out of the direct line. Then let the basin be filled with water; reflection will represent it in a place not its own. Therefore, to proceed, insert a mirror into the basin filled with water; I suppose the image will not be seen directly, or at equal angles, but obliquely. I do not know if this experiment cannot be set up in such a way that, with the mirror undetected by the eyes, the image appears in sight. Here novelty contends with beauty; with the image, like a spirit, about to occupy the air and be visible from there. For example, opposite a cistern or marsh, let there be placed

--- Page 493 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VIII. 453
be placed a picture of the devil or whatever you wish, yet so that the water is not perceived by the eyes, let a mirror be placed on the water. If from an oblique angle, the picture of the devil strikes the sight, not the water, you will have the likeness of the devil before you. Now for a long time among the Oxonians a rumor holds, that the Monk Roger Bacon passed through the air between two obelisks of two temples, which was then believed to have been done by means of optical glasses, although he was walking on the ground.

Various experiments concerning impulsion and percussion.

763. A heavy body, once moved, is more easily impelled than the first time when it was at rest. The reason is, partly because motion dispels the sluggishness of a solid body, which, besides the motion of gravity, also has in itself a natural appetite for rest; partly also, because a body at rest suffers a stronger compression of its parts from the resistance of the body in which it rests, than it would have from itself; so that a greater force must be applied to dislodge it from its state. For if a weighty body is suspended, even by a thread, the impulse will be equally easy as if it were entirely in motion.
764. A huge or very tiny body so

--- Page 494 ---
**FRANCIS BACON**
cannot be projected as far as one of me-
dium size, so that a force commensurate with the body
moved, which moves it, seems to be required according to the law of pro-
portion. The cause is, because
impulse does not occur without the power of the moving
body and the resistance of the moved; but a body,
if it is of enormous magnitude, yields more slowly;
if of smallness, it does not resist strongly enough.
    765. It is commonly known that no weight
presses and breaks so strongly if it is placed on another
body, as if it is impelled or struck into
it from above. Perhaps something is to be attributed
to the air in promoting percussion. But the principal
cause seems to me to be that the parts of the moved body, from impulse
or continuous motion of gravity, have in themselves an equal
compression downwards, as
they do forwards when projected and emitted through the air.
I also conceive that the swift relaxation of that motion
anticipates the resistance of the lower
body; the priority of forces everywhere
proving its efficacy, as appears in infinite
instances.

    *A solitary experiment concerning*
                *tickling.*

    766. Tickling is most perceived in
the sole of the foot, under the armpits, and in the lateral
ribs. The cause is the thinness of the skin, which these
                                            parts

--- Page 495 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VIII. 655
covers these parts, and also by their rare
touch. For every tickling is a slight
movement of spirits, which the thinness of the skin,
and sudden and rare contact promotes. Thus
a feather or a reed lightly
gliding over the lips or cheeks causes tickling, not a more
obtuse or harder contact. As for sudden
contact, it is clear that no one can tickle
himself; and the palm, though its skin is as thin
as the parts already mentioned, does not
admit tickling, due to the frequency of
contact. Tickling also causes laughter.
The cause is perhaps an emission of spirits and thus of the
soul, by the flight from tickling, in which a
recoil and drawing back of the part is always observed
to avoid it. In the nostrils also, when tickled
internally by a feather or straw, they cause sneezing;
which is a sudden emission of spirits,
and expels moisture. There is also a tickling
joined with pain, such that it cannot be
endured.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*the scarcity of rain in Egypt.*

767. It is strange that, while the Nile
inundates Egypt, as it is accustomed to do, scanty or no
rains are felt in that region. The cause can be
referred either to the nature of the water, or of the air, or of
both. Of the water, if also a longer [period] is
considered

--- Page 496 ---
456      FRANCIS BACON'S
a swift course is given, since water rapidly carried by the current exhales less than stagnant water; and its concoction, when properly concocted, does not evaporate as much as raw water, just as water boiling over a fire emits vapors more sparingly after a moderate interval from the first boiling than at the very beginning. It is also established that the waters of the Nile are found to be sweeter in taste than others, in the judgment of those who taste them; they are also recommended for calculus and hypochondriacal melancholy, from which a soothing virtue is inferred; and it flows through a hot climate, a flat region neither shaded by woods nor mountains; so that it is necessary for the Sun, strongly bearing down on the river, to remove its crudities. It can be attributed to the air (I conceive that its role in this scarcity of rain is primary) that it is thin by nature and thirsty, and eagerly absorbs watery moisture, and disperses it so thoroughly throughout its entire body that it does not allow it to remain in the form of vapors by which it might swell into rains.

      *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
            *clarification.*

      768. We have spoken under the heading of percolation (that is, internal percolation) that egg white and milk are used for clarifying liquids. The Egyptians prepare and clarify the waters of the Nile, drawn into cisterns or stone vessels, and agitated with a few

--- Page 497 ---

a few crushed almonds, with which they anoint the mouths of the vessels, and remove them when they have settled a little. It would be beneficial to transfer this experiment of clarification with almonds to fresh beer or must, so that the work of purification may be accelerated.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*plants lacking leaves.*

769. Scarcely are plants found which, devoid of leaves, have branches; unless coral is excepted. But the deserts of St. Macarius in Egypt nourish a plant, long, lacking leaves, of black color, branched like coral, except that its top is closed. That plant, when brought into houses and placed in water, unfolds in a wonderful way; and a superstition has seized the people living in the vicinity, that it helps women in labor.

*the material of glasses.*

*A Solitary Experiment concerning the*
*prevention of putrefaction and the long*
*preservation of cadavers.*

771. The preservation of cadavers for many years,
with the marks of their dimensions intact and not
escaping in any part, as appears in Egyptian mummies—
some of which are believed to have lasted three thousand
years—does not deserve ordinary observation. Indeed, their
method of removing the brain and the viscera (whose
corruption you can scarcely ward off) is well understood;
but that is not so significant as to express admiration. For
we see how soft a substance flesh is, and most easily prone
to putrefaction above the other parts of the body. But it
could be seen from our observation and axiom, which we
gave in the hundredth experiment, that putrefaction, in my
conception, the natural period of bodies, is only an accident;
nor is matter the cause of accelerated corruption. Hence
it is established that bodies in shining amber,
mercury, balsam (of which we have already spoken),
wax,

--- Page 499 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VIII. 459
wax, honey, gums, and perhaps snow-pits or snow-preservers, etc., to be preserved for a very long time. Nor is there need, if we recall here what was said in that experiment, of repeating those things which pertain to annihilation. For if the three things accustomed to cause putrefaction are prevented, corruption can be entirely kept away. The first is, that air be excluded, which silently undermines the body and, with its spirit, as it were, conspires towards dissolution. The second, that what is around and adjacent to the body should not be of the same material, but completely heterogeneous with respect to the body to be preserved; for thus, one can receive nothing, and nothing can proceed from the other. Such are Mercury, white amber (as seen) in herbs, flies, and suchlike bodies. The third, that the body to be preserved should not be of such a mass that it can spontaneously dissolve into corruption, even if nothing of it passes into an adjacent body. Therefore, it ought to be rather thin and small, rather than vast. And a fourth aid is given: if the body to be preserved is of such a size as it is usually seen, then the containing body should be endowed with the faculty of attracting and drying out the moisture of the contained body, lest putrefaction, begun internally, grow strong, even though nothing may escape. I remember Livy relating that two leaden chests were once found in a certain tomb; and in one had been enclosed the body of King Numa, and in the other the books of sacred rituals and the discipline of the Pontiffs. A singular observation concerning the abundance of niter on certain shores.

772. Near the fortress of Catia and the wells of

A singular observation concerning bodies which float on water.

773. The Dead Sea, yielding bitumen, is of such
density, that living creatures thrown into it with hands
and feet bound floated on it and were not submerged.
From this we learn that sinking under water is nothing
but the body's weight by which it exceeds the water's
weight; so much so that it can be made so weighty and
strong, perhaps from mercury or similar substances,
that it suffices for supporting iron. Of which thing I
see no use, but it gives occasion for deception. The
same principle shows that all metals, except gold, float
on mercury.

*Solitary Experiment concerning fuel which consumes little or nothing.*

774. They say that at the foot of a hill near the Dead Sea, a black stone is found (used by hermits as an aid in preparing fire) which, burning like coal, does not diminish, but increases in splendor and brightness. If this is true, I certainly do not wonder, since iron glows red from heat and is not consumed; but that it endures for some time, that is what one may wonder at; for the redness of iron, when removed from fire, immediately disappears. It would certainly be a matter of no small convenience and profit if a fuel were devised which, when ignited, both gives light and lasts for a longer period. Nor do I entirely deny that candles are made from Salamander's wool, a certain kind of metal, which, when inflamed, glows white-hot and is not consumed. The question is, what feeds the flame, and usually it is a tangible body consisting of weight. But it seems possible that a spirit or vapor (both devoid of weight) excites it in a body; such as the material of ignis fatuus. You might perhaps object that such vapor, about to expire quickly, would fade. A Solitary Economic Experiment concerning fuel of low cost.

775. Fossil coal burns longer than that from wood, and coal from roots, cut into large pieces, lasts longer than that commonly used from wood. Common turf and that from heather are of low cost, and are long-lasting, slow-burning fuels. Coal from branches and shrubs or thorns, when placed on top of coals from green wood, provides fuel for a long fire. Sedge is a fuel of low price, which is frequently used by brewers and bakers, but otherwise useless. Let earth or chalk mixed with fossil coal be investigated. This mixture (which coal-dealers are accustomed to use clandestinely), if it is applied to make the mass of coal greater, is a deception; but if only the desire for knowledge is considered, it would be a matter of economy.

A Solitary Experiment concerning the collection of wind for cooling.

776. The people of Gaza today insert tiles or earthenware vessels into walls, so that they may draw down the wind captured from the roof into lower places by means of extended small pipes; a cooling (method) usually employed against great heats. *Solitary Experiment concerning judgments*
*about the salubrity of the air or the opposite.*

777. One ought not to apply oneself idly to this,
that, whatever bodies or places you choose, the
salubrity of the air or the opposite may be explored,
both as regards the seasons of the year,

Nor would I rashly be persuaded that meat

Excellent are experiments which shed light on such
matters not yet fully understood: for they are useful to
natural prognostics of weather, better than the aids
of astronomical skill. Moreover, they teach men
what locations are to be chosen for habitation, so that health
may be safe, and better cared for.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the germination of coral.*

780. On the southern coast of the Sicilian sea many corals are collected. This is a submarine plant, lacking leaves, only branched under water, soft and green in color, but exposed to the air it hardens, with a shining redness mixed in, as is known. They say it also bears white berries, but not yet transported with the corals; perhaps considered refuse there. But the nature of the plant must be discovered by a more exact and deeper investigation.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the collection of manna.*

781. Calabria produces the best manna and in abundant yield, which it collects from the leaves of the mulberry tree, very different from those which grow in valleys. Manna, like other dews, falls onto the leaves during the night. Perhaps someone might think such dews are to be dispersed lest they remain, before they adhere to the leaves of trees in valleys. It might also seem that there is a coagulating power in the leaves of the mulberry tree,

--- Page 507 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VIII. 467
power, by which the dew might be thickened, because it is observed in no other tree besides that unique one. Silkworms, accustomed to being nourished by these leaves, also sufficiently show that its juice is delicate and uniform. Add to this, that the leaves (especially of the black mulberry) are a little hairy, and for that reason more suitable for preserving the dew. It would certainly be worthwhile to deem the dews accustomed to settling on mountain trees and herbs worthy of the diligence of accurate investigation. Perhaps it happens that many are dispersed before they reach the valleys. And I entirely conclude thus, that if the best May dew is to be collected for medicinal uses, it must be sought in the mountains.

A solitary experiment concerning
the correction of wine.

782. A method is circulated by which Greek wine is prepared, so that it may not evaporate or intoxicate, with a little sulfur or alum added; of which the former is unctuous; the latter astringent; nor is it doubted that these two prevent evaporation very well. Let that be transferred to other wines and beers of better quality, by adding things which are of a similar substance, while they are fermenting, so that they both evaporate less, and become less intoxicating.

*A solitary Experiment concerning the*
*substance of artificial fire [a] from sulfur,*
*bitumen, and gunpowder.*

783. A not improbable reason has been devised by some, why artificial fire (which is especially bituminous) cannot be extinguished by water, because bitumen first solidifies from fire and water mixed, but not sulfur. This is attested by a place near Puteoli, called the court of Vulcan, which, with water and fire mutually vexing each other in conflict, sends forth a horrible thunder, with the eruption of hot waters through siphons. Moreover, there is a great quantity of bitumen there; while the fires of Etna and Vesuvius and similar mountains, which are sulfurous, belch forth smoke, ashes, pumice, not water. They also report that bitumen mixed with glue and placed in water, as it were, hardens into the substance of an artificial rock.

*A solitary experiment concerning judg-*
*ment on the healing of certain*
*ulcers and wounds.*

785. The ancients recorded that in bodies full of humors and impure, wounds of the shins are healed with difficulty, but those of the head more easily. The reason is that ulcers and wounds on the shins require desiccation, which the downward flow of humors impedes, while ulcers and wounds of the head do not require it, but on the contrary, dryness prevents them from being conveniently consolidated. The observation of our time has found a similar difference between an Englishman and a Frenchman; the former having a humid, the latter a dry bodily constitution; so that a wound of the head in a Frenchman, and of the shin in an Englishman, is more difficult to heal.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
        *the Floating of Bodies.*

   790. Take two ounces of aqua fortis, and as many drams of quicksilver (for aqua fortis can sustain that weight). If you dissolve it, it will not bear a flint stone of the size of a nutmeg. Nevertheless, water increased in weight increases its carrying power; just as salt brine, having enough [salt], will carry an egg floating. I remember that baths from a certain mineral were used by a Physician for the cure of gout, etc. A body placed in such a bath did not descend as easily as in common water. But it seems the weight of quicksilver, though greater than that of the flint, does not compensate for the weight of the flint any more than the aqua fortis [does].

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
     *the Flight of an Unequal Body in the Air.*

   791. A body of unequal weight (such as wood and lead, or bone and lead), if it is thrown with the lighter end forwards, ob-

--- Page 513 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VIII. 473
turned forward, it will change its position, and the heavier end will precede, unless the excessive length of the body prevents it. The reason is, because a denser body suffers a more vehement pressure of its parts from the initial impulse; and this is the cause (although hitherto unknown, as often said) of all violent motion. And since the posterior part moves more quickly (because it suffers less compression of its parts) than the anterior part can yield its place, it is necessary for the body to turn: for, having turned, it is able to draw the lighter part forward more easily. Galileo rightly notes that if an open trough, full of water, is impelled more strongly than the water can follow, then the water collects in a heap towards the posterior part, from where the motion began. This (he) (confidently assuming the motion of the earth) established as the cause of the ebb and flow in the sea, because the earth moves more quickly than the water. Although this theory is false, yet the former experiment is true. The unequal pressure of parts clearly appears if you take iron or flint, but another body is wood, of the same magnitude and form; when projected with an equal exertion of forces, the wood will almost be left behind by the stone or iron which tend further.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning the power*
      *of imagination to imitate sense.*

   795. Those effects which senses, when struck, produce,
and which flow from actual things, in a certain way also
depend on imagination. Hence, he who observes another
eating sour and tart things, and those things by which teeth
become dull and blunted, carries an imagination imbued
with this object, so that from the sight of another's action,
he feels his own teeth blunted. Likewise, he who sees another
spun in long circles, or wheels often going in a circle, he
himself is seized by dizziness; and placed on high without
obstructing barriers or restraints (unless habit has made
it easy), will cling, wavering with uncertain steps. Many
also, from the sight of another's blood, torture, or
strangulation, suffer a fainting spell, as if their own blood
were flowing and they themselves were being afflicted.

   798. I call it the submersion of metal

of greater splendor and with some prerogative

separation. If anyone secretly works on this

off as a simple precious metal,
it is an imposture of adulteration. But if it is
attempted deliberately and without deceit, it would be a great
saving of the more precious metal.
I remember having heard from a man most skilled

But lead in silver (since it is a heavier metal) cannot be detected; if the excess of weight in the lead is above the weight of the silver.

**A solitary experiment concerning the fixation of bodies.**

799. Gold is a substance that contains nothing volatile, and yet melts without any difficulty. Liquefaction shows that it is not empty, or devoid of spirits, so that its fixation is not a defect of spirits, such that they exhale, but an equal distribution of tangible parts, and a tight compaction of them, whence there is less appetite for them, nor any reason for them to exit. It would therefore be expedient to try whether, if glass is re-melted, some weight departs, for the parts in glass are equally distributed but not as tightly bound as they are in gold; as is evident from the fact that it easily admits

--- Page 520 ---
FRANCIS BACON'S
may emit light, heat, cold, and be of small weight. Other fixed bodies are endowed with few or no spirits; so that nothing can exhale. Such is the material from which goldsmiths' [a] cupels are made, which they place in furnaces, unharmed by the force of fire. Therefore, there are three causes of fixation: an equal distribution of spirits, and of tangible parts, and their tight constriction, and the leanness and extreme comminution of spirits; of which the former two allow for the nature apt to be liquefied, but the last does not.

*A solitary experiment concerning the rest-*
   *lessness of natural things in themselves*
      *and the appetite for change.*

800. It is a profound contemplation of nature, if one considers the want (so to speak) and dissatisfaction of various bodies, and their appetite for admitting other things. Air imbibes light, sounds, odors, vapors; and it is manifest that this is done by it with a kind of eagerness, as if it were not content with its former consistency; otherwise, it would never admit them so easily and suddenly. Water and liquids suddenly receive dry and more earthy bodies proportionate to themselves; dry bodies in turn imbibe waters
                                                     & li-

and liquids; so that one (which he among the ancients said concerning terrestrial and aqueous substances) may be a glue to the other. Membranes, skins, garments, etc., receive liquids within themselves, although they are intact bodies, and by no means with parts so gaping as sand and ashes, nor porous to the senses. Metals themselves are readily imbued by strong waters, and these penetrate metals and stones in no other manner. Aqua fortis, effective on gold, languishes on silver and vice versa. Gold, which you would consider the most compact and solid body by weight, eagerly imbibes Mercury. Nor does this reception of other bodies seem violent; for it is often reciprocal and as if by consent. Concerning the causes of all these things, and to what axiom they can be referred, one must think carefully. That charming notion, that matter is like a harlot prostituting her body, because it desires all forms, is merely a vague notion. Flame alone does not admit any body, but either overcomes it, or converts it into its own nature as a conqueror, or destroys and extinguishes itself.
