CENTURY NINE.

Various experiments concerning perce-
ption in insensible bodies, ten-
ding towards natural divination
or subtle experiments.

[Large decorative initial I] Among the most thoroughly explored things is that all
bodies, whatever their nature, even those devoid of sense,
possess some faculty of perception. For when body is applied
to body, something akin to choice is found in admitting what is
agreeable, and in excluding and rejecting what is disagreeable.
Also, perception, always preceding operation, distinguishes the
altering body from the altered body; otherwise, all bodies would
be indifferent to each other. This power of perceiving far exceeds
the subtlety of sense, which, compared to it, comparison shows
to be crude. Thus, thermometers or the psychiologion reveal the
heat or cold of the air, even when varied very slightly, which
otherwise would exhaust men anxiously trying to detect it.
That perception is sometimes at a distance, sometimes by contact;
as when a magnet attracts iron; or a flame seizes Babylonian
naphtha from a great

                                                                            great

--- Page 523 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. IX. 483
...great interval/distance. Therefore, let investigating
curiosity not be ingloriously engaged, which with zeal grasps the subtlety
of perception; another key for unlocking nature,
along with sense, to which it is often preferred. It is also the foundation
of reason, which animates natural magic, and whatever
offers itself here beforehand, afterwards becomes manifest in great effects
of things. Nor does it serve so much for revealing secrets,
as it aids predictions of future events; as the subtlety of
many experiments teaches. For example, for one doubting
whether seeds are old or new, the reliability of sense fails.
If new ones are boiled in hot water,
you will distinguish them by their faster germination. Of better water,
taste is not the indicator, but its sudden consumption;

*A solitary experiment regarding the nature of appetite in the stomach.*

831. Cold and especially dry things are effective in exciting appetite. The cause is that cold is a kind of natural deficiency, requiring aid; dryness is similar to it. Hence all acidic things (such as vinegar, lemon juice, oil of vitriol, etc.) provoke hunger. The disease, which is called bulimia or canine appetite, is produced by an acidic and vitreous phlegm in the mouth of the stomach. Appetite also becomes more excited by acids, because they contract the nerves inserted into the mouth of the stomach; a great impetus towards hunger. That onions, salt, pepper cooked in foods invite appetite, arises from the titillation of the nerves we mentioned; for movement sharpens it. Wormwood, olives, capers, and other such things strong in bitterness, excite appetite by cleansing; so that four principal causes of appetite exist: cooling of the stomach combined with dryness, contraction, titillation, and cleansing. There is also hunger from inanition, however, more often from too long a fast.

*Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the sweet smell of the Rainbow.*

832. The ancients observed that wherever the Iris (rainbow), as if impending or leaning, descends, a sweet odor is exhaled. The cause is the nature of certain bodies, endowed with an inherent sweetness, which the gentle rainbow-dew elicits. Moderate showers produce the same effect, which imbue the earth with sweetness; but none are as delicate as the rainbow-dew, wherever it happens to fall, because sweetness is inherent in the water itself, since the Iris is nothing but agglomerated droplets, which cannot fall as rain except from a very low atmosphere, which can retain the fragrance of herbs and flowers, like distilled water, intact. For rain and other dew, falling from on high, cannot preserve the odor, which exhalation dissipated and lost during ascent. I also do not know whether water itself does not have some rudiment of sweetness. It is true, indeed, that such is not found in marshes, rivers, springs; but good earth, recently tilled, a pleasant vigor and

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*Fragrance.*

833. Fragrance requires both the heat of the matter to be concocted, and moisture to be dispersed through exhalations. As for heat, woods and spices are more fragrant in hot regions than in cold ones. As for moisture, it is manifest that things too dry lose their sweetness; and flowers, while germinating, bloom more sweetly in the morning than in the evening. For some, applied fire destroys fragrance, such as violets, pellitory, carnation, speedwell, and in general all flowers which consist of a cold and delicate spirit. For others, it remains unimpaired in fire and when removed from it, such as rose water, etc. The fragrance of some is scarcely elicited, or at least not so delicately, except with the aid of fire, such as juniper, and sweet gums, etc., and all odors which lie enclosed in hard bodies. **A solitary experiment concerning fragrance.**

833. Fragrance requires both heat for the material to be concocted, and moisture to be dispersed through exhalations. As for heat, woods and spices are more odorous in hot regions than in cold ones. **A solitary experiment concerning the corporeal substance of odors.**

834. It is beyond controversy that no odor is conveyed except by the effluvium of a corporeal substance; unlike what happens with light, colors, and sounds. For we see that the interval to which those others progress is not reached by the effused odor. It is indeed true that forests and plains thickly planted with citrus trees and rosemary are perceived by their odor transmitted over great spaces into the sea, perhaps up to twenty miles; but how small is this compared to what the sound of a cannon produces, fired in a small compass; when forests and plains often extend vastly. Moreover, odors adhere to hard bodies, as when they imbue sleeves, etc. Whence they are understood to be corporeal and to subsist for some time, while light and sounds vanish.

A Solitary Experiment concerning Fetid and Fragrant Odors.

835. The excrements of most animals stink, especially those which relieve themselves; for pigeons and horses, man excepted, we see that they are very well, if their stables and the places where they are fed are kept clean. I judge the same concerning birds which live enclosed in cages; and the cat removes its excrements, having hidden them from sight. This especially holds true in beasts which are nourished by meat. Dogs almost alone among beasts are delighted by fetid odors; which argues something peculiar in their sense of smell, differing from the sense of smell of other animals. The reason why excrements stink is obvious, because the body itself rejects them, and how much more the volatile spirit [within them]; nor are we ignorant that the excrements of the first digestion smell worst, such as the excrements of the belly; those of the second, less; and those of the third, so much less; for sweat is not of so malignant a nature as the other two; especially in men abounding in heat. A solitary experiment concerning
the causes of putrefaction.

836. Spirits are the cause of all putrefaction, especially internal, partly the ambient body, whether air, liquid, or whatever it may be. This latter happens in two ways: either by the ingress of substance from the ambient body into the putrefying body; or by the excitation and solicitation of the putrefying body and its parts from the ambient body. The received opinion, that cold or internal and preternatural heat causes putrefaction, is not far from trifles. For cold is most hostile to the putrefaction of inanimate things, although it extinguishes vivification, which always consists in attenuated spirits, which cold freezes and coagulates. As for external heat, it is well enough if adventitious heat, by excessive proportion, predominates over the natural and inherent heat and the body's spirits, leading to dissolution or manifest alteration. But it arises rather from the emission, suppression, or suffocation of the native spirits; and from the confused order and perverse situation of the tangible parts, and other unobserved things, which nature establishes by means of passages, not from a conflict of heats.

A solitary experiment concerning
    imperfectly mixed bodies.

  837. The consistency of bodies is varied: dense, rare, tangible, pneumatic, volatile, fixed, determinate, indeterminate, hard, soft, adhering and the opposite, congealable, non-congealable, apt to liquefy and not, fragile, tenacious, flexible and the opposite, tactile or ductile (drawn out lengthwise), intractable, porous, solid, equal and smooth, unequal, venous, fibrous, full of grains, integral, and many others.    *A solitary experiment concerning*
      *bodies apt to liquefy and the opposite.*

   840. Liquefaction is from the detention of spirits, which dwell in the body, and open it. Hence bodies most (full of) spirits

--- Page 547 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. IX. 507
...swollen with spirits, or where they are more strictly imprisoned, or again, where they dwell more calmly and undisturbed, are apt to liquefy; since bodies behaving in these three ways do not allow the escape of spirits. An example of both of the former properties is found in metals, and of the latter in tallow, pitch, sulfur, butter, wax, etc. The inclination not to liquefy comes from the easy emission of spirits, which contracts the coarser parts. Hence bodies devoid of spirit, or which lose their spirit more easily, do not liquefy, such as wood, clay, hewn stone, etc. However, many of these bodies, though incapable of liquefying, become thoroughly or quickly soft, like iron on the anvil; and a rod hidden in hot ashes acquires greater flexibility. There are also those which liquefy or are dissolved by fire, such as metals, wax, etc. Others are dissolved in water, such as salt, sugar, etc. The cause in the former is the dilation of spirits by heat; in the latter, the loosening of tangible parts, which admit liquid. There are also those in which both methods are effective for dissolving, such as gum, etc. And these either swell with abundant spirit, or have tangible parts that lack moisture; the former serves the expanding spirits to receive fire; the latter stimulates the parts to admit moisture.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
      *fragile and tenacious bodies.*

   841. Some bodies are fragile,
some tenacious and not fragile; and if you try
to break some, they separate at the place
where the force strikes; others separate in such a way
that they fly apart into various pieces. The cause
of fragility is an inability, not enduring extension;
thus stone is more fragile than metals; and earthenware
more fragile than crude earth; dry wood, than green.
The cause of inability in extension is a small
quantity of spirits, which promote the extension
and dilation of bodies, and is usually
conjoined with porosity and dryness in the tangible parts.
Conversely, in tenacious bodies, the spirits are more
abundant and the pores fewer, and the tangible parts
more humid. Hence membrane or leather endures
extension, paper does not; likewise, a woolen
garment endures it, a linen one scarcely.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
        *hard and soft bodies.*

   844. We see that some bodies are hard, some soft. Hardness is chiefly brought about by jejune spirits, and their unevenness with the tangible parts. Softness, on the other hand, is afforded by a greater quantity of spirits (the sole cause of yielding) and a more even distribution into the tangible parts, whence they become more ductile and slippery, as in gold, lead, wax, &c. The second [species] of those which by yielding change their capacity, such as water or other liquids, certainly yield easily to a stone or other body thrown in, but universally rise up; by a spurious yielding, since it occurs in place, not in the body itself.

the latter are carried longer in the womb,
and there they are nourished
and grow; whereas with birds, once the egg
is laid, nothing further regarding growth and
nourishment is provided by the mother;
for incubation vivifies, it does not nourish.

A Solitary Experiment concerning

854. Partly in the preceding sections, we

thinner part of a shoot is inserted inverted, it produces
fruits with very small or no stones at all.

*A Solitary Experiment regarding*

860. Tradition has almost universally held the belief about the Salamander, that it lives in fire and is able to extinguish it. The other is extreme cold, and an extinguishing power in the body of that animal, which suffocates the fire. It has been found that artificial fires are better extinguished by milk than by water poured on, because it penetrates more.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning the color of the sea and of any water.*

874. Motion makes sea water or any other water turbid; rest, more transparent. The reason is, because motion does not allow rays of light to pass straight through, whence it becomes darker; whereas rest transmits the received rays straight through. Moreover, in brightness there is a degree of brilliance, especially if there is a moderate reflection. For a steel mirror shines more brightly than plain glass. This experiment deserves to be extended further, by investigating in what way motion impedes sight.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning scaly fish.*

875. Antiquity gave scaly fish a place among insects. The reason for this fact escapes me. For they are distinguished by sex like other fish, nor are they generated from putrefaction, especially those that move. It is certain that oysters, snails, and mussels, which lack motion, are not separated by that distinction. Investigate, at what time and how they are generated? Oyster shells seem to grow where none Z 4 were before.

*Solitary Experiment concerning the Left or Right Side.*

876. The efficacy of sense does not vary in the right or left side, but the limbs on the right are stronger. The cause is perhaps, that the brain, the instrument of sense, is equally for both sides; but movements, and the faculties that aid them, borrow some aid from the liver, which has its seat in the right side, or because the senses are led to exercises indifferently on either side from the time of birth. However, we use the limbs of the right side more; so that nevertheless we acknowledge some dominion of custom here. Thus it is clear that some are more left-handed, because they have used their left hand very much.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*shadows.*

879. A shadow is seen trembling at its
extremities. The cause is, the continuous motion of
atoms in the Sun, even when the wind is not
perceptible to the senses. Therefore, that motion at
the boundary of light and shadow, from light into
shadow, and from shadow into light, represents
the shadow as trembling, because motion is present
in the medium.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning the un-*
*dulation of the sea, and shallows within it.*

880. Shallows and narrow places break waves more
than the depth of the sea, extending in every
direction. The cause is, the impulse is the same
on both sides; except that where there is more water
and space, it moves more slowly, with less unequal
ascent and descent, or with less mountainous or
steep undulation. But where there is less both
of water and space, and it is more dashed against
the bottom, it moves more quickly and precipitously,
which every breaking of waves generates.

A solitary experiment concerning the sweetening of salt water.

881. The ancients relate that salt water, if it is boiled down, and, once boiled, is cooled, becomes more suitable for drinking than if it were raw; although salt, having undergone the distilling fire, does not rise among the exhaled vapors, and distilled water is sweet. The reason might be that part of the salt water rises partly in the form of foam, and partly goes into sediment, and seeks the bottom; so that it should rather be called separation than evaporation. But its thickness prevents it from rising into vapors, and bitterness also prevents it from rising; as simple waters of wormwood and similar things, when distilled, lose their bitterness.

A solitary experiment concerning the return of saltiness into wells dug on the shores.

882. We have said [a] before, that from wells dug on the shore, sweet water is drawn, having been filtered through the sands by the saltiness of the sea. But other ancients note that in certain places in Africa, with the passage of time, the water in those wells becomes salty. The reason is that after a period of time, the sands are imbued with salt by the marine

883. Antiquity testifies that salt thrown into salty water

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*subterranean heat.*

885. Water in wells is warmer in winter than in summer, as is also the air in caves. The cause is, because in parts of the earth not interior, or nearer to the surface, there is a certain degree of heat (as sulfurous veins, etc., show) which winter intensifies by keeping it more tightly enclosed, while summer diminishes it, being dissipated by exhalation.

887. That purple powder provides a dye.

*Solitary Experiment concerning the ascent of water by means of flame.*

889. An experiment much talked about in common, but the cause is hidden. Take a pot, or rather a glass, so that you may observe the movement in it, and place a lit candle at the bottom of a basin filled with water, and invert the mouth of the pot or glass over the candle, causing the water to rise. Those who attribute it to the attraction of heat deviate from the truth, since it is clear that the movement is due to the connection, which they call 'to prevent a vacuum', which proceeds thus. When the covered candle flame begins to be suffocated by the compressed air, it diminishes gradually, and then the water rises moderately, the flame gradually occupying less space, and the rise of water corresponds to the decrease [in flame volume]. But at the very instant when the candle is extinguished, a large part of the water suddenly rises, because the body of the flame no longer fills any space; and thus air and water take its place. The same will happen, if instead of water, you place flour or sand in the basin...

Observation principally records four influences of the Moon: the provocation of heat, the induction of putrefaction, the increase of humidity, and the excitation of motion in spirits.

890. As for the provocation of heat, we previously directed that hot water be taken, a part of which is to be exposed to Lunar rays, and another part, under the pretext of an interposed umbrella, is to be kept away from them, so that you may explore whether that exposed to the Moon cools more quickly. But because this interposition is of little moment (although in the Sun, shadow contributes greatly to the matter), it would be better to try the same with the Moon shining and not shining; in hot water in a glass flask as well as in a dish; in cinders or hard residues from mineral coal and glowing iron, etc.

891. One may try putrefaction with meat or fish exposed to Lunar rays, and again exposed to the air when the Moon is not shining; in both cases for an equal space of time, so that what accelerates corruption may be recognized. Also, examine a capon or other fowl placed outdoors, to see whether it is mortified more quickly and becomes more tender; and from dead flies and worms, by pouring a little water over them, you will discern the speed of putrefaction; as also from a common apple or a citron.

    Solitary Experiment concerning ani-
    mals which hibernate through the whole winter.
    899. There are various animals for which the whole winter is slept, the bear, hedgehog, dormouse, bee, etc., which grow fat in sleep, and excrete nothing. The cause of fatness during sleep could be a defect of assimilation, since whatever is not assimilated is changed into sweat or fat. These animals have been observed for some period of sleep to not move at all, but in the remaining time to move indeed, but not from their place; and they seek warm and enclosed retreats for their sleep. It was observed by the Dutch wintering in Novaya Zemlya that bears fall asleep around mid-November, and then foxes come out, previously terrified. I find it recorded by ancient writers that a pregnant bear [a] gives birth to her cubs during her sleep; and that a pregnant one is rarely seen.

TENTH CENTURY.
Various experiments concerning the trans-
mission and influence of immaterial
virtues and the power of ima-
gination.
[Large decorative initial P] he philosophy of Pythagoras, driven mad by super-
stitions, gave birth to that monster of imagination
which the school of Plato and others
afterwards fostered: namely, that the world
is one, entire, and perfect animal endowed with life;
so much so that Apollonius of Tyana, a prophet from the
tripod of the Pythagoreans, affirmed that the ebb and
flow of the sea is the respiration of the world, drawing in
water like a breath, and expelling it again.
And these people proceed and build upon that statement: if the world lives,
it has a soul and a spirit, which, according to their opinion,
exists, and is called the spirit of the world. Nor do they
designate God by this word (although the Deity was not unknown to them),
but only the soul, and the essential form of the world.
With this foundation established, they were free to fabricate
whatever specious error might suggest. For in living
beings, even those of vast bulk (e.g., in a
whale)

--- Page 593 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. X. 553
whale) sensation and affection of any part in the body is instantly diffused through the entire body. Nor did they wish anything else to be implied by that madness of invention, than that magical operations overcome any distance of place, nor adhere to the failure of unprepared matter; but that (e.g.) Europe would receive the sensation of a thing done in China, and an effect could be produced without and contrary to what matter would allow, with no help of angels or spirits, but by that unity alone which the consensus of nature brings forth. There were those whom error did not deceive only up to this point, but drove them wandering further from the straight path of reason, while they thus establish; if the spirit in man (whom they call a microcosm), about to make a suitable impression, flows into the spirit of the world, that the power and efficacy of imagination, and firm persuasion, can dominate nature. For Paracelsus and some ignoble authors of magic attribute to exalted imagination the virtue of miraculous faith. That vast and from foul absurdities concocted trifling has breathed upon many with an amiable madness.
But we, constantly proceeding by the footsteps of God impressed upon His works, nor deviating from sense, which is the lamp of God (and this the breath of man), will soberly and strictly inquire whether nature anywhere permits such a transmission and influx of immaterial virtue; what the power of imagination is, whether into the body whence it itself arises, or into another. It is indeed a labor not unlike the Herculean toils in cleansing the Augean stable, so that nature may stand on its own rights and be cleansed of superstitious magical observations; if not to be received with applause, certainly it will not be entirely condemned. And although in ranging through this matter occasion will be given everywhere, yet now it pleases to open the entrance to other things.

*Various cautionary experiments concerning*
*the transmission of spirits and the power*
*of imagination.*

901. People should be warned not to discredit operations arising from the transmission of spirits and the power of imagination, merely because the outcome sometimes fails. For just as contagion, transmitted from body to body, is often received, yet sometimes the strength and good habit of the passive body repels it before the disease takes hold; so much the more does an impression from soul to soul, or from spirit to spirit, often triumph victoriously; but the suffering soul and spirit may recollect itself, and having struggled free from the bonds of an as yet unsolidified dominion, may overcome it, before the dominant affliction refuses to be dislodged. That power is most effective in languid minds and spirits, such as those of women, the sick, the superstitious, children, and animals of tender age.
     *I know not what eye bewitches my tender lambs.*
The poet speaks not of sheep but of lambs. That Kings and Lords of lands are protected by the reverence for their high station against these impressions, could be attributed (besides the principal reason, namely, the watchfulness of God, cherishing His vicars in full security) to the imagina-
                                                  tion's

--- Page 595 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. X. 555
...imagination's impotence, here abandoning the one who imagines [it]. For it is scarcely possible that witches and sorceresses gain credence, when they want it to be believed that even they themselves are vulnerable to harm.

902. Again, men must be restrained from the danger of credulity, lest they lean too rashly towards this with misplaced faith, because they often see the outcome respond to the operations. For the cause of success is often to be referred to the powers of emotion and imagination in the acting body, which can act upon a different body by a certain secondary reason. For example, if someone carries around a planetary sign, or a ring, or a piece of an animal, certainly persuaded that it will be an aid to him in promoting love affairs, or that he will be preserved from danger or a wound in battle, or that he will emerge superior in competition, etc., he can thereby sharpen his wit, and stimulate diligence, or nourish confidence and support constancy, by which (without it) he might perhaps have failed. Now indeed, who is ignorant of what industry and a mind tenacious of purpose signifies, especially in civil affairs? For we see men of a more tender and weaker spirit shrink back from the assaults of another's audacity, and the state of things in this world fluctuates with a condition so easily varied, that often the persistence of urging an attempt even to a miraculous

937. It would be advisable to stir up healthy air within houses. Windows should not be moved too close to the arch (when it is elaborated elegantly and for display), but should be low. Stone walls are unhealthy; wooden ones contribute more to health; but especially brick ones. To some, the thickness of walls, with chalk interspersed between bricks, for preventing evaporation, succeeded very well.

are rather things that accompany audible
and visible species, than their effects.
Sixth, they are of a tender and weak nature,
since they only affect a slender and thin

    Now we undertake to explain the powers of
imagination on the body of another; and in what ways
it is strengthened when exalted. I understand
imagination to be a representation of individual
thought; and it is threefold. The first is connected
with faith in a future thing; the second with memory

Whatever happens, all authority ought to be born from itself, turned (as has been said) either into art or into a person. Where that [authority] is derived into another, that person must be ignorant, not learned, or fantastical. Such are usually witches and superstitious people, whose faith is so bound to teachers and traditions that reason or experience cannot convince them. Hence, magic usually employs boys and younger people, into whose spirits faith or imagination is easily transferred or impressed.

Now indeed, there are three ways of strengthening the imagination: authority, from which faith is derived; reasons by which imagination may be excited and confirmed; and means by which it may be repeated and renewed.

948. We have spoken of authority. As for the reasons strengthening and exciting the imagination, in magic there are usually employed (if in the use of these things there is anything merely natural): garments, characters, words, seals, certain parts of plants and animals, specific hours, gestures and movements, incenses, odors, chosen company (which intensifies the imagination), diets, and preparations for a certain space of time. The words are always either barbarous, signifying nothing, lest they disturb the imagination; or

   951. If you attempt anything through the imagina-

   952. Because you cannot discern the intimately

   953. The imagination of him at whom you aim your

      958. It is a very common belief that a corpse, in the sight of the murderer, emits blood anew through an inflicted wound. Various experiments concerning the secret power of Sympathy and Antipathy.

960. Many things act upon human spirits by the powers of Sympathy and Antipathy. It is an old and universally received opinion that precious stones, commonly worn as ornaments, possess admirable faculties, and that effects of curious vanity are attributed to them. So far so good, that stones contain subtle spirits, which their splendor proves, so that by consent they can act upon human spirits, refreshing and cheering them. Of these, the most attested virtues in this kind are the diamond, the emerald, the Oriental hyacinth, [a] the gold stone and the green Topaz. But that they attribute special properties (to them) is from vanity, and deserves no credit. It is manifest that light has the primary role above all else in refreshing human spirits, and it is very probable that by varying the splendor of light, the same effect is produced, and indeed with greater grace of novelty. And this is one of the reasons why precious stones comfort. It would therefore be useful to dye lanterns or umbrellas made of glass with green, blue, yellow, scar-

one day that she wished to remove whatever warts disfigured her hands. Afterwards she took a small piece of bacon, with the rind not removed,
with the fat of which she anointed all the warts;
and among them, the one which had almost been coeval with me up to that point. Then, having affixed the piece of bacon with a nail to the post of her bedroom window,
which faced south, she exposed it to the sun
to be putrefied. The result was that all
the warts completely vanished within seven months; even that one which surpassed the others
in age. I do not wonder that those born in a short time quickly died off; but the destruction of that one which had clung to my hand, surviving through so many years, still occupies my mind.
The same effect is attributed
to Elder, if you apply a green stick from it for rubbing warts, which afterwards,
placed in dung, should rot. It could be tried on corns of the feet and scrofula and similar excrescences; also in parts of
animals which are most akin to excrescences, such as the combs and spurs of roosters,
          Cc 3                    beasti-

...of beasts' horns, etc. The method of testing should be twofold: either the parts are rubbed with lard or elder, as in the aforementioned cases; or, those parts being cut into smaller pieces, you may have what remains to be consumed, and you may observe what the consumption of a separated particle can achieve in one that was once joined.
     998. Among many, the opinion has prevailed that by anointing the iron and whatever inflicted the wound, the wound itself is healed. From the report of a most trustworthy man (although hitherto I cannot be induced to believe the experiments), you will note the following. Firstly, the weapon salve consists of various ingredients, among which are most remarkable and most difficult to procure: moss from the skull of an unburied corpse, bear's fat, and a she-bear killed in childbirth. In the latter two, I easily suspect that a refuge was sought, so that if the cure did not succeed, it could be pretended that the beasts had not been killed at the proper time. Ireland supplies a great quantity of moss from bodies killed, heaped up, and unburied. The remaining ingredients are hematite reduced to powder, and certain other things that stop blood; which moss also does. A description of the entire ointment exists in Crollius's Chymical Dispensatory. Secondly, that ointment is applied not to the wound, but

--- Page 647 ---
SVLV. SYLVAR. Cent. X. 607
but applied to the weapons themselves to exert its power.
Thirdly (which greatly pleases me), for the preparation
of the salve they do not require a certain con-
stellation; a usual refuge for ignorance
in magical medicines; if they are disappointed,
[they can say] it was not prepared under that sign, which in
the sky is destined for its preparation. Fourthly, it can
be applied to weapons, even if the patient is far removed
at long intervals. Fifthly, it does not seem
necessary that the imagination of healing concurs;
since the injured person can be cured even without any
knowledge of what is intended. And up to this
point, experience testifies that, for example, when the salve
was wiped off the weapons, the wounded person being unaware,
the pains recurred until the weapons were again anointed.
Sixthly, they assert that if the weapon itself is not available,
it is sufficient if an iron or wooden instrument, not
dissimilar in form, is inserted into the wound so that it
draws blood; the anointing of which is equally important for
healing. I think that is fabricated, so that the wondrous
method of healing may be more sought after, and usurped.

608          FRANCIS BACON
placed. Ninth, that the salve, wiped from the sword and preserved, can double its service; its virtue rather increased than diminished. Tenth, that it heals much faster than other wound salves. Lastly, that the cure in man and beast will be with equal success; which pleases me above all, since the whole matter can be more easily investigated.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
           *hidden properties.*

   999. I would like men to know that, although I reprehend the gross negligence in seeking the causes of things when they are attributed to hidden faculties and properties (a hindrance and a deadly slumber to the investigation instituted for further knowledge), I do not, however, assert that much should not be left to proof by experiments in the practical part of knowledge, where judgment does not penetrate so exactly; and that not only in general, but in specific cases. Thus in Medicine, if you wish to cure the royal disease, it is not enough to say that the medicine should not be cooling, since it impedes deobstruction, which the disease requires; nor should it be hot, since it exasperates bile, so that it penetrates to the gallbladder, for in it the obstruction adheres, the cause of the disease, etc. But from experien-

--- Page 649 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. X. 609
ence is to be received, that powder of ground-
pine or similar, taken in beer, cures the king's
evil (jaundice). Again, a prudent physi-
cian will not continuously apply the same medicine,
but will vary it, if the first medicine disappoints
the hope of success. For remedies
for the king's evil, stones, fevers, &c.,
which are beneficial in one place, are harmful in another; according
to the suitability that intervenes between the medicine and the
individual body.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*the general sympathy of the spirit*
*of man.*

1000. The pleasure which popularity,
fame, honor, submission,
and subjection of minds, wills,
and affections generate in men (although another
end may be proposed for desiring these things) seems a
grateful thing and agreeable to human nature,
nor does it admit of further contemplation
of a more widely extending consequence. But
indeed, to one who pays attention, a deeper
significance occurs, as if all human
spirits and minds have proceeded from one divine source.
Otherwise, indeed, how would man be so greatly
affected by those things which others conceive in their minds and bring
forth? The best temperament and con-
stitution of the mind seeks solidly good fame and
Cc 5 ve-

--- Page 650 ---
610      Fʀ. Bᴀᴄᴏɴɪ Sʏʟᴠ. &c.
true honor; a lighter [mind] catches the popular breeze, and enjoys the title and applause of a public servant. A worse [mind] seeks subjection and contrives tyranny, as is evident in conquerors most laden with affected glory, and in the world's agitators. Yet this is even more evident in Arch-heretics, since the introduction of novelty in the doctrine of salvation is a kind of tyrannical domination over human intellect and faith.

A remedy for gout devised by Bacon, to which Exper. 60 pertains, consists in this order.

I. Prescription for a Poultice.

Take about three ounces of fine flour bread, only the crumb finely shredded; let it be cooked in milk until it coalesces into a small poultice. Add at the end a drachm and a half of red rose powder. Ten grains of saffron. An ounce of rose oil. Let it be spread on a linen cloth, and applied warm, and continued for three hours.

II. Bath or Fomentation.

℞. Half a handful of sage leaves. Six drachms of chopped hemlock root. Half an ounce of bryony roots. Two handfuls of red rose leaves. Let them be cooked in a pot filled with water in which steel has been quenched, until the liquid has been reduced to a quarter. After per-

--- Page 652 ---
612
percolation, add half a handful
of black salt; let it be applied with a scarlet
cloth or scarlet wool dipped
in the warm liquid, the application repeated seven times.
Let these things be done in the space of a quarter (of an hour)
or a little more.

III. Plaster.

℞. Plaster of Diacalciteos,
as much as is sufficient for the part to be covered.
Let it be dissolved in oil of roses to such a con-
sistency that it adheres; let it be spread on a thin linen cloth
and applied.

TO THE READER
Greetings.

[Large decorative initial F]The most honorable author fashioned this fable of New Atlantis with the intention that in it he might present a certain model and description of a College, established for the interpretation of nature and the greatness and power of works; and that he might distinguish it by the name of Solomon's House, or the College of the Works of the Six Days. And he extended the thread of his discourse thus far, until he completed this. The model, (I confess) according to the custom of Poetics, is grander and loftier than that which, in all things, might be open to imitation; yet truly, in most things, the industry of men should not despair of itself. He also intended, in this very fable, a book concerning
          a 2               legi-

--- Page 704 ---
4           TO THE READER.
laws, or concerning the best state of the Commonwealth, he had intended to write; but since he foresaw this work would be extensive; and also, being swept away by the desire for collecting Natural History and composing other parts of the Instauration (which he considered far more important), here he stopped.
    New Atlantis, as far as the English edition is concerned, found its place here by my Lord's decision, because of its large part affinity with the Natural History, which is prefixed.

            VV. RAWLEY.

He led the way, and looking back at us, he said, certainly most kindly: that he was merely our servant for our convenience; and a guide for the way. But he led us through three streets, very beautiful: and along the whole way which we traversed, many of the people gathered on both sides, standing in an orderly fashion; but in such a civil manner that they seemed to have gathered not so much for an idle spectacle, as to congratulate us on our arrival. The house of strangers is a beautiful and spacious building, constructed of bricks, (similar to) ours, but a little more purple in color: with elegant windows, some of glass, but others of delicate linen cloth, dipped in oil. First he led us into a rather elegant dining room, located up steps: then he asked us: how many of us there were in number? And, how many of our men were sick? he led us back to the dining room, and raising his rod a little, (which was their custom, whenever Ministers report the commands of Superiors,) he spoke to us thus.
   I inform you that the custom of this Kingdom requires that after the present day and tomorrow, (which we permit you for transferring men and your goods from the ship) you keep yourselves within these doors for three days. However, let this not disturb you, nor on that account imagine yourselves to be confined within a prison: but rather that this is a privilege, by which you may refresh and restore your spirits from your journey, you will lack nothing: Indeed, six servants have also been assigned, who will minister to you, and attend to your affairs.
   We thanked him, with all affection and humility: and said: God is undoubtedly manifested in this land. We also offered him twenty gold pieces, but he also, smiling, said only this: What, do you wish me to be a man of double salary? Thus he departed. A little later, our dinner was brought: which certainly provided a sufficiently lavish and wholesome fare, both in respect of food and drink: certainly better and more abundant than according to the standard of any College, as far as I know, in Europe. ...and the New World, we have sailed past. And whether it will be granted to us to behold Europe again, is known only to God. There is still more; for they (though in a humane manner) have confined us within the enclosures of this house for three days. Who knows whether they do this to test our conduct: if they find us wicked, they will immediately order us to be exiled; but if upright, they will grant us a longer stay here.

In the course of which days, we were also constantly cheered by the recovery of our sick men.     On the morrow after those three days had passed, a new man came to us, whom we had not seen before, clothed in a blue garment, just like the previous one, except that his Turban was white, with a small red cross on the top. Thus he departed from us, not without tears, which welled up from the tenderness of his spirit; and he also left us confused and struck with joy and a feeling of gratitude, and we said to one another, that we had come into a land of Angels, who appeared to us daily, and anticipated us with consolations which we could not even have conceived, much less expected.

About twenty years after the Ascension
of the Lord, it happened that there was seen
by the people of Renfusa (a maritime city
situated on the Eastern side of our Region),

On the day of the festival, after the divine Liturgy has been celebrated, the Tirsanus proceeds into a certain spacious hall, where the solemnities of the festival are performed. This hall has a single step of ascent on its upper part. There, against the wall, in the middle, a chair is placed, with a table and a covering over it. Above the chair, a canopy is extended, round or oval, made of ivy; ivy certainly, compared to ours, very much whitish in color, not unlike the leaf of the poplar which we call silver poplar, but somewhat more splendid; for it is green through winter. The canopy, moreover, is elegantly woven with silver threads and byssus threads of various colors, which bind the ivy together; and the work is usually that of one of the daughters of the family. At the top, it is veiled with a fine net of byssus and silver; but the material of the canopy is real ivy, from which, after the solemnity is finished, friends of the family love to pluck off some leaf or a small branch.

Within a few following days, I formed a friendship and familiarity with a certain merchant of that city, whose name was Ioabin. He was however a Jew and circumcised. which, having participated in the blessing of that festival, have always flourished wonderfully afterwards. But now, listen carefully, and I will tell you what I know. You will understand that scarcely any nation under the sun can be found so chaste as this one of Bensalem, nor so pure from all stain and pollution. I would plainly call her the virgin of the world. I remember having read, in one of your European books, about a holy Hermit among you, who desired to see the spirit of fornication, and immediately a small, deformed, and foul Ethiopian appeared to him: but if he had desired to see the spirit of Bensalem's chastity, without a doubt it would have appeared to him in the form of some beautiful and glorious Cherub. For nothing among mortals is beautiful or worthy of admiration compared to the most chaste souls of that nation. Therefore, I want you to know that there are no brothels among them, no houses of prostitution, no hired harlots, nor anything of this kind. Indeed, not without a certain detestation do they wonder that you in Europe tolerate such things. They say that you have overthrown marriage from its proper office; for marriages were instituted as a remedy for illicit concupiscence, but natural concupiscence is like a goad to marriage. But, with men

--- Page 757 ---
N O V U S A T L A S.          57
when a remedy more pleasing to men, with their desires corrupted, is at hand, marriages are almost driven out. Therefore, it is possible to see countless among you who do not take wives, but rather prefer an impure and lustful celibacy to the honorable yoke of marriage. Furthermore, many who do take wives do so late, when both the flower and strength of youth have vanished. But if by chance they do contract marriage, what else is marriage to them than a mere business transaction? In which kinship, or a dowry, or reputation is sought, with some desire (but nevertheless as if for something unimportant) for offspring; but by no means does that faithful nuptial union between man and woman, which was instituted in the beginning, come to mind. Nor can it happen that for those who have so vilely wasted such a great part of their age and strength, children (our other self) are at all held in esteem. Nay, and even during the bond of marriage, does this situation indeed improve, as it ought to have, if those excesses were tolerated only for the sake of necessity? --- Page 766 ---
plas, and deep, of various depths. The deepest of them extend down to six hundred fathoms. And some of them have been dug out under great mountains, so that if you combine the height of the mountain with the depth of the cavern, some of them have a depth of three miles. For we have found that the height of the mountain down to the plain, and the depth of the cavern from the plain, are in effect the same, both being equally removed from the Sun, and celestial rays, and open air. We call these caverns the lowest region. Moreover, we use them for all coagulations, indurations, refrigerations, and conservations of bodies. We also use them to imitate natural mines; and for the production of new artificial metals, from materials and compounds which we prepare there and bury for many years. We sometimes use them (which might seem strange) for the cure of certain diseases, and the prolongation of life, in some Hermits who prefer to live there, well supplied with all necessary things, and who are certainly very long-lived; from whom we also learn many things.

of natural substances and materials, not in any hollow, but in the contiguous earth itself, where we bury many compounds, just as the Chinese bury their porcelain.       We have very high Towers, the highest of which rise, by a perpendicular line, up to the height of half a mile. Some of them, however, are situated upon high mountains, so that, if you combine the height of the mountain and the height of the tower, the altitude in some of them extends up to at least three miles. These places, moreover, we call the supreme region, considering the entire tract of air, between the supreme and the lowest, as the middle region of the air. We use these towers, as is suitable for their various heights and locations, for insolation (exposure to the sun), cooling, preservation, and for observing various meteors, such as winds, rains, snows, hailstones, and some of the fiery meteors. We have ponds, in some of which fresh water is filtered from salt water, but in others, by artificial means, fresh water is changed into salt water. We also have swift whirlpools and waterfalls for the use of many violent motions; for a similar use, we have many machines which receive, multiply, and strengthen winds.

We have breads from various grains, roots, nuts, and acorns, some also from dried meats and fish, with various kinds of ferments and seasonings, some of which, wonderfully, excite the appetite, others are so nutritive that many live on them alone, without other food, who nevertheless are usually long-lived. We have foods which we so pound, tenderize, and break down, yet without any degree of putrefaction, that the weak heat of the stomach easily turns them into good chyle, no less effectively than the strong heat of the stomach can work on common foods. We have certain kinds of food, bread, and drink, which, when consumed, will enable one to tolerate fasting longer than usual: also others, to which those who become accustomed, become harder and more solid in flesh than before: and then their strength, for any movement, is increased and intensified.
  We also have dispensaries, or workshops of medicines: in which it is easy to imagine, since we have such a great abundance and variety of plants and animals, beyond what you have

--- Page 775 ---
N O V U S A T L A S.          75
...than you in Europe we abound (for we know well what is found among you), that likewise simple remedies, drugs, and ingredients for medicines ought to be so much more varied and manifold. There also we have drugs of different ages and of long fermentation. But as for the preparations of medicines, we have not only all kinds of exquisite distillations and separations, but especially through gentle heats and percolations, through various linens, wools, woods, and even more solid substances, but much more excellent methods of compounding, by which we achieve such an incorporation of compounds that they appear almost as natural simples.

We also have several mechanical arts unknown to you, and materials made by them, such as papers, linens, silks, textiles, stitched from feathers of most elegant and wonderful splendor, most beautiful dyes and colorings, and many other things. Indeed, we also have workshops for some of the aforesaid arts, both those which have not been adopted for common use, and those which have. For you ought to know, from those things which I have already recounted,

many [such things] are in use throughout the whole kingdom, although, if they originated from our invention, we sometimes keep copies of them in our house, as if they were originals and most excellently elaborated.

	We also have very diverse furnaces, and which exhibit and maintain diverse degrees of heat, namely, of a sharp and swift quality, robust and persistent, gentle and moderate, blown, tranquil, humid, dry, and similar [qualities]. But above all, we administer heats, in imitation of the heat of the Sun, and of celestial bodies, which pass through multiple inequalities, and as it were, orbits, progressions, and periods, through which we bring forth wonderful works. Nor do we lack imitations of the heat of dung; and of the bellies of animals, and of their blood and bodies themselves: of hay, and of herbs piled up and enclosed while they are humid: of quicklime, and of other things. Likewise, we have instruments which excite heat, by motion alone: and moreover, places for strong insolation, and again, subterranean places, which, either by nature or by art, excite heats. We exhibit these diverse heats, as the nature of the operation, which we design, demands.

We also have houses of perspective,
where we display experiments of all
sorts of colors; and from transparent
and colorless bodies, we represent
individual colors: not shimmering in the form of rainbows
(as happens in gems and prisms), but
by themselves, simple and constant.
Furthermore, we display every multiplication
of rays, so that we project light
to great distances; and we have imparted
to it such power and strength,
that by means of such light, the finest
lines and points can be seen. We display
every kind of tinted and colored
lights, and all illusions and deceptions
of sight, in figures, sizes,
motions, colors; all demonstrations
of shadows, and of images
floating in the air. We have also discovered
several means, unknown to you, of producing
original light from various bodies.
Again, we have discovered devices by
which very distant objects may appear to the eyes,
as if in the Sky, and other remote
places. Indeed, we also show what is near
as if from afar, and what is far
as if near, displaying fabricated distances
at will.

  We also have houses of perfumes and

we produce forces stronger and more powerful than

men, quadrupeds, birds, fish, and serpents. Finally,
we have other movements, remarkable for their evenness
and subtlety.

   We also have a house of illusions,
where we exhibit all kinds of tricks, impo-
stures, and illusions, and their deceptions.
But you will easily believe that we, who
possess so many truly natural things that
excite admiration, could also impose countless
things upon the senses of men, if we wished
to adorn and exalt them into a miracle.
But we hate all imposture and falsehood.
Moreover, we have strictly forbidden all
members of our house, under penalty of igno-
miny and fine, from displaying anything
from natural things falsified by artificial
apparatus; but only what is pure, and free
from all deceit and affectation of miracle.
And these are, (my son), the riches of
Salomon's House.
   As for the functions and duties of our
members, we have twelve who sail to
foreign regions, under the name of other
nations (for we do not reveal our land):
who bring books, materials, and models
of experiments to us

if you yourselves have not seen them, to make descriptions of them would be too long, and then in rightly understanding them, it will be easy to err. For indeed to the inventor of every more worthy thing, we soon erect a statue, and to him we bestow a sufficiently generous honorarium. Of those statues, some are of bronze, of marble, and Lydian stone, others of cedar, and certain other precious woods, gilded, and adorned, others of iron; others of silver, some of gold.

We also have certain hymns, and forms of liturgies, which we daily sing, and recite; with which we resound praises and jubilees, and thanksgivings to God, because of His wondrous works: likewise certain forms of prayers, with which we implore His help and blessing, that He may deign to direct and illuminate our labors, and convert them to good and holy uses.

Finally, it is customary among us, from time to time to visit and frequent the principal cities in the kingdom, in which, (as opportunity offers itself) we reveal such useful inventions, as we deem fit. We also predict, before they arrive, (which pertains to natural divinations,) epidemic diseases,

   And while he had said these things, he raised
himself to his feet: but I, as I had been instructed, knelt
down, whereupon, placing his right hand on my
head, he said: "May God bless you, my
son, and may God likewise bless this account which I
have made. I grant you permission to
publish it for the good of other nations.
Indeed, we live here in the bosom of God;
a nation entirely unknown to others."
Having said these things, he departed: But he had assigned
about two thousand Aurei, as a gift,
to be counted out to me and my companions. For they are great
givers, wherever they may come, etc.
